cases.title: Whitney Museum ISP Suspension / Palestine Performance Cancellation
cases.artist: Noel Maghathe, Fadl Fakhouri, Fargo Tbakhi (ISP 2024–25 fellows); Sara Nadal-Melsió (ISP associate director)
cases.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
cases.description: The ISP 2024–25 fellows scheduled a performance, “No Aesthetic Outside My Freedom: Mourning, Militancy, and Performance,” addressing Palestinian mourning, for May 14, 2025. On May 12, curators were told the performance would not proceed; Whitney Director Scott Rothkopf had objected to a preface instructing attendees who support Israel to leave — reportedly before confirming whether that language would appear in the final staging. ISP Associate Director Sara Nadal-Melsíó’s position was subsequently dissolved. On June 2, 2025, Rothkopf announced the suspension of the entire Independent Study Program for the 2025–26 academic year. His stated rationale attributed the suspension to a leadership gap following ISP director Ron Clark’s 2023 retirement and the ongoing search for a new director; his letter did not directly cite the performance cancellation. The cohort and 300+ ISP alumni contested that framing, characterizing the suspension as censorship retaliation for the Palestine-related performance. The causal link between the cancellation and the suspension is disputed: Rothkopf’s stated reason (leadership gap) and the cohort’s retaliation claim are both on record. Cohort members withdrew or altered works and canceled appearances. In June 2026 the museum announced the ISP would reopen under new director Soyoung Yoon.
cases.outcome: Performance canceled May 12, 2025 (scheduled May 14). ISP suspended June 2, 2025 for 2025–26 academic year. Nadal-Melsíó position dissolved. 300+ alumni signed open letter. ISP to reopen under new director Soyoung Yoon (announced June 16, 2026). Original cancellation decision not reversed; no institutional accountability statement issued. Causation between cancellation and suspension remains contested.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Institutional crisis

cases.title: "Black Artists Matter" mural (E. 11th St, 2021/2024); Pride/rainbow crosswalks (W. 4th & Colorado St); "TEXAS" street mural (Guadalupe St / "the Drag," UT Austin, 2024); plus other decorative crossings (Lake Austin Blvd river crosswalk; Zilker "Fairy Alley")
cases.institution: City of Austin streets, Texas; Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT)
cases.date_controversy: Oct. 8, 2025 (Abbott directive) – June 2026 (TxDOT denial; June 22 deadline)
cases.description: TxDOT — acting on Gov. Greg Abbott’s Oct. 8, 2025 directive to remove "political ideologies" from roadways (mirroring the July 2025 federal "SAFE ROADS Initiative" under US DOT Sec. Sean Duffy/FHWA) and a new Texas MUTCD clause banning road markings with "political or advocacy messages of any nature" — denied Austin’s Nov. 2025 request to keep ~15 decorative street markings. A May 18, 2026 TxDOT letter to Austin Transportation & Public Works director Richard Mendoza declared six locations non-compliant, including the "Black Artists Matter" mural (E. 11th St), the W. 4th St rainbow Pride crosswalk, and the "TEXAS" mural on Guadalupe St near UT Austin, and ordered the city to submit a removal timeline/action plan by June 22, 2026 or risk losing state and federal road funding (~$175M+ in grants). The city says it will comply; community members call it "erasure" of history and expression.
cases.outcome: Exemption request denied (TxDOT letter, May 18, 2026). City ordered to submit a removal time frame and action plan by June 22, 2026 or risk losing state/federal road funding. Mayor Watson says Austin will comply while pursuing "creative" alternatives on city-owned infrastructure (banners along Bettie Naylor St, painted sidewalks, utility-pole fixtures). Zilker "Fairy Alley" allowed to fade over time; some sites may remain if made compliant with curbing/improvements. Community objection ongoing; red paint was previously thrown on the rainbow crosswalk (counter-protest vandalism).
cases.tags: Removal, Censorship, Funding dispute, Political interference, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Public art, Historical erasure

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC
cases.date_controversy: June 14-15, 2026 (algae return); pool declared complete June 6, 2026
cases.description: NYT (June 15, 2026) reported that days after the $14.2M no-bid renovation was declared complete (June 6), algae blooms returned over the June 13-15 weekend, turning Trump’s "American flag blue" Reflecting Pool green again after several hot, humid days. The Interior Dept. (spokeswoman Katie Martin) says a newly installed "nanobubbler" water-treatment system has killed the algae and that it is being vacuumed up, calling the pool fixed "for good"; a week earlier the agency had called the algae "residual" from supply lines that sat dormant during the work. NPS workers and Pearl Purity Water Solutions (the pool’s water contractor since 2021) skimmed algae on June 14-15. The two no-bid vendors were Atlantic Industrial Coatings (joint-sealing/waterproofing, completed June 4) and Ohio-based Greenwater Services (upgraded purification system).
cases.outcome: Pool declared complete June 6, 2026; algae blooms returned June 14-15, 2026 (green again). Interior says the nanobubbler killed the algae and it is being vacuumed; characterizes the fix as permanent — efficacy disputed in practice within ~8 days of completion. TCLF lawsuit pending (Case 1:26-cv-01593, DDC; Judge Nichols ruling awaited). "Trump Promenade" announced but unbuilt.
cases.tags: Conservation, Political interference, Architectural preservation, Funding dispute

cases.title: Kyiv Pechersk Lavra — Dormition Cathedral (UNESCO World Heritage Site); Mystetskyi Arsenal (Old Arsenal, contemporary art centre); Kharkiv Art Museum; Dovzhenko Film Studio costume collection (and further sites in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro)
cases.artist: N/A (heritage sites and collections; Kharkiv Art Museum noted for Taras Shevchenko and Ilya Repin works)
cases.institution: Kyiv (Lavra, Mystetskyi Arsenal, Dovzhenko Film Studio), Kharkiv (Kharkiv Art Museum), Dnipro — Ukraine
cases.date_controversy: June 13–15, 2026 (weekend into Monday; Kharkiv museum hit June 14; Lavra/Arsenal overnight into June 15)
cases.description: Over the weekend of June 13–14 into Monday June 15, 2026, a massive Russian missile-and-drone barrage struck multiple Ukrainian cultural sites. Overnight into June 15 a drone strike set ablaze the roof of the 11th-century Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra — a UNESCO World Heritage site and a centre of Orthodox monasticism revered by both the Ukrainian and Russian churches. UNESCO cited possible significant damage to the cathedral's exterior and interior and to adjacent historic structures, including elements of the Lavra's fortification complex and the Ivan Kushnik Tower. The adjacent Mystetskyi Arsenal — an 18th-century complex now a national contemporary art centre — had a large part of the Old Arsenal's left-wing roof seriously damaged by a Shahed drone that hit the tower and exploded on the roof (per director-general Olesia Ostrovska-Liuta). In Kyiv, the "largest and oldest costume collection of Ukraine" was reported destroyed at the Dovzhenko Film Studio. The Kharkiv Art Museum (famous for Shevchenko and Repin; most significant works evacuated in 2022) was hit Sunday June 14, with paintings carried out of the building after the strike. Culture minister Tetyana Berezhna reported damage across Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Dnipro. President Zelensky, who visited the Lavra and the Arsenal on June 15, said two Russian drones deliberately targeted the area and called the attack "Russian barbarism" and "an attack on the Christian community and on the cultural heritage of humanity," reporting 11 killed and 53 wounded nationwide (35 injured in Kyiv). Russia's foreign-ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova called reports that Russia hit the Lavra "fakes," claiming — citing Russia's defence ministry — that the site was struck by an American Patriot air-defence missile supplied to Ukraine.
cases.outcome: Dormition Cathedral roof fire extinguished; UNESCO and Ukraine assessing damage to the Lavra, Mystetskyi Arsenal, Kharkiv Art Museum, and the (reportedly destroyed) Dovzhenko costume collection. Restoration pledged (Metropolitan Epiphanius). Damage assessment ongoing as of June 15, 2026; Russia denies targeting the Lavra. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Heritage destruction, Wartime destruction, Geopolitics, Conservation, Religious site, Historical erasure, Russia-Ukraine war

cases.title: Monumento à Literatura Brasileira (a.k.a. Monument to Carlos Drummond de Andrade and Mário Quintana), 2001
cases.institution: Praça da Alfândega, Centro Histórico, Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul (near MARGS and Casa de Cultura Mário Quintana)
cases.date_controversy: Recurring; most recent datable incident July 20, 2022 (theft 2015; "vandalized several times")
cases.description: Backfill / recurring-vandalism entry. A bronze ensemble — a bench and two life-size figures, Drummond standing and Quintana seated, evoking a casual encounter between the two poets — commissioned by the Câmara Riograndense do Livro for the 47th Porto Alegre Book Fair and inaugurated October 26, 2001. The work has been vandalized repeatedly: a main part was stolen in 2015, and on the morning of July 20, 2022 both figures were found covered in yellow paint poured over the writers' heads and thrown across the bodies (removed the same day by the prefeitura; humid, foggy weather slowed drying). Portuguese-language sources note it has been "vandalized several times." No perpetrator or stated motive has been reported for any incident.
cases.outcome: 2022 paint removed same day by the city; status of the 2015 stolen part unclear; the monument remains in situ. Recurring-vandalism pattern with no perpetrators identified.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Public sculpture

cases.title: Tänzerinnen-Brunnen ("Dancers' Fountain" / "Dancing Girls Fountain"), 1922
cases.institution: Georg Kolbe Museum, Berlin (deaccessioned); sold at Grisebach, Berlin
cases.date_controversy: Looted/forced sale 1941; restituted spring 2026; sold June 4, 2026
cases.description: Backfill / restitution-cluster entry. Kolbe's 1922 bronze-and-limestone fountain — a white female dancer borne aloft by three crouching Somali men, which the museum itself describes as reflecting the artist's "reliance on colonial representation" — was commissioned by Heinrich Stahl, director of Victoria Insurance and a prominent member of Berlin's Jewish community, and installed at the Villa Stahl in Berlin-Dahlem. In 1941 Stahl was forced under Nazi racial laws to sell his home and the fountain far below value; he was deported to Theresienstadt and murdered, while his widow Jenny survived and emigrated to the US. The dispersed work (the dancer reached Madrid via a Bulgarian consul) was reassembled and acquired by the Georg Kolbe Museum in 1978–79 with German Class Lottery Foundation funds, becoming a garden centerpiece for nearly five decades. A 2001 waiver by grandson Werner Stahl was later found not to bind the wider family; a 2024 museum research project ("Der Brunnen/The Fountain") concluded the fountain was "cultural property looted as a result of Nazi persecution." In February 2026 the museum offered full restitution under the 1998 Washington Principles; the heirs accepted, took possession in spring 2026, and consigned the work to Grisebach, where it sold on June 4, 2026 for a record €4m (with fees) — the highest price ever for a Kolbe, well above the prior €1.4m record. It has left public display.
cases.outcome: Resolved. Restituted to the Stahl heirs (spring 2026) by amicable agreement under the Washington Principles; sold at Grisebach June 4, 2026 for a record €4m and removed from public display.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Deaccessioning, Nazi-looted art, Financialization, Provenance, Colonial representation

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing demolition — DC Circuit appeal
cases.institution: White House; U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit
cases.description: On June 5, 2026, a three-judge DC Circuit panel heard oral argument in the National Trust for Historic Preservation's suit over the ~$400M ballroom built on the demolished East Wing site. The panel appeared skeptical of the administration's claim that no court could review or block the project; one judge likened the government's position (no standing once a structure is already destroyed) to "move fast and break things," invoking a hypothetical about demolishing the Statue of Liberty, and the panel signaled that only Congress can authorize such a project. A ruling is expected in the coming weeks.
cases.outcome: DC Circuit June 5 oral argument held; panel skeptical of DOJ's no-review / national-security claims; ruling pending as of June 15, 2026.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Demolition, Legal challenge, Political interference

cases.title: SAIC graduate course assignment — case study (per 166); Hyperallergic editorial
cases.institution: School of the Art Institute of Chicago (SAIC)
cases.description: Hyperallergic editor-in-chief Hrag Vartanian published an opinion essay, "They Want to Control Our Imagination," on the SAIC matter logged in 166. It specifies the triggering assignment: a professor asked students to imagine a way to help someone they might encounter — which SAIC leadership reportedly found "beyond the pale." The piece frames the institution's response as an attempt to police students' imaginative and empathetic capacity. (Appears to concern the same SAIC case as 166; the professor there is on paid leave with an investigation ongoing.)
cases.outcome: Opinion essay published June 2026 adding the assignment specifics; the underlying SAIC matter (166) — professor on paid leave, investigation ongoing — remains unresolved.
cases.tags: Censorship, Institutional crisis, Labor dispute, Academic freedom

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed, ~250 ft) — Section 106 consultation and public comment
cases.institution: Memorial Circle, George Washington Memorial Parkway (NPS); National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC)
cases.description: The NPS Section 106 consultation meeting for the arch is set for June 15, 2026 — ten days after public comments opened on June 5 — and the public-comment period on the Assessment of Effects Report closes the same day (11:59 p.m. Mountain Time). Six preservation organizations — the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the Committee of 100 on the Federal City, the DC Preservation League, the Cultural Landscape Foundation, the National Parks Conservation Association, and the American Institute of Architects — formally requested inclusion in the Section 106 consultation but, per The Art Newspaper, had received no reply from the NPS. The NCPC's next monthly meeting is July 9 (it recesses in August).
cases.outcome: Section 106 meeting and public-comment deadline both June 15, 2026; six preservation groups' consultation-inclusion requests unanswered by NPS; no decision yet.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Political interference, Design controversy, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Cali municipal mural-erasure program (broader context to 137's "falsos positivos" memory mural)
cases.institution: City of Cali / Alcaldía de Cali (Mayor Alejandro Eder); program run via Uaesp ("promotores de residuos cero")
cases.date_controversy: Late May 2026 (El Tiempo coverage); program ongoing
cases.description: El Tiempo coverage broadens 137 from a single May 24 incident to a documented citywide pattern: youth and street-art collectives say the Eder administration is systematically covering their murals and painting walls gray. Councilwoman María del Carmen Londoño (Pacto Histórico) alleged the mayor's office has spent roughly COP $20.252 billion on a program — run via Uaesp "promotores de residuos cero," linked to Diego Hau — that contracts people to roam the city erasing murals and painting bridges and walls gray, including messages critical of Eder and of "uribismo." Street artists call it censorship of artistic expression; regional politicians counter that the murals are illegal/unauthorized and carry "proselytizing" ("tintes proselitistas") content. Complaints have been filed with the Procuraduría General de la Nación against congressmen (e.g., Alfredo Mondragón) who accompanied the artists.
cases.outcome: Dispute ongoing; municipal gray-over program continuing; Procuraduría complaints pending; no resolution as of mid-June 2026.
cases.tags: Censorship, Removal, Political interference, Protest art, Historical erasure

cases.title: "Funk: Um Grito de Ousadia e Liberdade" (exhibition; originally developed by the Museu de Arte do Rio / MAR)
cases.artist: N/A (group exhibition; curator Renata, surname not confirmed in coverage)
cases.institution: Museu da Língua Portuguesa (Estação da Luz), São Paulo; managed by IDBRASIL Cultura, Educação e Esporte
cases.date_controversy: May 31, 2026 (early closure); MP complaint filed late May 2026
cases.description: On Sunday May 31, 2026, the Museu da Língua Portuguesa closed "Funk: Um Grito de Ousadia e Liberdade" roughly three months early (it opened November 2025 and was scheduled through August 30, 2026). The early closure followed a representação to the Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) by city councilman Lucas Pavanato (PL) and state-deputy pre-candidate Felipe Sertanejo (PL) (one outlet also names state deputy "Tenente Coimbra," PL-SP), objecting to images of women in short clothing, references to sexuality, drug-consumption symbols, and works said to allude to "narcocultura," and alleging violations of the Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA) and of the show's indicative rating (14+), emphasizing reported school visits. The MPSP opened a preliminary apuração and sent ofícios to the museum, the municipal Education Secretariat and the state Culture Secretariat, but stated it had not ordered any alteration, interruption, censorship or closure. The museum publicly framed the closure as routine scheduling ("to enable two new shows this year"; "Funk ran six months, the average run for temporary shows"). The exhibition's curator (Renata) said the early closure was not the curatorial team's decision and that she learned a replacement show had been arranged without prior discussion. The show was originally created by the Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR), where it ran for over a year.
cases.outcome: Exhibition closed May 31, 2026, ~3 months ahead of schedule; MPSP preliminary investigation open as of mid-June 2026; museum denies political motive (cites scheduling), while the curator and critics attribute it to far-right political pressure.
cases.tags: Censorship, Removal, Political interference, Institutional crisis, Religious objection

cases.title: "Man in the Garden" (2025), Clarence Heyward -- NYT enrichment
cases.institution: Houston Museum of African American Culture (HMAAC)
cases.date_controversy: May 21, 2026 (vandalism); NYT report June 13, updated June 14, 2026
cases.description: New York Times coverage (June 13, updated June 14) adds detail to 176. The two young white men, dressed in black and carrying a bag, used a screwdriver or scissors to scrape and puncture the 4-by-4-foot canvas (valued at $23,000; damage estimated at ~$4,500). Before the attack they visited a show by artist Kandy G. Lopez (also Black) and had themselves photographed giving the middle finger to one of her works. The museum's security cameras were not operating that day -- a repair work order had been filed the day before. HPD is investigating a report filed the day after; no arrests. The damaged work was returned to view on the exhibition's final day, June 6.
cases.outcome: HPD investigation ongoing, no arrests as of June 14, 2026; damaged work shown on the exhibition's closing day, June 6.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Resistance, Security failure
outlets: The New York Times (Derrick Bryson Taylor)

cases.title: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts -- name-removal appeal posture
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington, DC
cases.description: After the facade name was fully removed (completed ~noon Saturday, June 13, under a granted ~12-hour weather extension), the fight shifted to the appeal. The DC Circuit panel (Judges Katsas, Millett, Wilkins) denied the administrative stay June 12 in a brief, unsigned order but set a briefing schedule running through ~June 29 before ruling on whether Judge Cooper's order stays in effect for the duration of the appeal; the panel left open that Trump's name could be restored if DOJ ultimately prevails. DOJ argued repeated name changes would confuse the public and that removal jeopardizes donor funds given to the Center because of Trump's name.
cases.outcome: Name fully removed June 13, 2026; DC Circuit to rule on a stay pending appeal after briefing through ~June 29; restoration legally possible if DOJ prevails.
cases.tags: Political interference, Legal challenge, Historical erasure, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Italian nationwide arts and culture sector strike -- June 12 (held)
cases.artist: ANGA (Art Not Genocide Alliance); Federculture; Italian arts unions and collectives
cases.institution: Nationwide, Italy
cases.description: The nationwide arts-and-culture strike called for June 12, 2026 was held. Cultural-sector employees under Federculture and at the Ministry of Culture struck for the full day, affecting museums and cultural institutions. Backed by ANGA, Mi Riconosci?, Art Workers Italy, the Italian Association of Museum Educators and others, the action combined demands over precarious labor and low wages with opposition to "genocide normalisation" in culture and cultural-sector ties to the arms industry, building on the May 8 Venice Biennale strike.
cases.outcome: Strike held June 12, 2026. Turnout figures and any government response not yet reported.
cases.tags: Labor dispute, Protest art, Political art, Geopolitics

cases.title: "Au Grand Maure" wrought-iron shop/house sign (enseigne) depicting a Black man's head in profile; in place ~60 years
cases.institution: Cite district (old town), Lausanne; owner Etablissement cantonal d'assurance (ECA); destined for Musee historique de Lausanne
cases.description: The owner of the building, the Etablissement cantonal d'assurance (ECA), announced ~June 10, 2026 that it will remove the roughly 60-year-old "Au Grand Maure" wrought-iron sign -- a stereotyped profile of a Black man's head -- from a street in Lausanne's historic Cite quarter after months of public debate, and donate it to the Musee historique de Lausanne together with a commissioned historical study of the object.
cases.outcome: Removal announced ~June 10, 2026; sign to be transferred to the Musee historique de Lausanne with an accompanying historical study. Not yet physically removed.
cases.tags: Removal, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Historical erasure, Adaptive reuse

cases.title: Franco-era monument (monumental sculpture)
cases.institution: Rambla / Avenida Francisco La Roche, Santa Cruz de Tenerife (public space)
cases.date_controversy: BIC denial reported ~June 10-11, 2026 (expediente opened Oct 2024; related court ruling June 28, 2024)
cases.description: The Canary Islands government's Consejo de Patrimonio Cultural declined (~June 10, 2026) to declare the Juan de Avalos Franco-era monument a Bien de Interes Cultural (BIC), finding it lacks the heritage values required for the highest tier of protection. Without that protection the monument is expected to be removed under Spain's Law of Historical Memory. The decision follows a June 2024 court ruling and an expediente opened by the Cabildo in October 2024. The memory association ARMH-Tenerife gathered 1,400+ signatures urging removal and proposed relocating the piece to the Museo Historico Militar de Canarias (Cuartel de Almeida).
cases.outcome: BIC protection denied (~June 10, 2026); removal under the Memory Law now likely but not yet executed; relocation to the military museum proposed.
cases.tags: Removal, Iconoclasm, Political interference, Landmark dispute, Historical erasure

cases.title: 25 bequeathed works incl. 8 Rembrandts (e.g. "Saul and David," "Two African Men")
cases.artist: Rembrandt van Rijn; Jan Steen; Jan van Goyen; and others
cases.institution: Mauritshuis, The Hague
cases.description: The District Court of The Hague ruled June 10, 2026 that the Mauritshuis is not required to return 25 works bequeathed by former director Abraham Bredius (d. 1946) to the descendants of his sole heir, Joseph Kronig. The heirs argued the museum breached a condition that all 25 works (incl. 8 Rembrandts) remain on permanent display; 15 are kept in storage. The court read Bredius's French-language will ("devront rester exposes exclusivement dans ledit Musee") as granting the museum exclusive display rights and barring loans elsewhere, rather than imposing a permanent-display obligation, finding the wording left "room for uncertainty."
cases.outcome: District Court of The Hague ruled June 10, 2026 in the museum's favor; the 25 works stay at the Mauritshuis. Heirs may appeal.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Deaccessioning, Copyright/ownership, Conservation

cases.title: Ai Weiwei design for the Miss Read book fair (rejected) — reportedly rejected for resemblance to a swastika
cases.institution: Miss Read (Berlin Art Book Fair / art-book fair), Germany — venue to confirm
cases.date_controversy: June 2026 (per Ai Weiwei Instagram post; exact date unconfirmed)
cases.description: According to a post on Ai Weiwei's Instagram account (reported to the tracker by R. Shields; no press pickup located as of June 13, 2026), a design he created for the Miss Read book fair in Germany was rejected by organizers because the design resembled a swastika. Details of the design, the rationale, and whether the rejection cited German law or organizer risk-aversion are not yet confirmed.
cases.outcome: Design rejected by Miss Read organizers over swastika resemblance, per Ai Weiwei's Instagram. Social-media report only as of June 13, 2026; no organizer statement or press coverage confirmed.
cases.tags: Censorship, Design controversy, Self-censorship
outlets: Ai Weiwei (Instagram, @aiww) — reported by R. Shields

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed, 250 ft) — archaeological / Section 106 review; Memorial Circle on Columbia Island
cases.artist: N/A (administration project; rendering by Harrison Design)
cases.institution: Memorial Circle, Columbia Island, Washington, DC; National Park Service / DC Historic Preservation Office
cases.date_controversy: June 12, 2026 (report coverage); Section 106 meeting set for June 15, 2026
cases.description: An NPS report in the arch's historic-preservation review warns that construction could disturb precolonial archaeological deposits beneath Memorial Circle on man-made Columbia Island (landfill roughly 10–14 ft deep; moorings would need to reach bedrock about 75 ft down), an area of "moderate to high" archeological sensitivity for intact precolonial and historic resources. Thirteen documented archaeological/historic sites lie within a mile on the Virginia side (including Arlington House; War of 1812 associations). The detailed archaeological appendix was withheld as "sensitive" and not posted on the public-comment portal; DC HPO archaeologist Ruth Trocolli said protecting site locations "does make sense" given active looters. A Section 106 review (National Historic Preservation Act of 1966) is required; a Section 106 meeting is set for June 15 — ten days after public comments opened. Six preservation groups (National Trust for Historic Preservation, Committee of 100 on the Federal City, DC Preservation League, Cultural Landscape Foundation, National Parks Conservation Association, American Institute of Architects) asked to be consulting parties but had received no reply. NPS plans a programmatic agreement with the DC HPO, the NCPC and the ACHP — the latter two now stacked with Trump appointees. The US Commission of Fine Arts approved the arch on May 21 despite roughly 99.5% unfavorable public comments.
cases.outcome: Section 106 review underway with a June 15, 2026 meeting; detailed archaeological appendix withheld as "sensitive"; six preservation groups await consulting-party status; programmatic agreement pending. Construction approvals unresolved as of June 13, 2026.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Archaeological site, Political interference, Landmark dispute, Conservation

cases.title: National Park Service interpretive signs, films and materials nationwide (e.g., slavery plaques at Independence NHP; climate sign at Fort Sumter; Indigenous-history sign at Acadia)
cases.institution: National Park Service / national parks nationwide; U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts
cases.description: Judge Angel Kelley (D. Mass.) on June 12, 2026 temporarily blocked the NPS from removing or revising signs, films and other materials to comply with Trump's executive order targeting content that "inappropriately disparage[s] Americans" or casts the United States "in a negative light," and ordered restoration within three weeks of any dismantled or altered exhibits. The 63-page ruling called the removals "a dangerous precedent of censorship and sanitization." Plaintiffs were a coalition including the Coalition to Protect America's National Parks (suit filed Feb 2026). Removed items had included slavery plaques at Independence NHP (Philadelphia), a climate sign at Fort Sumter (SC), and an Indigenous-history sign at Acadia (Maine). Interior signaled an appeal; an NPS official directed regional supervisors to pause implementation pending further guidance.
cases.outcome: Nationwide removals/revisions temporarily blocked June 12, 2026; NPS ordered to restore altered/removed exhibits within three weeks; implementation paused; Interior signaled appeal. Litigation ongoing.
cases.tags: Censorship, Historical erasure, Political interference, Legal challenge, Removal

cases.title: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts — facade name-removal compliance
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington, DC
cases.description: After Judge Christopher Cooper's May 29, 2026 ruling that only Congress can rename the Center, the Trump-appointed board voted June 11 to appeal and sought a stay. Both the district court and a federal appeals court denied an immediate stay on June 12. Granted a roughly 12-hour extension past the midnight June 12 deadline (the Center cited summer storms that delayed scaffolding), workers removed Trump's name from the white marble facade in the early hours of Saturday, June 13, 2026 (letters began coming down just past 3 a.m.); executive director Matt Floca filed a sworn declaration confirming removal. The DOJ stay motion (AAG Brett Shumate) warned that removal would threaten donor fundraising tied to the 'Trump' name and echoed the president's own cadence. The name was already gone from the website and YouTube page; Rep. Joyce Beatty was present at the plaza for the removal.
cases.outcome: Trump's name physically removed from the facade early Saturday, June 13, 2026, after both the district and appeals courts denied a stay and a ~12-hour extension; Floca filed a sworn compliance declaration. Merits appeal continues at the DC Circuit; the separate two-year closure/renovation dispute also remains live.
cases.tags: Political interference, Legal challenge, Historical erasure, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation; new "Trump Promenade" pedestrian bridge (announced)
cases.institution: Lincoln Memorial / National Mall, Washington, DC
cases.description: Trump declared the Reflecting Pool renovation complete on June 6, 2026 (filled June 5, touting "clean, beautiful water") and announced a new "Trump Promenade" — a pedestrian bridge connecting the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac, framed as fulfilling the early-20th-c. McMillan Plan. Sen. Blumenthal's June 9 letter cited the pool's "resealing" among projects that bypassed legal review.
cases.outcome: Pool declared complete June 6, 2026; "Trump Promenade" announced, not yet built; legal-review concerns raised. Active.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Political interference, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed, ~250 ft), Memorial Circle near the Lincoln Memorial
cases.institution: Memorial Circle / National Mall area, Washington, DC
cases.description: A fast-tracked historic-preservation review of the arch began Friday June 5, 2026; a 24-page National Park Service preliminary assessment (released the week of June 8) describes year-round construction up to 20 hours/day in two 10-hour shifts, tower cranes up to 320 ft, and a roughly 3-year build. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) wrote Interior Sec. Doug Burgum and acting NPS director Jessica Bowron on June 9 citing "persistent lack of transparency" across the arch, ballroom, and Reflecting Pool — none of which went through usual legal reviews or Congress. Trump said construction would start "within two months."

cases.title: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts — name-removal appeal & stay denial
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington, D.C.
cases.description: On June 11, 2026 the Kennedy Center's Trump-allied board voted to appeal Judge Christopher Cooper's May 29 ruling, which ordered removal of Trump's name (added Dec 2025) by June 12 and temporarily blocked the planned two-year closure. Lawyers filed a notice of appeal and sought a stay, arguing that removing then reinstating the name would waste time and money and confuse the public; Rep. Joyce Beatty, whose suit prompted the ruling, called it a frivolous "eleventh-hour" gambit. On June 12 Cooper denied the stay, finding the center's partial compliance (name scrubbed from website and branding) undercut any claim of irreparable harm; the administration then filed an appeal with the D.C. Circuit. Cooper's 94-page order held that only Congress can change the name and that the board had been "derelict" in reviewing the closure.
cases.outcome: June 11: board votes to appeal and seeks stay. June 12: Cooper denies stay (partial compliance = no irreparable harm); administration appeals to D.C. Circuit. Name-removal deadline June 12; appeal pending.

cases.title: Poisoning the Country's Lungs (The Battle of Eat Street) (2026)
cases.institution: Eat Street / Minneapolis (protest site); Starring America News (independent media project)
cases.description: On January 24, 2026, artist and courtroom sketch artist Isabelle Brourman was documenting anti-ICE protests in Minneapolis as part of the long-term project Starring America News (with partner Peter Hambrecht and collaborator Jeannette Berlin) when a masked federal agent spotted her sketching, dropped to one knee, and fired pepper balls at her at point-blank range. Brourman raised her drawing board just in time, deflecting the projectile — which left a hole and dent through the wood and paper. This occurred on the same day hospital nurse Alex Pretti was killed by federal agents. Brourman produced the drawing Poisoning the Country's Lungs (The Battle of Eat Street) (2026) from the experience. The Art Newspaper profiled her on April 9, 2026. The trio continued their documentary work and are developing a longer-form documentary; they discussed touring the country with drawings and video in a makeshift mobile gallery.
cases.outcome: Brourman uninjured. No charges filed against agent. Documentary work ongoing as of June 2026.

cases.title: N/A (institutional collective action — Walker Art Center, Minneapolis Institute of Art, Weisman Art Museum, and others)

cases.description: On January 22–23, 2026, leading art museums and galleries in Minneapolis and St. Paul participated in a citywide general strike ('Day of Truth and Freedom') to protest violent ICE operations under Operation Metro Surge. The Walker Art Center, Minneapolis Institute of Art, Weisman Art Museum, Minnesota Museum of American Art, Museum of Russian Art, Praxis Photo Arts Center, and numerous smaller institutions closed on January 23. The Walker canceled a scheduled performance by Nile Harris. The strike followed the January 8 killing of Renee Good by ICE agent Jonathan Ross, subsequent escalation of ICE operations (including the detention of a 5-year-old as 'bait'), and the January 24 killing of hospital nurse Alex Pretti. The art community's participation stood in stark contrast to the silence of institutions in LA, NYC, Chicago, Denver, and DC, whose dependence on federal funding made them reluctant to act. Dreamsong gallery called ICE's operations 'unconstitutional attack on our populace.'
cases.outcome: Strike completed January 23, 2026. Institutions reopened January 24. No known government retaliation against participating institutions.
cases.tags: Labor dispute, Political interference, Resistance, Institutional crisis, Artist safety

cases.title: No Ice in the Cup (poster campaign, multiple works)
cases.artist: Cristy Road Carrera (NYC), Angel Faz (Dallas), Chris Stewart (LA), Hana Natsuhara (Seattle), Johann C. Muñoz-Tapasco (Miami), and artists from 10 US host cities
cases.institution: Nationwide (US FIFA World Cup host cities); noiceinthecup.us
cases.description: The Horizons Project, a pro-democracy organizing network, launched 'No Ice in the Cup' on May 6, 2026 — a campaign using commissioned protest poster art to oppose the deployment of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents at 2026 FIFA World Cup events. Artists from 10 of the 11 US host cities contributed posters available for free download and remix. Works use soccer imagery, local themes, and direct anti-ICE messaging: NYC's poster (Cristy Road Carrera) shows a soccer squad facing off against ICE agents in tactical gear; Seattle's (Hana Natsuhara) riffs on Starbucks; Miami's (Johann C. Muñoz-Tapasco) features an alligator crushing a football with 'No Ice in Our Waters.' The campaign responds to: ICE's planned deployment at stadiums; a WaPo/UMD poll showing ~2/3 of Americans oppose ICE at World Cup venues; an April 23 travel advisory by 120+ civil society groups; and ICE killings of civilian bystanders (Renée Good, Alex Pretti) during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. Federal officials stated ICE will not conduct operations in Los Angeles during the tournament. The Art Newspaper covered the campaign June 9, 2026.
cases.outcome: Campaign active. World Cup June 11–July 19, 2026. Posters freely downloadable and remixable.

cases.title: Bayeux Tapestry loan to British Museum — French Supreme Court ruling
cases.institution: Conseil d'État (French Supreme Administrative Court)
cases.description: UPDATE: The French Conseil d'État (Supreme Administrative Court) dismissed a legal challenge by heritage nonprofit Sites & Monuments, which had filed an appeal in December 2025 to halt the Bayeux Tapestry loan to the British Museum. The court ruled it lacked jurisdiction, finding that Macron's decision to loan the tapestry constitutes an 'act of government' (acte de gouvernement) inseparable from France's conduct of international relations — and therefore not subject to administrative review. The loan proceeds: the tapestry is scheduled to travel to the British Museum for display September 2026 through July 2027, while the Bayeux Museum undergoes renovation for its reopening before William the Conqueror's 1000th birthday in 2028. Additional controversy: France had sought free admission for French citizens and the return of the Rosetta Stone in exchange; Britain refused both requests.
cases.outcome: Legal challenge dismissed. Loan proceeds. Exhibition September 2026–July 2027.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Conservation, Legal challenge, Geopolitics

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Chuck Redd lawsuit dismissed
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington DC
cases.description: Two significant developments: (1) REDD LAWSUIT DISMISSED: On June 6, 2026, DC Superior Court Judge Tanya Jones Bosier dismissed the Kennedy Center's breach-of-contract lawsuit against jazz drummer Chuck Redd, who had canceled his annual Christmas Eve Jazz Jam performance in December 2025 after the Board voted to rename the center. Redd had hosted the event since 2006. The Kennedy Center sought $1M in damages, calling the cancellation a 'political stunt.' Judge Bosier found no valid breach-of-contract claim — Redd had not signed the 2025 contract. She dismissed under both standard contract law and DC's anti-SLAPP statute, ordering the Kennedy Center to pay Redd's legal fees and court costs. (2) NAME REMOVAL PROCEEDING: The Kennedy Center website logo has removed 'Trump' from its branding as of approximately June 8. Physical facade signage (still reading 'Donald J. Trump') must be removed by the June 12 court deadline per the general counsel's internal memo. Staff instructed to update all materials, email signatures, brochures, and signage.

cases.title: Miniluv (mural, in progress)
cases.institution: Sunday Home furniture store, Roscoe, Town of Rockland, Sullivan County, NY
cases.description: Sullivan County artist Seth Indigo Carnes was commissioned in summer 2025 by the Sunday Home furniture store to paint a mural on the building's exterior in Roscoe, Town of Rockland. The mural — part of Carnes's long-running Miniluv project (text-based political/conceptual works) — was still in progress when Rockland Town Supervisor vocalized objections and instructed the town code enforcer to issue an irrelevant citation under the town's signage ordinance. A town council member then asked whether the artist would modify the work to reflect the town's tourism branding. The pressure led to the project's suspension. After seven months, the work-in-progress was destroyed. Carnes filed a federal First Amendment lawsuit in the Southern District of New York on February 26, 2026 (Carnes v. Town of Rockland, 7:2026cv01619). On June 4, 2026, NCAC and Artists Equity Group publicly condemned the town officials' actions.
cases.outcome: Mural destroyed after suspension. Federal lawsuit active (SDNY). NCAC condemned town June 4, 2026.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Community objection, Legal challenge

cases.title: Staffordshire Potteries historic industrial buildings (275+ listed buildings, 16 officially at risk)
cases.institution: Stoke-on-Trent, UK
cases.description: Stoke-on-Trent City Council declared the UK's first-ever 'heritage emergency' in January 2026, releasing a prospectus (The Potteries: A National Heritage Emergency) calling for £325M in public and private investment over 10 years to prevent the collapse of the city's ceramics industrial heritage. The city holds 275+ listed buildings, 22 conservation areas, and five scheduled monuments — many tied to Wedgwood, Spode, Royal Doulton, and other historic ceramics manufacturers whose decline has left factory buildings in severe disrepair. At least 16 sites are officially at risk; Chatterley Whitfield colliery complex alone may require up to £150M. Key at-risk sites include Burslem Indoor Market, the Wedgwood Institute, and Falcon Works. The council is appealing to central government, Historic England, and private investors. The Art Newspaper ran a feature June 8, 2026 as TAN's first substantial coverage of the emergency.
cases.outcome: Heritage emergency declared January 2026. £325M funding appeal ongoing. No central government commitment announced as of June 2026.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Funding dispute
