cases.title: Portrait of Fräulein Margarethe Lieser (1917–18)
cases.institution: Im Kinsky auction house (Vienna); New York State Supreme Court
cases.description: Patricia J. Leahy, a South Carolina-based descendant of the Lieser family, filed suit in New York State Supreme Court on June 5, 2026 against Vienna auction house Im Kinsky and current possessor Eva Ropper, alleging the long-lost Klimt portrait was looted from the Jewish Lieser family during the Nazi era. The portrait — unfinished at Klimt's death in 1918, and unseen publicly since 1925 — resurfaced when Im Kinsky sold it for $37.5M in April 2024, setting an Austrian auction record. The Hong Kong collector who bid withdrew after the sale. Leahy alleges Im Kinsky deliberately altered the title (dropping 'Margarethe') to obscure its Holocaust provenance, conducted a sham restitution process that excluded her as direct heir, and warned her not to approach the press. The suit names Austria's weak restitution laws as enabling the scheme.
cases.outcome: Lawsuit filed June 5, 2026. Case pending in New York State Supreme Court.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Art market fraud, Market opacity, Legal challenge

cases.title: Smithsonian 'American Aspirations' / Bunch's possible last curation
cases.artist: Lonnie G. Bunch III (Smithsonian Secretary); curators Abeer Saha and Harry Rubenstein
cases.institution: Smithsonian Castle, Washington DC
cases.description: NYT (Robin Pogrebin, May 28, 2026) profiles Lonnie Bunch III, Smithsonian Secretary, as he walked through 'American Aspirations,' an exhibition he curated for the institution's 250th anniversary contribution, which opened at the Smithsonian Castle on June 2. Bunch characterized it as 'probably the last exhibit I will curate, there's no doubt about that.' The Trump administration has asserted the Smithsonian is too negative about the US and is working to install allies on the board; Bunch acknowledged Trump allies could hold a board majority by fall. The exhibition features 30+ objects from five Smithsonian museums and includes complex, race-forward framing: a Douglass broadside recruiting Black soldiers, the Treaty of Canandaigua with the Iroquois Confederacy, and a Bartholdi Statue of Liberty model framed around slavery (the statue originally stood on broken chains). Bunch said: 'Did I pull punches? Not really. I'm never going to run from race.' The show runs through July 26. Separately confirmed: the exhibition 'Many Americas, Many 1776s' (which was to highlight non-colonial-white founders) was canceled; the Smithsonian's traditional National Mall Folklife Festival has been ceded to Trump's Great American State Fair. The Smithsonian has also been quietly removing politically sensitive wall text from National Portrait Gallery exhibitions (see 012-C).
cases.outcome: Exhibition open through July 26. Bunch anticipates departure. Trump allies may hold board majority by fall.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Museo Dolores Olmedo reopening after six-year closure and collection relocation controversy
cases.artist: Olmedo family trust; Carlos Phillips (son, trust president); Defendamos al Olmedo collective
cases.institution: Museo Dolores Olmedo, Xochimilco, Mexico City, Mexico
cases.description: The Museo Dolores Olmedo, which holds the world's most extensive collection of Frida Kahlo (26 works, including The Broken Column and Henry Ford Hospital) and Diego Rivera works (98 works), reopened May 30, 2026 after a six-year closure. The museum was first closed during the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2021, its governing trust — run by Olmedo's descendants — announced plans to relocate part of the collection to a new venue in Chapultepec's Parque Aztlán, sparking public backlash for going against Olmedo's expressed wishes for her collection to remain at the hacienda site. The trust ultimately announced in July 2025 that the museum would reopen after 'extensive cataloguing, maintenance and research.' The reopening honored Olmedo's legacy with newly opened private spaces. Community advocates from the collective Defendamos al Olmedo gathered outside for celebrations; the group is now pursuing a heritage declaration for the Mexico City site to further protect it. Questions remain about future loans and whether the collection will eventually be split: the museum declined to answer questions about future relocation plans.
cases.outcome: Reopened May 30, 2026. All art on display. Relocation question unresolved — museum declined to answer.
cases.tags: Institutional crisis, Deaccessioning, Repatriation

cases.title: Arson attempt at Boston Museum of African American History / African Meeting House
cases.artist: Unknown suspect (white male, caught on CCTV)
cases.institution: Museum of African American History, African Meeting House, 46 Joy St., Beacon Hill, Boston, USA
cases.description: At approximately 8:07 a.m. on June 4, 2026, a suspect stole a package from outside the Museum of African American History's Boston campus (the African Meeting House, the oldest surviving Black church building in the United States), opened the package, scattered its contents, and set them on fire in a nearby alley. The package contained materials for the museum's upcoming Juneteenth celebration, including Juneteenth-themed puzzles, decorations, bingo sets, and event supplies. Boston Police, the National Park Service, and federal authorities are investigating as a suspected hate crime; the Civil Rights Division of the Boston Police Department is leading the investigation. Security video shows the suspect, described as a white male in a dark jacket and white sneakers. Museum president and CEO Dr. Noelle Trent called it a 'sobering reminder' that the museum's work continues to be necessary. Boston Mayor Michelle Wu condemned the act and stated 'hateful acts of violence will never be tolerated.' No arrests as of the scan date.
cases.outcome: Investigation open. Suspect not yet identified or arrested. Museum building undamaged.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Censorship

cases.title: Alma Allen accuses publicist David Resnicow of undermining US Pavilion
cases.institution: US Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy
cases.description: On June 8, 2026, artist Alma Allen published an Instagram post doubling down on prior accusations against veteran art-world publicist David Resnicow, alleging he had advised others not to support Allen's US Pavilion. Allen claimed two of the three galleries that withdrew their support from his pavilion did so 'on the advice of David Resnicow,' and that Resnicow's name came up from arts writers, museum directors, funders, and curators who said he had warned them not to support the 2026 American pavilion. Allen said he has 'never met' Resnicow. Resnicow's firm had represented the US Pavilion six times previously. ARTnews reports Resnicow called Allen's claims 'baffling.' This is the second time Allen has publicly named Resnicow; the first was in a NYT article from March 2026. Allen's pavilion was already embattled: his two main galleries (Mendes Wood DM and Olney Gleason) dropped him after he accepted the commission; he now shows with Perrotin.
cases.outcome: Allen's public accusation issued June 8. Resnicow denies. No legal action announced.
cases.tags: Institutional crisis, Market opacity

cases.title: CFA chairman Rodney Mims Cook Jr. at St. Petersburg International Economic Forum ('Russian Davos')
cases.artist: Rodney Mims Cook Jr. (chair, US Commission of Fine Arts)
cases.institution: St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF), Russia; US Commission of Fine Arts
cases.description: On June 4, 2026, Rodney Mims Cook Jr., the chairman of the US Commission of Fine Arts — the body that has approved Trump's triumphal arch and White House ballroom — participated in a two-hour roundtable titled 'Russia-US: Dialogue of Cultures' at Putin's St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF), known as 'Russian Davos.' He was the first US official to participate at SPIEF in nearly a decade. The roundtable was moderated by Mikhail Shvydkoy, Putin's international cultural envoy and the architect of Russia's controversial Venice Biennale return. Seated next to Cook was Mikhail Piotrovsky, director of the State Hermitage Museum, EU-sanctioned for supporting Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Also on the panel: Russian Culture Minister Olga Lyubimova (EU- and US-sanctioned), conductor Valery Gergiev (director of both the Mariinsky and Bolshoi theatres), and actor Steven Seagal (Russian passport holder, Putin appointee). Cook spoke for nearly 20 minutes about his love of Russian culture, heritage projects near Moscow, and a dacha he built in Atlanta in 'Russian village style.' He also presented Trump's ballroom and arch proposals. Cook had delivered a copy of the Sitka Icon of the Theotokos to a St. Petersburg monastery as a gift from Trump ahead of the summit. Secretary of State Rubio denied knowledge of the US delegation. The panel was broadcast live on Rutube (Gazprom-Media).
cases.outcome: Cook attended SPIEF June 4. No response from Cook or CFA. Rubio denied knowledge.
cases.tags: Political interference, Geopolitics, Political art

cases.title: Triumphal arch — NCPC June 4 vote / public testimony
cases.institution: National Capital Planning Commission / Memorial Circle, Washington DC
cases.description: The Art Newspaper (Helen Stoilas, June 5) provides the fullest account of the June 4 NCPC hearing. Nearly 1,700 written comments were submitted, vast majority negative. More than two dozen people spoke directly, including multiple military veterans. Key testimony: (1) Former Marine Jimi Shaughnessy called the arch 'fodder for the vain.' (2) Veteran Stephen Eubank called it 'a monumental disgrace' and invoked Ozymandias. (3) Former CIA analyst Holly Berkley Fletcher compared it to 'tacky, bombastic strongman vanity' of African dictatorships she grew up observing. (4) Architect David Parker submitted drawings showing the 1930s-approved columns that were never built were only 14ft in diameter, vastly smaller than the arch. NCPC chair Will Scharf (simultaneously Trump's White House staff secretary) argued the Height of Buildings Act does not apply to federal construction, citing two 1932 precedents — the Masonic Temple (got a Congressional waiver) and the National Archives (built to 166ft without one). Only Commissioner Evan Cash (DC City Council member) voted against, questioning the lack of any framework for what the arch commemorates. The NCPC scheduled its next hearing for July 1.
cases.outcome: NCPC voted 9-1 to advance conceptual plans. July 1 is next NCPC hearing. Trump says construction begins 'in next two months.'
cases.tags: Political interference, Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Community objection

cases.title: Pace Gallery layoffs / model correction — additional coverage
cases.institution: Pace Gallery (global)
cases.description: Additional coverage from The Art Newspaper and Hyperallergic (June 4–5) confirms details logged in parent entry 150. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher publicly characterized the cuts as a 'model correction,' telling ARTnews: 'Galleries need a model correction.' The Art Newspaper commentary (Melanie Gerlis) framed the move as potentially signaling that 'shrinking is the next growth model' for mega-galleries, questioning whether 'constant expansion and rising prices in the primary market are unfixable.' The Hyperallergic piece framed the layoffs in the context of 'the disastrous collapse of crypto-backed art ventures, of which Pace was an early adopter.' Total confirmed: approximately 50 artists dropped and 50 staff let go.
cases.outcome: Confirmed: ~50 artists and ~50 staff released. Glimcher framing = 'model correction.'
cases.tags: Financialization, Art market fraud, Market opacity, Labor dispute

cases.title: Bayeux Tapestry loan to British Museum — controversy and study
cases.artist: Bayeux Museum; British Museum; French government; UK government
cases.institution: Bayeux Museum (France) → British Museum (London, UK)
cases.description: The planned loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum for an exhibition (September 2026–July 2027) has generated overlapping controversies: (1) Conservation/transport risk: French art historians and conservators have argued the 950-year-old, 70-metre textile — with 24,000 stains, 16,445 creases, and 10,000+ holes — is too fragile to transport. A May 2026 ARTnews report confirms a French study asserts the transport is safe; critics contest the 2mm/second vibration limit as based on 'utmost generality.' (2) Insurance controversy: UK Treasury is insuring the tapestry under the Government Indemnity Scheme for an estimated £800 million ($1 billion+), the highest GIS cover in history, triggering public debate about taxpayer risk. (3) French public opposition: A petition of 40,000+ French signatories characterized the loan as a 'heritage crime.' The Macron government announced the loan during his July 2025 state visit to the UK. In exchange, British artifacts including Sutton Hoo treasures and Lewis chess pieces will travel to Normandy. An April 2025 simulation of the tapestry's removal from its technical room was conducted using a facsimile.
cases.outcome: Legal challenge dismissed (Conseil d'État, June 2026). Exhibition proceeds September 2026–July 2027.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Conservation, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Italian nationwide arts and culture sector strike — June 12
cases.artist: ANGA (Art Not Genocide Alliance); Italian arts unions and collectives
cases.institution: Nationwide, Italy
cases.description: Italian labor unions, cultural workers' associations, and grassroots collectives have called a nationwide 24-hour strike across Italy's arts and culture sector for Friday, June 12, 2026. The action was announced by ANGA (Art Not Genocide Alliance) and allied groups. Strike participants cite unstable working conditions, low wages, and public investment in arms over culture — and explicitly link the action to Palestinian solidarity, framing it as 'the next step' after the Venice Biennale ANGA strike of May 8. A separate government source (Federculture) confirmed cultural-sector employees under Federculture and the Ministry of Culture will strike nationally on June 12. The June 12 action expands beyond the Venice context to include editorial workers, entertainment professionals, and all arts-adjacent labor.
cases.outcome: Strike called for June 12. Action has not yet occurred as of this scan (June 8).
cases.tags: Labor dispute, Political art, Geopolitics

cases.title: Jerry Gogosian / Hilde Lynn Helphenstein — death in São Paulo
cases.institution: Rosewood São Paulo, Brazil (death); art world at large
cases.description: Hilde Lynn Helphenstein, 40, creator of the art-world satirical Instagram account 'Jerry Gogosian' (145,000–156,000 followers), was found dead in her room at the Rosewood São Paulo hotel on May 31, 2026. She had been in São Paulo for three weeks for a cosmetic procedure. The death was registered as suspicious by the 78th Police Station; Brazilian forensic authorities and police opened an investigation. Prescription pills, an empty vodka bottle, and broken glass were found at the scene. Launched in 2018 under an anonymous persona, Jerry Gogosian became the art world's most influential satirical voice, skewering gallery power dynamics, auction house excess, and market opacity. Helphenstein had recently retired the Jerry Gogosian persona. She had previously run an LA gallery, collaborated with Sotheby's, and hosted the Art Smack podcast. Her identity was revealed by Artnet News columnist Kenny Schachter in 2020.
cases.outcome: Death confirmed, suspicious circumstances. Police investigation open. Cause of death not yet determined.
cases.tags: Market opacity, Financialization

cases.title: Penn Station redesign / Trump name carved into marble
cases.artist: PAU (Practice for Architecture and Urbanism), Vishaan Chakrabarti (lead architect); Penn Transformation Partners (Vornado, Halmar)
cases.institution: Pennsylvania Station, New York City, USA
cases.description: On June 8, 2026, Penn Transformation Partners and Amtrak released official renderings for the nearly $8 billion Penn Station redesign, confirming that the name 'Donald J. Trump' will be carved into marble next to a presidential seal at the new 31st Street/Eighth Avenue entrance. The design was helmed by architect Vishaan Chakrabarti (PAU). Renderings feature Beaux-Arts-inspired architecture, large American flags, gold-accented railings and escalators, and raised ceilings of up to 50 feet. The master developer was selected in a competitive process. Earlier (May 29, Gothamist), leaked internal renderings had first disclosed the Trump branding. White House officials had floated renaming the station 'Trump Station' but this was not adopted in the official renderings. Financing is unresolved: Amtrak hopes the federal government will cover most of the $7–8 billion cost. Trump has ordered construction to begin by end of 2027.
cases.outcome: Official renderings released June 8. Trump branding confirmed. Financing unresolved. Construction target end-2027.
cases.tags: Political interference, Architectural preservation, Design controversy

cases.title: Chichén Itzá — reopening after 13-day vendor closure
cases.institution: Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
cases.description: RESOLUTION: Chichén Itzá reopened June 1, 2026 after an unprecedented 13-day closure (May 19–June 1) triggered by protests from 666 registered artisans against their mandatory relocation to the new Visitor Attention Center (CATVI), built adjacent to the Maya Train station. An agreement was reached after intensive negotiations among the Yucatán state government, federal authorities (INAH), and the Indigenous Council of Pisté. Key terms: no vendor evictions; artisans retain a presence at the site; the CATVI market is operational; no new artisan entries will be permitted beyond the 2025 census. Industry estimates put daily losses at approximately 800,000 pesos during the closure. During the shutdown, Chichén Itzá briefly lost its title as Mexico's most visited archaeological site.
cases.outcome: RESOLVED June 1. Site open. Agreement reached preserving artisan presence at site.
cases.tags: Community objection, Indigenous rights, Demolition, Adaptive reuse

cases.title: Hungary cultural de-Orbánization — June status
cases.institution: Ludwig Museum and broader Hungarian cultural sector, Budapest
cases.description: STATUS CHECK (Monday June 8): As of today, Dr. Julia Fabényi remains listed as director of the Ludwig Museum — Museum of Contemporary Art in Budapest. The Ludwig Museum website still shows her as director. Zoltán Tarr has been confirmed as Minister of Social Relations and Culture under PM Péter Magyar since May 9, 2026. Magyar reorganized the culture ministry into the Ministry of Social Relations and Culture. No director resignations at major Orbán-era cultural institutions have been confirmed since the May 31 voluntary-resignation deadline passed. The government is reportedly in active negotiation or proceeding administratively to replace loyalist directors.
cases.outcome: Fabényi still listed as director. Tarr now minister. No forced removals confirmed yet.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis
outlets: Ludwig Museum website; Wikipedia (Hungary Minister of Culture)

cases.title: Kennedy Center name removal / compliance
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington DC
cases.description: Kennedy Center general counsel issued a June 4 memo instructing staff to immediately remove Trump's name from email signatures, letterhead, and documents, and to complete all signage, website, and brochure updates by June 12 deadline. As of June 8 (today), the website and YouTube page have been updated, but Trump's name remained on the exterior building facade. The Board stated it is 'complying with the court's order while evaluating all legal options.' No appeal has been filed as of the scan date.
cases.outcome: Compliance underway. June 12 is the court-ordered deadline for all physical signage. Board has not confirmed or denied appeal.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Censorship

cases.title: N/A (gallery operations — artist roster and staff reductions)
cases.institution: Pace Gallery (New York, London, Hong Kong, Seoul, Geneva, Palm Beach)
cases.description: Pace Gallery, one of the world's largest commercial art galleries ("mega gallery"), announced it is dropping approximately 50 artists from its roster and laying off approximately 50 staff members as a "model correction" in response to unsustainable growth and market contraction. CEO Marc Glimcher told ARTnews: "Galleries need a model correction." The cuts follow years of aggressive expansion by mega galleries including Pace, Hauser & Wirth, and David Zwirner. Pace had grown to represent more than 100 artists across global locations. The announcement comes in the context of a broader art market contraction: blue-chip sales remain strong (Lucian Freud nude estimated at $47M) but the contemporary primary market for younger and emerging artists has weakened significantly, and the gallery sector more broadly is under financial pressure. Tiwani Contemporary (London/Lagos, dedicated to African art) announced it was ceasing operations May 28. The New School layoffs (148-A) represent the educational-institutional counterpart of the same market contraction.
cases.outcome: Approximately 50 artists dropped, 50 staff laid off. Restructuring ongoing.
cases.tags: Art market, Labor dispute, Institutional crisis, Financialization

cases.title: Persepolis (2007 animated film) and graphic novel (2000); body of work
cases.institution: N/A (obituary / retrospective)
cases.description: Marjane Satrapi, Iranian-French cartoonist, graphic novelist, and filmmaker, died June 4, 2026, at age 56, reportedly in Brazil. Satrapi was best known for her autobiographical graphic novel Persepolis (2000–2003) and its 2007 animated film adaptation, which recounted her childhood in revolutionary Iran and exile in Europe. Persepolis was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature — making Satrapi the first woman nominated in that category. The work itself has been a notable target of censorship: Chicago Public Schools attempted to ban Persepolis in 2013; it remains on challenged and banned book lists in the US. Iran banned the film outright. The work is a foundational text for art-as-political-testimony and for understanding how state censorship shapes artistic biography. Satrapi's death during an active period of Iranian cultural conflict (entry 037, entry 065) gives her legacy particular resonance.
cases.outcome: Death confirmed June 4, 2026. Cause of death not publicly reported.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political art, Historical erasure, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Graduate arts programs nationwide — federal earnings test (gainful employment / earnings threshold rule)
cases.institution: The New School (New York City) — Parsons, New School for Social Research, College of Performing Arts; affected institutions nationwide
cases.description: UPDATE: The New School confirmed June 4 it is laying off 87 staff and faculty (approximately 15% of workforce) as part of a restructuring driven by a $48M deficit. 19 tenured or tenure-track faculty are among those laid off; 10 are tenured. The institution is consolidating from four colleges to two: liberal arts/social research combined; design/performing arts/media combined. Programs discontinued include the Master's in Arts Management and Entrepreneurship. The AAUP New School chapter called layoffs "a major gutting" and said some appear "politically motivated and retaliatory." The layoffs are structurally distinct from the earnings test (entry 148) but occur in the same environment: New School enrollment is down 20% from 2021 peak, and S&P downgraded its bond rating in February 2026. Separately, the earnings test proposed by the Department of Education (to be implemented July 1, 2026) would threaten federal loan access for programs where graduates earn less than peers with bachelor's degrees — Yale's MFA, NYU's Tisch programs, and many conservatories would fail the test.
cases.outcome: Layoffs proceeding June 2026. 87 total affected. Restructuring to two colleges. Arts Management program discontinued.
cases.tags: Labor dispute, Funding dispute, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: National Mall; National Parks nationwide (source of diverted funds)
cases.description: UPDATE: Washington Post investigation (published ~June 3) confirmed the Trump administration has diverted at least $90 million in National Park Service entrance fees — collected at parks including Yellowstone and Yosemite — to Washington DC construction projects. Of this: approximately $60M went to restoration of nine ornamental fountains around DC; $7M to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation (some sources say $13M including non-fee sources); $1.6M for a July 4 fireworks display (five times the standard budget). Federal law permits up to 20% of park entrance fee revenue to be used at non-fee-collecting sites, making this technically legal — but between December 2025 and March 2026, more than 90% of all NPS recreation-fee funds went to DC-based projects. National Parks Conservation Association: Interior Secretary Burgum "is determined to divert millions of dollars to projects that President Trump can see out his window." The Reflecting Pool's no-bid contract — awarded to a Virginia company at a reportedly inflated profit margin — was previously reported by NYT in late May. National park system carries $24B in deferred maintenance backlog.
cases.outcome: Diversion confirmed. $90M+ redirected. Renovation underway. No legal challenge to fee diversion. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Political interference, Landmark dispute, Design controversy, Architectural preservation

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed)
cases.institution: National Capital Planning Commission; Memorial Circle, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: NCPC voted June 4 — not final approval but a list of staff concerns to be addressed before final decision. NCPC chair Will Scharf (simultaneously Trump's White House staff secretary — ongoing conflict of interest) said "the project team has some homework to do," requesting additional illustrations of sightlines from multiple observer points and a formal legal justification for bypassing the Heights of Buildings Act. Staff raised issues about the arch's height, sightlines, legal authority, and environmental impacts. Scharf himself argued the Height Act may not apply to federal construction — a legal opinion not yet formalized. Preliminary surveys and ground testing of the Memorial Circle site reportedly began the week before. Separately, Trump told Politico construction will begin "sometime in the next two months" — targeting ahead of July 4. National park revenue: $90M in entrance fees from Yellowstone, Yosemite, and other parks have been diverted by the administration to Washington DC construction projects including a $76M Reflecting Pool renovation and $1.6M fireworks display.
cases.outcome: NCPC voted June 4 to approve list of concerns — not final approval. Administration must address sightline illustrations, legal authority question, environmental issues before final NCPC vote. Veterans lawsuit active. Trump says groundbreaking in "next two months." [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Political art, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian presidency, parliament; Magyar/Tisza government; cultural institutions broadly
cases.description: UPDATE: The May 31 voluntary-resignation deadline for Orbán-era institution heads passed without significant compliance. Most prominently, President Tamás Sulyok refused to resign, citing constitutional obligations and awaiting the Venice Commission's opinion. Magyar announced constitutional amendment proceedings to remove Sulyok. Also refusing to resign by the deadline: Constitutional Court President Péter Polt, Supreme Court (Curia) President Zs. András Varga. Magyar and Justice Minister Márta Görög met Sulyok June 1. As of June 5, constitutional confrontation ongoing. On the cultural institutions front: the government is proceeding separately under Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr (installed May 13). EU-Hungary agreement reached in Brussels on release of €16.4B in frozen EU funds — a significant structural leverage unlocked. No major cultural institution director changes (including Ludwig Museum director Júlia Fabényi) have been announced post-deadline. The cultural de-Orbánization appears to be proceeding more cautiously and separately from the political showdown.
cases.outcome: Sulyok refused. Constitutional confrontation ongoing. Cultural de-Orbánization proceeding cautiously under Tarr. Fabényi still in post at Ludwig. EU funds unlocked. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Funding dispute, Self-censorship

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale — 100+ artists legal action over Visitors' Lions ballot
cases.artist: Walid Raad, Laurie Anderson, Pio Abad, Alfredo Jaar, Yto Barrada, Rosana Paulino, Meriem Bennani, Cauleen Smith, and 100+ others
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Giardini and Arsenale
cases.description: UPDATE: On June 3, 2026, more than 100 artists participating in the 61st Venice Biennale threatened legal action against the Biennale Foundation for including their names on the Visitors' Lions ballot despite repeated formal requests to be withdrawn. The group — 67 artists from "In Minor Keys" and 39 national pavilion participants — first wrote to the Foundation on May 9 requesting removal; a second letter went May 20 after no acknowledgment. On May 14, the Foundation emailed ticketed visitors inviting them to vote on the Visitors' Lions, with withdrawn artists' names still on the ballot. The Foundation told the NYT that artists are included on the ballot but "these votes will not be considered" — a position the artists call contradictory and disrespectful. Signatories include Walid Raad, Laurie Anderson, Pio Abad, Alfredo Jaar, Yto Barrada, Rosana Paulino, Meriem Bennani, and Cauleen Smith. The legal threat is the first formal accountability mechanism directed at the Foundation itself rather than at specific national pavilions.
cases.outcome: Legal action threatened as of June 3. Foundation says votes for withdrawn artists "will not be considered" but has not removed names. Visitors' Lions vote ongoing through November 22 closing.
cases.tags: Geopolitics, Protest, Boycott, Institutional risk, Legal challenge

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott
cases.institution: Kennedy Center, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: Kennedy Center staff instructed June 4 to begin removing Trump's name per Judge Cooper's summary judgment order (May 29). Internal memo from KC general counsel set June 12 deadline to replace exterior/interior signage, email signatures, letterhead, furniture, and all materials bearing Trump-affiliated name. KC VP Roma Daravi: "We are complying with the court's order while evaluating all legal options to preserve this revitalization and recognize President Trump's leadership." Parties ordered to file joint status report on next steps by June 5 (today). KC Board has signaled appeal. Trump blasted Cooper, saying he should "be ashamed of himself." Trump appeared resigned to name removal, framing it as building badly needing repair. D.C. Preservation League parallel challenge denied by Cooper. Renovations may proceed; Board could revote on closure with proper process.
cases.outcome: Staff removing Trump name per June 12 court deadline. Board appealing. Closure injunction in effect. Joint status report due June 5.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Legal challenge, Censorship

cases.title: Proposed 250-foot triumphal arch, Memorial Circle, Washington DC
cases.artist: Harrison Design (architect Nicolas Leo Charbonneau); Commission of Fine Arts (Trump-stacked, approved); National Capital Planning Commission (Trump-stacked, vote Thursday June 5); Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA); military veterans (plaintiffs); historic preservationists
cases.institution: Memorial Circle / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: The Washington Post published the first 3D visualization of the arch's interior on June 3, 2026, based on blueprints by Harrison Design submitted to the NCPC in May 2026. Key new details: the arch would include an observation deck accessible by elevator or stairs, offering 360-degree views; a planned underground pedestrian tunnel was abandoned after Fine Arts Commission questions; the Commission of Fine Arts (Trump-stacked) has already voted to approve the design. The National Capital Planning Commission — also packed with Trump deputies — is scheduled to vote Thursday June 5 to potentially approve the design. The White House is not seeking congressional approval and has declined to provide cost estimates, saying a mix of taxpayer and private funds will be used. A Washington Post–ABC–Ipsos poll (April 2026) found 52% of Americans oppose the arch vs. 21% in favor. Military veterans have filed suit over the arch's impact on Arlington National Cemetery visiting experience. Rep. Beyer has warned of traffic disruption. A 60-foot Lady Liberty statue and other golden statuary would top the structure.
cases.outcome: NCPC vote scheduled Thursday June 5, 2026. Veterans lawsuit active. No congressional approval being sought. Cost undisclosed.
cases.tags: Political interference, Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Design controversy

cases.title: Graduate arts programs nationwide — federal earnings test (gainful employment / earnings threshold rule)
cases.artist: US Education Department; Senate education committee; Juilliard School; Yale MFA/music; Harvard museum studies; Bard Center for Curatorial Studies; Association of Independent Colleges of Art and Design; New York Film Academy
cases.institution: National (US Education Department)
cases.date_controversy: June 2, 2026 (NYT reporting); July 2026 (agency deadline to finalize)
cases.description: The US Education Department is finalizing guidelines for a revised earnings test that would penalize nearly half of all graduate programs in visual arts, music, and performance. Programs whose alumni fail to earn more than the median salary for 25–34-year-old bachelor's degree holders — measured four years after graduation — would lose federal loan eligibility if they fail the test twice in three years. Programs that lose eligibility cannot enroll students using federal loans, likely causing sharp enrollment decline and program closures. Preliminary analysis shows Yale's MFA and music master's programs would fail; Harvard's museum studies master's would fail; Juilliard's undergraduate and graduate music programs would fail. The test was inserted into last year's domestic policy bill on party lines. The Education Department has a July 2026 deadline to finalize guidelines, with possible implementation fall 2027. An estimated 644,000 students would be affected; arts master's students in failing programs currently hold approximately $311 million in federal loans. Previous threshold compared alumni earnings to median high school diploma holders — a substantially lower bar.
cases.outcome: Pending finalization; Education Department has July 2026 deadline. If finalized as written, takes effect fall 2027.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Censorship, Institutional crisis

cases.title: 61st Venice Biennale — Visitors' Lions awards / artist ballot dispute
cases.artist: 100+ artists in In Minor Keys (incl. Laurie Anderson, Alfredo Jaar, María Magdalena Campos-Pons, Walid Raad); Venice Biennale Foundation; Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy
cases.description: More than 100 artists participating in In Minor Keys have threatened legal action against the Venice Biennale Foundation after the Foundation included their names on the Visitors' Lions ballot despite their explicit prior requests for withdrawal. After the full jury resigned (April 30) and the Foundation replaced the Golden Lions with a public Visitors' Lions vote, over 50 artists immediately announced withdrawal from the new awards. When voting opened on May 14, artists discovered their names remained on the ballot. A letter to Foundation president Buttafuoco dated May 20 — signed by ~67 artists including Laurie Anderson, Alfredo Jaar, Campos-Pons, and Walid Raad — received no official reply. The Foundation's stated rationale: names were kept on the ballot to 'guarantee all visitors their freedom of expression,' and votes for refusing artists 'will not be taken into consideration.' Artists reject this as a violation of their rights. Legal action threatened via e-flux announcement published June 3. ARTnews and Artforum both reporting.
cases.outcome: Legal action threatened as of June 3, 2026. Foundation has not removed names from ballot. Visitors' Lions vote ongoing through November 22.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Censorship, Political interference, Geopolitics

cases.title: 61st Venice Biennale — In Minor Keys (critical reception)
cases.artist: Koyo Kouoh (posthumous curator); Naomi Beckwith; Beatrix Ruf; Diana Campbell Betancourt; Ekow Eshun; Francesco Manacorda; Tai Shani; Hammad Nasar
cases.institution: Venice, Italy
cases.description: The Art Newspaper published a critical roundup on June 3, 2026 gathering responses from seven prominent curators and art world figures on In Minor Keys and the 2026 Biennale. Consensus broadly positive on Kouoh's curatorial vision: praised for decentering Western art history, centering women artists of the African diaspora, and building a 'polyphony' rather than a single thesis. Recurring references: Édouard Glissant's 'Tout-Monde,' the healing metaphor of *rimarginare* (Manacorda), and the emotional charge of mourning Kouoh within the exhibition itself. Dissenting note from Tai Shani: the ANGA strike on May 8 was 'the largest in the Biennale's history' (27 pavilions closed or partially closed), yet was 'wilfully underreported.' Shani explicitly names the resignation of the International Jury, the mass protest, and the closure of the Israel pavilion as the defining features of this Biennale. The Russian pavilion remained shut to the general public for the entire run. The Visitors' Lions (replacing Golden Lions after jury mass resignation) will be announced November 22.
cases.outcome: Biennale runs through November 22, 2026. Visitors' Lions to be announced on closing day.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Geopolitics

cases.title: Hungarian cultural institutions — de-Orbánization process
cases.artist: Magyar government (PM Péter Magyar); Orbán-era institution heads; Hungarian Academy of Arts; Ludwig Museum; Hungarian National Gallery
cases.institution: Budapest, Hungary
cases.description: STATUS CHECK (Wednesday June 3): Hungary's new Tisza government is actively dismantling Orbán-era governance structures. Today, Modern Diplomacy reported that the Magyar government is moving to abolish the Sovereignty Protection Office, established in 2023 to monitor alleged foreign political interference — widely seen as a tool targeting civil society and opposition media. No specific cultural institution leadership changes confirmed as of today. The Hungarian National Gallery website shows active exhibition programming continuing under current directorship (Fabényi still appears to be in post — no resignation announcement identified in today's search). The voluntary-resignation deadline for Orbán-era cultural institution heads (May 31) apparently produced no major public exits. Cultural sector reform is proceeding through institutional restructuring (Sovereignty Protection Office abolition) rather than forced personnel changes so far.
cases.outcome: De-Orbánization ongoing. No major cultural institution director resignations confirmed post-deadline. Sovereignty Protection Office dissolution in progress.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship

cases.title: Seattle Art Museum Workers United (SAMWU)
cases.artist: SAM Workers United / AFSCME; SAM management (Director Scott Stulen)
cases.institution: Seattle Art Museum, Seattle, WA
cases.description: AFSCME confirmed on approximately May 26, 2026 that SAM Workers United has formally organized as a union. The May 27 voluntary-recognition deadline expired without public SAM management acknowledgment (logged as 096-G). Per AFSCME, the workers filed for an NLRB election as a parallel track, meaning the union drive will proceed through formal election process since voluntary recognition was not granted by the deadline.
cases.outcome: NLRB election petition filed. Formal election process underway. No voluntary recognition granted.

cases.title: Arts Council England (ACE) — institutional leadership
cases.artist: Dawn Airey CBE (incoming chair); Nicholas Serota (outgoing chair); Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy
cases.institution: Arts Council England, London, UK
cases.description: On June 2, 2026, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy appointed Dawn Airey CBE as the new chair of Arts Council England, succeeding Nicholas Serota. Airey — a media executive whose CV includes Channel 5 (CEO), Sky, ITV, Yahoo!, and Getty Images — will serve a four-year term beginning August 1, 2026. The appointment follows the Hodge Review's critical assessment of ACE's Let's Create strategy (already logged as 133). Serota, whose tenure was extended beyond its original end date to ensure stability during the review, will step down. Some arts sector observers noted Airey's media background is a departure from ACE's tradition of museum-sector leadership; critics (including Slipped Disc) expressed concern about her lack of classical arts background.
cases.outcome: Appointment confirmed June 2, 2026. Airey begins August 1, 2026.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Institutional crisis

cases.title: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
cases.artist: Kennedy Center Board (Trump appointees); Rep. Joyce Beatty; Trump administration; Judge Christopher Cooper
cases.institution: Washington, DC / US Court of Appeals DC Circuit (anticipated)
cases.description: Following Judge Cooper's May 29, 2026 ruling (logged as 005-AC) — which permanently blocked renaming and preliminarily blocked closure — the Kennedy Center Board announced it will appeal. Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi stated the Center 'will review the decision carefully' and expressed confidence the appeals court would 'uphold the Board's will to recognize President Trump's historic contributions.' President Trump blasted Cooper on Truth Social, calling the judge 'shameful.' Separately, Trump floated putting Congress back in control of the Center — potentially a strategic maneuver to reframe the dispute. The name-removal 14-day deadline (from May 29) runs to approximately June 12, 2026. As of June 3, no compliance action confirmed.
cases.outcome: Appeal signaled by Kennedy Center Board. June 12 compliance deadline for name removal approaching. Cooper injunction against closure remains in effect pending appeal.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Legal challenge

cases.title: Marine, Amsterdam (1874) by Claude Monet; portrait of Adolphe Monet (by Monet)
cases.artist: Wildenstein & Co.; Monet heirs; Larry Ellison (Oracle founder, current owner of Adolphe Monet portrait)
cases.institution: Rouen Judicial Court, France; New York
cases.description: ARTnews published a detailed account on June 2, 2026 of the May 28 Rouen jurisdictional ruling (already logged as 056-E), adding a significant new detail: the Adolphe Monet portrait at the center of the 2004 exchange has since been sold by Wildenstein & Co. to Oracle founder Larry Ellison. If the Rouen court ultimately voids the 2004 transaction on grounds of 'vitiated consent,' Wildenstein would be required to return the Adolphe Monet — but the painting is no longer in their possession. The article also notes that the Monet family's heir was 'very attached' to the Adolphe Monet painting and agreed to the exchange only to enable fair distribution of inheritance between children.
cases.outcome: Active litigation; jurisdiction confirmed May 28, 2026. Case proceeds on merits. Adolphe Monet portrait now owned by Larry Ellison — complicates any potential restitution.
cases.tags: Art market fraud, Market opacity, Legal challenge

cases.title: Artists' works held in storage at commercial galleries
cases.artist: UK artists generally; commercial gallery sector
cases.institution: United Kingdom
cases.description: The Art Newspaper published an analysis on May 29, 2026 documenting that artists in the UK are poorly protected when a commercial gallery goes bankrupt — works held in storage can be seized by administrators to satisfy gallery debts, even when the artist retains legal ownership. The article is prompted by ongoing gallery sector instability. UK insolvency law does not automatically protect consigned artwork from being treated as gallery assets in administration proceedings.
cases.outcome: Ongoing legal gap; no legislative remedy currently in place in UK.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Labor dispute, Art market fraud

cases.title: Liangzhu Archaeological Site; associated cultural heritage administration
cases.artist: Liu Bin (archaeologist, former director of Liangzhu Archaeological Research); unnamed third parties
cases.institution: Zhejiang Province, China
cases.description: Chinese archaeologist Liu Bin — known for his work at the UNESCO World Heritage Liangzhu site (inscribed 2019), one of China's most significant prehistoric archaeological discoveries — pleaded guilty on June 1, 2026 to corruption charges. He is accused of accepting approximately $700,000 in bribes and embezzling approximately $45,000. Liu had been a leading figure in Liangzhu excavations documenting a 5,000-year-old civilization that supported Chinese government claims of a continuous 5,000-year civilization.
cases.outcome: Guilty plea June 1, 2026. Sentencing pending.

Xinhua (implied)

cases.title: Colorado Artist Company Act (SB26-133)
cases.artist: Sen. Jeff Bridges (D) + bipartisan sponsors; Yancey Strickler (Kickstarter co-founder, originator)
cases.institution: Colorado State Capitol, Denver, CO
cases.description: Colorado Governor Jared Polis signed Senate Bill 133 into law on June 2, 2026, creating 'Artist Companies' (A-Corps) — a new type of LLC designed specifically for artists. The law guarantees artists at least 51% ownership stake in their creative enterprise, allows IP assignment as capital contribution, and provides a legal structure matching how artists actually operate. Colorado is the first US state to enact this structure. Implementation begins August 2026; conversion from other structures available by July 2027. Artists from any state or country can incorporate in Colorado.
cases.outcome: Signed into law June 2, 2026. Implementation from August 2026. First state in the US to enact this structure.
cases.tags: Copyright/ownership, Labor dispute, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Pattie Gonia brand/persona (drag queen/activist persona of Wyn Wiley)
cases.institution: US District Court, Central District of California
cases.description: Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia filed a federal trademark infringement lawsuit in January 2026 against drag queen and environmental activist Pattie Gonia (Wyn Wiley), alleging that Wiley's September 2025 trademark application for 'Pattie Gonia' — covering apparel, advocacy, and events — breached a 2022 agreement and infringed Patagonia's famous mark. Patagonia seeks $1 in damages plus attorneys' fees. Wiley publicly escalated on May 27, calling the suit 'a corporation trying to erase an activist,' and on June 2 publicly rejected Patagonia's proposed settlement. As of June 3, no resolution.
cases.outcome: Active litigation; Patagonia settlement proposal rejected by Wiley June 2, 2026. NLRB election petition filed as alternative track.
cases.tags: Copyright/ownership, Legal challenge, Defamation

cases.title: Yemeni cultural heritage sites (multiple)
cases.institution: Yemen (multiple sites)
cases.description: The Art Newspaper published a feature (June 1, 2026) on Yemen's cultural heritage challenges after years of civil war (2015–present). The feature notes renewed momentum in heritage preservation efforts, with women playing a key role. UNESCO and international heritage organizations have been involved. Yemen's UNESCO World Heritage Sites include the Old City of Sana'a, Old Walled City of Shibam, and the Historic Town of Zabid — all affected by conflict. Coverage notes progress despite ongoing instability under the Houthi/internationally recognized government divide.

cases.title: Untitled Matisse work (title not confirmed)

cases.description: Brazilian police announced on June 1, 2026 that they have identified the suspected architect of a Matisse theft at the Biblioteca Mário de Andrade (São Paulo's main public library). According to ARTnews/police, a voicemail on the suspect's phone contained an apparent admission — the suspect reportedly described himself as a specialist in rare books. The theft appears to have occurred in late 2025. The suspect has not been named in initial coverage.

cases.title: Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888) (watercolour) by Cézanne
cases.institution: Fondation Beyeler, Basel, Switzerland
cases.description: An heir has claimed that a Cézanne watercolour on loan to the Fondation Beyeler's Cézanne exhibition (which closed May 26, 2026) was lost to Nazi persecution. The 1888 work depicting Montagne Sainte-Victoire was on loan to the Beyeler show. The heir claims it belonged to Jewish businessman Gustav Schweitzer (or related party) and was lost due to persecution. The Art Newspaper (Catherine Hickley) reported the claim. Further details on the claimant, the current owner of the work, and the legal/restitution process not yet confirmed from initial report.
cases.outcome: Claim made against Cézanne watercolour on loan to Beyeler. Exhibition closed May 26. Restitution process status unknown.

cases.title: Chichén Itzá archaeological site
cases.institution: Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
cases.description: Chichén Itzá, Mexico's most visited archaeological site and UNESCO World Heritage Site / New Seven Wonders of the World, was closed for 13 days (approx. May 19–June 1, 2026) following protests by vendors and artisans over the construction of a new 16-hectare visitor complex called 'Catvi.' The conflict centered on the forced relocation of 600+ vendors who had sold within the site for decades. The site reopened June 1 after negotiations. INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History) administers the site. The dispute highlights tensions between tourism development — Chichén Itzá is the main income source for surrounding Mayan communities — and local economic livelihoods.
cases.outcome: Site reopened June 1 after 13-day closure. Vendors relocated to Catvi complex. Underlying tensions over commercialization vs. local livelihoods unresolved.
cases.tags: Indigenous rights, Community objection, Heritage site

cases.title: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center
cases.institution: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center, Chicago IL
cases.description: UPDATE: DuSable Museum President Perri Irmer filed a formal legal response to the whistleblower lawsuit (ARTnews, June 1, 2026). Irmer and the museum are accused of misusing funds intended for the education program. Details of the response not fully available from initial coverage — ARTnews article behind paywall. Case continues in litigation.
cases.outcome: Irmer has responded to whistleblower lawsuit in court filing. Litigation ongoing.

cases.title: Jewish Culture Month lecture on Ancient Israel and Judah
cases.artist: Paul Collins (BM keeper, Dept. of Middle East)
cases.institution: British Museum, London, UK
cases.description: UPDATE: Director Nicholas Cullinan issued a public statement on June 1 defending the May 28 postponement of the Jewish Culture Month lecture. Key points: (1) Up to 50% of registered attendees were suspected protesters; (2) The museum 'balanced competing obligations' — visitors' right to attend the lecture vs. the curator's right to deliver it vs. school groups in the building at the time; (3) The talk has been rescheduled to early June; (4) Cullinan wrote the answer 'cannot be to abandon difficult conversations' in 'uneasy times.' His statement distinguished 'postponement' from 'cancellation.' Historian Simon Schama had publicly called the original decision 'absolutely the wrong decision' on X.
cases.outcome: Lecture rescheduled to early June. Director issued public statement defending postponement decision.

cases.title: Comedian (2019)
cases.institution: Centre Pompidou-Metz, Metz, France
cases.description: UPDATE: The banana element of Cattelan's Comedian was stolen from the Centre Pompidou-Metz on May 30, 2026, during the exhibition 'Endless Sunday — Maurizio Cattelan and the Centre Pompidou Collection' (runs until January 25, 2027). A museum security guard discovered the disappearance of the 'perishable element.' The banana was quickly replaced and the work restored. The museum filed a complaint with authorities; perpetrators unknown. The museum's statement distinguished between the perishable element and the work's value: 'The value of the work lies in its certificate of authenticity and the protocol governing its presentation rather than in its perishable element.' This is the latest in a series of banana-removal incidents (Justin Sun purchased a banana edition in 2024 for $6.2M and ate it at Art Basel Hong Kong).
cases.outcome: Banana replaced; complaint filed; perpetrators unknown.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Security failure

cases.title: Seattle Art Museum Workers United organizing campaign
cases.institution: Seattle Art Museum, Seattle WA
cases.description: POST-DEADLINE STATUS: The May 27 voluntary recognition deadline expired. No public announcement of voluntary recognition from SAM management confirmed as of June 2. Per prior entries (096-E/F), management declined to voluntarily recognize by deadline. Workers had pre-filed an NLRB petition (case listed as open, proposed unit of 138 employees covering SAM downtown, Seattle Asian Art Museum, and Olympic Sculpture Park; excludes security, supervisors, casuals). The NLRB election process is now the likely path forward. AFSCME/WFSE confirmed May 26 that workers 'formed union with AFSCME' per AFSCME website — language suggests the organizing is proceeding under the NLRB petition track. Background: SAM security workers (SAM VSO Union) organized separately in 2022 and won their first contract after a 12-day strike in 2024.
cases.outcome: Voluntary recognition deadline expired without recognition. NLRB petition filed and open. NLRB election process underway.
cases.tags: Labor dispute, Institutional crisis

cases.title: 'Adolphe Monet lisant dans un jardin' (1867) and related exchange works
cases.institution: Tribunal judiciaire de Rouen, France
cases.description: JURISDICTIONAL RULING: The Rouen court ruled on May 28–29, 2026 that it has jurisdiction over the case — the trial will be held in France, not the United States. Wildenstein & Co. had argued for US jurisdiction; Monet heirs' counsel argued France (the heirs' domicile at time of transaction, Mont-Saint-Aignan, near Rouen). The ruling aligns with EU consumer contract law: the trial must be held at the consumer's domicile. Monet heirs' lawyer: 'At each new stage we win. Now it would be good for the gallery to acknowledge its error.' The ruling came as the Normandie Impressionniste 2026 festival opened. The merits of the 'vitiated consent' claim — whether Monet heirs were misled about the condition of Marine, Amsterdam (1874) — have not yet been decided.
cases.outcome: Rouen court has jurisdiction. Merits trial on 'vitiated consent' claim still pending.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Art market fraud, Market opacity, Authenticity

cases.title: Wyland Whaling Wall 82 / 'Ocean Life' (1999)
cases.institution: 505 N. Akard St., Downtown Dallas, TX
cases.description: LAWSUIT FILED: Wyland formally filed a $25 million federal lawsuit on June 1, 2026 (CBS Texas). Defendants: FIFA, FIFA (Americas) Inc., FWC2026 US Inc., 3PZ Property Company LLC, and Slate Asset Management. The suit seeks to vindicate Wyland's rights under VARA (Visual Artists Rights Act), alleging the 17,000-square-foot mural was destroyed without consent, consultation, or advance notice. The lawsuit also alleges the mural was destroyed without proper notice in violation of VARA's written-waiver requirement. Wyland stated he will donate any proceeds to local charities. The city of Dallas claimed it had notified Wyland prior to work; Wyland called the claim 'a lie with a capital L.' As of CBS Texas report (June 1), the North Texas FIFA World Cup Organizing Committee had not publicly committed to moving forward with the planned replacement mural.
cases.outcome: $25M VARA lawsuit filed June 1, 2026. Case active in federal court.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Removal, Community objection, Political art

cases.title: Hungarian cultural institutions / Orbán-era appointments
cases.institution: Budapest, Hungary
cases.description: DEADLINE OUTCOME: The May 31 voluntary-resignation deadline set by PM Péter Magyar expired with President Tamás Sulyok and Prosecutor General Gábor Bálint Nagy both refusing to resign. Sulyok stated he would await the Venice Commission's opinion and insisted the matter must be handled constitutionally. Magyar announced he and Justice Minister Márta Görög would visit Sulyok at 8am Monday (June 1) to press the issue. The confrontation frames a broader constitutional dispute: the new government argues it holds a mandate to dismantle the Orbán patronage network; Sulyok argues constitutional offices cannot be removed on political grounds. No major cultural institution director changes confirmed as of June 2. Note: the May 31 deadline applied primarily to judicial/executive officials, not cultural directors specifically — the cultural de-Orbánization process under new Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr (in office since May 9) is slower and distinct.
cases.outcome: Sulyok refused to resign. Constitutional confrontation ongoing. Magyar/Görög meeting with Sulyok June 1. Cultural de-Orbánization proceeding separately under Tarr.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis

cases.title: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington DC
cases.description: RULING ISSUED: Judge Christopher Cooper (USDC for DC) issued a 94-page summary judgment on May 29 (Kennedy's birthday). (1) PERMANENT injunction halting the renaming: the board lacked authority to rename the KC 'Trump Kennedy Center'; only Congress can change the name. Admin must remove all Trump signage, website references, and withdraw trademark applications within 14 days (by June 12). (2) PRELIMINARY injunction halting closure and programming wind-down through July 4/6. Cooper blocked the board's March 16 decision to close the doors on July 6, noting the board overstepped statutory authority. He carved out an exception: the $257M congressional repair appropriation for necessary maintenance is not enjoined. (3) Cooper denied a second preliminary injunction on the DC Preservation League's separate suit and ordered parties to file joint status report by June 5. Trump responded on Truth Social calling Cooper 'a Barack Hussein Obama Judge.' Rep. Beatty: 'The Kennedy Center belongs to the American people, not to Donald Trump.'
cases.outcome: Permanent injunction issued re: naming; preliminary injunction halting closure. Name removal deadline June 12. Joint status report due June 5. Trump signaled he is 'washing his hands' of the institution. Separate DC Preservation League suit continues.
cases.tags: Political interference, Legal challenge, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Comedian (2019) — banana duct-taped to the wall
cases.institution: Centre Pompidou-Metz, Metz, France (exhibition “Endless Sunday — Maurizio Cattelan and the Centre Pompidou Collection,” to Jan 25, 2027)
cases.description: Maurizio Cattelan’s Comedian (2019) — a banana duct-taped to the wall — was reported “stolen” from the Centre Pompidou-Metz on May 30, 2026 when a security guard noticed the “perishable element” (the banana) was missing from the exhibition “Endless Sunday — Maurizio Cattelan and the Centre Pompidou Collection” (on view to Jan 25, 2027). The museum replaced the banana and restored the work “as quickly as possible,” and filed a complaint with authorities; the perpetrators remain unknown. The museum emphasized that the work’s value resides in its certificate of authenticity and the protocol governing its presentation — not in the perishable banana — and that no irreversible damage occurred. The banana has previously been eaten by a visitor at the same museum (2025), by performance artist David Datuna at Art Basel Miami Beach (2019), and by a student at the Leeum Museum, Seoul (2023). Comedian sold at Sotheby’s in November 2024 to crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun for $6.2m.
cases.outcome: Banana reported stolen May 30; immediately replaced and work restored. Complaint filed with authorities; perpetrators unknown. No irreversible damage per the work’s presentation protocol.
cases.tags: Theft, Security failure, Authenticity, Financialization

cases.title: “Ancient Israel and Judah in the British Museum” lecture (Jewish Culture Month) — director’s public response
cases.artist: N/A (lecturer: Paul Collins, keeper, Dept. of the Middle East)
cases.institution: British Museum, Bloomsbury, London
cases.description: Following the British Museum’s postponement of a May 28 Jewish Culture Month lunchtime lecture on the kingdoms of Israel and Judah (led by Paul Collins, keeper of the Department of the Middle East) over fears of disruption — the museum estimated up to 50% of registered attendees were suspected protesters — director Nicholas Cullinan publicly defended the decision in a June 1 statement, framing it as “stewardship,” not censorship, and stressing the talk was postponed, not cancelled, and rescheduled for early June. He argued the museum faced competing obligations (thousands of visitors and school groups in the building, the curator’s right to speak without organized attempts to silence him) and warned against interpreting “every operational decision through the lens of ideology.” The original postponement was criticized by commentators including historian Simon Schama, who called it “absolutely the wrong decision.” Jewish Culture Month (Board of Deputies of British Jews; 100+ events from May 16) also involves the Tate, V&A and Museum of the Home.
cases.outcome: Lecture postponed May 28 over disruption fears; rescheduled for early June (details to be posted). Director Cullinan defended the move as “stewardship, not censorship” (June 1). Debate ongoing over protest, intimidation and free expression in UK cultural institutions.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Religious objection, Geopolitics, Community objection

cases.title: “Guadalajara es Mundialista” mural (2026 FIFA World Cup commemorative mural)
cases.institution: Periférico y Calzada Independencia, Guadalajara, Jalisco
cases.description: On May 23, 2026, three young people were detained for spray-painting graffiti over the “Guadalajara es Mundialista” mural, one of the city’s prominent works commemorating the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Rather than a conventional sanction, authorities ordered the three to repair the damage through community and artistic work (restorative justice).
cases.outcome: Three detained May 23; ordered to repair the mural via community/artistic work (restorative justice) rather than punitive sanction.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation

cases.title: “Mural de la memoria de las víctimas” / falsos positivos memorial mural (“7837 almas”)
cases.artist: Young community muralists (names not reported); accompanied by Rep. Alfredo Mondragón
cases.institution: Carrera 1ª between calles 25–26, under the old railway bridges (Puerto Rellena / Puerto Resistencia sector), Cali
cases.description: On May 24, 2026, a group of young people painted a memory mural in Cali honoring victims of “falsos positivos” (civilians killed by the military and falsely presented as combat deaths), bearing the figure “7837 almas” (the JEP’s count of victims). Mayor Alejandro Eder ordered police to the site to stop the intervention; officers confiscated the painters’ paint and reportedly attempted to detain one of them. The mural was subsequently erased. Pacto Histórico congressman Alfredo Mondragón, who accompanied the artists, framed it as an exercise in historical memory and denounced the police action; on-site arguments erupted over the JEP, Iván Cepeda and Álvaro Uribe.
cases.outcome: Mural painted May 24; police intervention same day; mural erased. No charges reported. Political dispute ongoing (mayor’s office vs. Pacto Histórico).
cases.tags: Censorship, Removal, Political art, Historical erasure, Resistance

cases.title: N/A (institutional / directorship of the Centro Galego de Arte Contemporánea)
cases.institution: Centro Galego de Arte Contemporánea (CGAC), Santiago de Compostela; Xunta de Galicia
cases.description: On May 20, 2026 the Xunta de Galicia (PP-led regional government) announced the appointment of Eva López Tarrío — a secondary-school art teacher (catedrática de instituto) in Vigo and practicing artist, with a PhD in Fine Arts but no significant curatorial or international museum experience — as director of the CGAC in Santiago de Compostela, replacing Santiago Olmo, who had led the institution for 11 years and had publicly clashed with the regional Dirección Xeral de Cultura. The cultural sector denounced the selection as a “dedazo” (politically directed appointment) and “injerencia política,” criticizing an opaque, closed process whose terms were modified to open the post to any civil servant (funcionario), allegedly to “tailor” the position. An open letter by the Asociación Cultural Vegliota gathered 1,300+ signatures; three CGAC advisory-board members (Silvia García, Agar Ledo, Cecilia Pereira) had already resigned on April 17 in protest. On May 22 protesters disrupted an exhibition opening attended by culture councillor José López Campos with “SOS CGAC” signs and chants (“El CGAC no se vende, el CGAC no se compra”).
cases.outcome: Appointment announced May 20, pending formal publication in the Diario Oficial de Galicia. Sector in open revolt; 1,300+ signatories; advisory-board resignations; May 22 protest. López Tarrío to assume post; Xunta defending the decision. Unresolved.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Resistance

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions (May 31 deadline outcome)
cases.institution: Hungarian cultural institutions; Office of the President; Constitutional Court (Budapest)
cases.description: The May 31, 2026 voluntary-resignation deadline set by PM Péter Magyar’s Tisza government — applied to Orbán-era appointees including cultural-institution heads as well as the President and the heads of other key institutions such as the Constitutional Court — passed without voluntary resignations from the highest-profile targets. President Tamás Sulyok publicly refused to step down, saying he would await the Venice Commission’s opinion and that constitutional offices cannot be removed on political grounds. Magyar announced he and Justice Minister Márta Görög would meet Sulyok on the morning of June 1. Tisza has begun advancing constitutional-amendment proposals (including a retroactive eight-year PM term limit aimed at barring Orbán’s return), signaling a shift toward formal/constitutional removal mechanisms.
cases.outcome: Deadline passed May 31 without voluntary resignations from the most prominent Orbán-era officeholders; President Sulyok refused (citing Venice Commission/constitution). Magyar–Görög meeting Sulyok June 1. De-Orbánization shifting to constitutional-removal mechanisms. No confirmed cultural-institution-director resignations reported as of this scan.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC
cases.description: NYT May 29 investigative piece (Gamio, Fahrenthold, Joselow) provides the most detailed technical account to date of the renovation's underlying problems and the scope of what the current work is — and is not — fixing. Key findings: (1) The expansion joint sealing by Atlantic Industrial Coatings twice failed pressure tests in mid-May; on May 29, Interior Secretary Burgum posted that a new solution had been developed with Army Corps of Engineers consultation and the joints would be sealed within days. (2) The fundamental problem — broken 12-inch supply/return pipes under the surrounding parkland — is NOT being addressed by the current contract. Trump's first term identified pipe replacement as the only real fix; the second term's contract deferred this to 'fall,' with no details given. (3) The blue-tinted sealant being applied to the pool's concrete slabs was not listed in prior Park Service analyses as a solution to the leakage problem; water leaks primarily between slabs, not through them. (4) The no-bid contract to Virginia company Atlantic Industrial Coatings covers expansion joint sealing and an upgraded ozone system ($1.7M); the $35M Obama-era renovation also failed to solve algae and leaks. (5) Former NPS director: 'It's like pouring water into a colander.' (6) If pipes aren't fixed, algae could return and obscure the newly blue-coated floor.
cases.outcome: Gap-sealing approach failed two mid-May tests; Burgum announced May 29 that Army Corps-consulted solution passed. Expansion joint sealing nearing completion. Pipe replacement (fundamental problem) deferred to fall with no contract details. TCLF lawsuit pending.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Design controversy, Funding dispute, Political interference

cases.title: San José galleon (1708) and its cargo (gold, silver, emeralds)
cases.institution: Seabed, Cartagena coast, Colombia; ICANH (Colombian Institute of Anthropology and History)
cases.description: The San José, a Spanish galleon sunk in 1708 by the British carrying gold, silver, and emeralds (estimated value $10-20B+), was discovered by Colombia in 2015 and has been contested ever since. In May 2026, the oversight group VNPCS issued an open letter to Colombia's attorney general alleging looting and unauthorized interventions at the site in 2016 and 2022, and claiming state-secret coordinates had been disclosed. The allegations build on a 2020 comparative imagery analysis by archaeologist Rodrigo Pacheco Ruiz showing sediment disturbances between 2015 and 2016 dives. A November 2025 retrieval of a cannon, porcelain cup, and three coins by underwater robotics drew criticism for lack of scientific justification. ICANH denied looting. Multiple ongoing legal disputes: Sea Search Armada (US salvage company) seeks $10B through Hague Permanent Court of Arbitration, claiming 50% of cargo; Spain claims the galleon as a warship; Colombia's Wayuu Indigenous community claims cultural heritage rights. The galleon was designated a protected archaeological area in 2024, banning private involvement.
cases.outcome: Site designated protected archaeological area 2024. November 2025 partial retrieval conducted. Looting allegations renewed May 2026. PCA arbitration pending. No resolution.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Conservation, Geopolitics, Indigenous rights, Art market, Legal challenge, Colonial legacy

cases.title: Pattie Gonia drag persona and merchandise / trademark application
cases.institution: US Federal Court, Los Angeles
cases.description: The outdoor clothing brand Patagonia sued drag queen and LGBTQ+/environmental activist Pattie Gonia (Oregon-based Wyn Wiley, 1.8M Instagram followers) in January 2026 for trademark infringement, after she filed a trademark application for her parody name 'Pattie Gonia' covering merchandise and motivational speaking. Patagonia claimed she violated a prior agreement by commercializing the name, and likened the filing to actual copycat brands 'Fratagonia' and 'Petagonia.' Pattie Gonia publicly responded in late May 2026, denying any formal agreement existed beyond a one-time project collaboration, and framing her persona as performance art with a long history of parody. Patagonia is seeking $1 plus attorneys' fees, estimated by Pattie Gonia at ~$1 million. She has raised nearly $5 million for nonprofits expanding outdoor access for LGBTQ+ and BIPOC communities. Activists are calling for a brand boycott. Pattie Gonia's merchandise (since removed from her website) does not appear to visually resemble Patagonia's logo; the company's lawsuit cited social media posts where she held fan art mimicking the logo.
cases.outcome: Lawsuit filed January 2026. Pattie Gonia went public May 2026. Boycott campaign active. No ruling yet.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Copyright/ownership, LGBTQ+, Defamation, Community objection

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions

cases.title: Caesar Rodney equestrian monument (1922, James Edward Kelly) + 12 soldier statues, Freedom Plaza
cases.artist: Original Rodney statue by James Edward Kelly (1922); new installation by NPS / Dept. of the Interior
cases.institution: Freedom Plaza, Washington DC; National Park Service / Department of the Interior
cases.description: ARTnews detail (reported May 27, 2026) on the May 22 Freedom Plaza installation: the Trump administration erected 13 statues, including an equestrian monument to Revolutionary War figure and enslaver Caesar Rodney (who owned 200 enslaved people at his Byfield plantation) that had been removed from Rodney Square in Wilmington, Delaware, in June 2020 during the Black Lives Matter movement.
