cases.title: National Museum of Sudan and 20+ additional museums — UNESCO implementation update
cases.institution: National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums (NCAM); Kerma, Gebel Barkal, Red Sea, El Damer, Sennar museums; Sudan
cases.description: Marking International Museum Day (May 18, 2026), UNESCO detailed its emergency response to Sudan's heritage crisis since the 2023 war. Through the Heritage Emergency Fund and in coordination with NCAM, UNESCO completed damage and risk assessments of five priority museums (Kerma, Gebel Barkal, Red Sea, El Damer, Sennar), created digital inventories of 1,737 artefacts to strengthen protection against trafficking, and securely relocated El Damer Museum's collections to Kerma. Specialized anti-trafficking training reached 500 heritage professionals, customs officials, judiciary, and law enforcement. UNESCO reported 20+ museums looted or damaged. A separate market analysis (Benchmark Journal, May 10) cited Sudan's antiquities authority estimating roughly $150 million in looted treasures moving through cross-border smuggling and online resale.
cases.outcome: Implementation of the April 8-9 consultation recommendations underway: five priority museums assessed, 1,737 artefacts digitally inventoried, El Damer collection relocated to Kerma, 500 professionals trained. National Museum recovery continues; thousands still missing; trafficking ongoing.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Geopolitics, Historical erasure, Security failure, Repatriation

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott — Cooper summary-judgment ruling
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington DC; U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia
cases.description: On May 29, 2026, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued a 94-page summary-judgment ruling in Rep. Joyce Beatty's lawsuit. He held the Board overstepped its statutory authority by unilaterally renaming the Center after Trump — 'Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it' — and ordered Trump's name removed from the facade, signage, and websites within two weeks. He temporarily blocked the planned two-year closure for renovations (tied to the post-July 4 shutdown), finding the Board had not adequately weighed the statutory duty to maintain continuous programming, though renovations may proceed and the Board could later revote on closure with proper process. He ruled the Board unlawfully stripped Beatty of her ex officio voting rights and ordered them restored. In a separate decision the same day, Cooper denied a parallel challenge by the D.C. Preservation League. Trump signaled he would back down and transfer control of the Center to Congress.
cases.outcome: Core claims resolved May 29, 2026: renaming blocked, name/signage to be removed within two weeks, two-year closure blocked, Beatty's voting rights restored; D.C. Preservation League challenge denied. Appeal possible; Board may revote on closure with proper process. Trump signaled transfer of control to Congress.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Legal challenge, Institutional crisis, Funding dispute

cases.title: Ancient Levant and Egypt gallery displays; "Ancient Israel and Judah in the British Museum" lecture (Jewish Culture Month)
cases.institution: British Museum, Bloomsbury, London
cases.description: The British Museum became the site of two overlapping controversies in 2026 over the ancient Levant and competing pressures around Palestine and Israel. (1) LABEL REMOVAL (February 2026): Following a letter from UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI), the museum removed references to "Palestine" from its ancient Middle East displays and changed "Palestinian descent" to "Canaanite descent" in multiple gallery panels, including Gallery 57 and the Egypt galleries. The museum stated the term Palestine was "in some circumstances no longer meaningful" and that "audience testing" had driven the change. Former curators said the changes were driven by scholarship refreshes; UKLFI said it had simply raised accuracy concerns. More than 200 academics, artists, and cultural figures — including musician Brian Eno, historian William Dalrymple, and former Central Saint Martins head Jeremy Till — signed an open letter condemning the changes as "historical revision and potential erasure," linking them to the museum's broader "complicity in Israel's genocide." Protesters demonstrated outside the museum in February 2026. The Art Newspaper reported that museum sources said the changes preceded UKLFI's letter and were not driven by the complaint. (2) LECTURE POSTPONEMENT (May 28, 2026): A sold-out Jewish Culture Month lecture titled "Ancient Israel and Judah in the British Museum" — scheduled for May 28 — was postponed after the museum learned that "a significant proportion of registered attendees were individuals intending to deliberately disrupt the event." Jewish Artists for Palestine were reportedly among those registered. The Board of Deputies of British Jews called the postponement "highly regrettable." Museum chairman George Osborne shared the museum's statement on X. Lord Wolfson (Conservative) said publicly-funded institutions should not "fold to pressure." The museum rescheduled the event "early next month." Jewish Culture Month (May 16 – June 15) was created by the Board of Deputies amid rising antisemitism in Britain since October 7, 2023.
cases.outcome: Gallery label changes in effect since February 2026; 200+ signatory open letter (March 10). Jewish Culture Month lecture on Ancient Israel and Judah postponed May 28 over disruption fears (up to 50% of registrants suspected protesters); director Nicholas Cullinan publicly defended the move as “stewardship, not censorship” (June 1) and rescheduled it for early June. Free-expression debate ongoing. (See 131-A.)
cases.tags: Censorship, Historical erasure, Geopolitics, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Community objection, Protest art

cases.title: N/A (gallery closure)
cases.institution: Tiwani Contemporary, Cork Street, Mayfair, London; and Lagos, Nigeria
cases.description: Tiwani Contemporary, the pioneering London- and Lagos-based gallery dedicated to art from Africa and its diaspora, announced closure on May 28, 2026, after 15 years. Founded in Fitzrovia in 2011 by Greek-Cypriot Maria Varnava — who grew up in Lagos and was guided by the late Nigerian curator Bisi Silva — the gallery helped launch careers of Joy Labinjo, Michaela Yearwood-Dan, Emma Prempeh, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Simone Leigh, Kapwani Kiwanga, and others. In 2022 it opened a Lagos outpost; in 2023 it moved to larger Mayfair premises. Director attributed closure to "wider market uncertainties" and rising operational costs: the commercial model was "no longer sustainable." Tiwani is the second major London gallery to close in the past year, after Stephen Friedman Gallery (February 2026). The gallery had been due to take part in Liste Basel next month but withdrew its application. Artists on its roster at time of closure include Dawit L. Petros (2026 Toronto Biennial) and Theo Eshetu (in the Koyo Kouoh-curated Venice Biennale main exhibition).
cases.outcome: Closed May 28, 2026. London gallery shuttered; Lagos restructuring. Artists seeking new representation.
cases.tags: Art market, Institutional crisis, Funding dispute

cases.title: England national museums foreign visitor admission fee proposal — museum opposition documented
cases.institution: UK national museums (British Museum, National Gallery, Natural History Museum, V&A, etc.); UK government / DCMS
cases.description: The Art Newspaper (May 22) documented that most major English museums oppose the government's proposal to charge international visitors admission fees, which is currently under consultation. The Cultural Policy Unit (an independent think tank led by former Art Newspaper editor Alison Cole) published a 2025 report arguing such charges would be "logistically complex as well as ideologically at odds with the global collections that the UK has accumulated" — a direct reference to colonial acquisition. A "two-tier entry system would fundamentally undermine our commitment to universal access," according to museum opponents. The UK government subsidy for national museums declined 18% between 2010 and 2023; charging overseas visitors has been floated since 2024. Proposed fees range from £15–£20 per visit; the policy is not yet in force. Government update expected before end of 2026. Entry fees would require a digital ID system to distinguish citizens from international visitors. The restitution connection is significant: countries involved in active repatriation claims (Greece/Parthenon Marbles, Nigeria/Benin Bronzes) would be charged to view their own cultural property.
cases.outcome: Policy under consultation. Most museums oppose. Government response expected before end of 2026. Not yet in force. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Repatriation, Ethical museum

Judge Cooper's ruling on the name change itself remains pending — Cooper previously ruled on the Beatty participation issue but has deferred the name change question. cases.title: Louvre Crown Jewels Heist / Institutional Crisis — film adaptation announced

cases.description: French filmmaker Romain Gavras (Athena, Sacrifice) announced he will direct a feature film adaptation of the Louvre crown jewels heist, based on the investigative book Main basse sur le Louvre (A Grab at the Louvre, Flammarion, May 27, 2026), co-written by journalists from Le Parisien, Le Monde, and Paris Match. cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, National Mall, Washington DC; NYT investigation
cases.description: NYT investigation (May 27) reveals new details about the no-bid Reflecting Pool contract: (1) A Park Service contracting specialist analysis found Atlantic Industrial Coatings charged an excessive 20% profit margin — vs. the typical 6–12% on federal construction contracts — adding at least $850,000 to typical contract cost. The analysis called the combined 20% overhead and 20% profit 'excessive.' A higher-up Park Service official nonetheless approved the full $13.1 million bid, reasoning the contractor deserved it for accepting a difficult job on a tight deadline. (2) The contractor also failed at least two attempts to seal the gaps between the pool's concrete slabs — a central purpose of the repair. Its original foam-plug approach failed testing; it had to chisel out the material and start again. Interior has declined to say if a working solution has since been found. (3) The government has used a rarely-applied 'letter contract' mechanism — contractor starts work first, haggles over price later — designed for genuine emergencies. Contracting experts call this mechanism an abuse when used to avoid competition. (4) National park entrance fees ($7 million) and 'senior pass' sales are being used to partly fund the project. (5) Trump defended spending at a Cabinet meeting, falsely claiming Obama administration spent 'hundreds of millions' trying to fix the pool.
cases.outcome: Renovation underway. Cost: $13.1M. Contractor charged excessive margins. Gap-sealing approach failed twice; status unclear. TCLF lawsuit pending (Judge Nichols ruling expected). [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Design controversy, Political interference

cases.title: Proposed $250 Federal Reserve note featuring Trump portrait; $100 bills bearing Trump signature (currently printing)
cases.artist: Iain Alexander (British painter, mock-up designer); Bureau of Engraving and Printing (institutional)
cases.institution: Bureau of Engraving and Printing, Washington DC; US Treasury
cases.description: Trump administration political appointees at the Treasury Department — US Treasurer Brandon Beach and senior adviser Mike Brown — repeatedly pressured staff at the Bureau of Engraving and Printing to design a $250 bill featuring Trump's portrait. Bureau director Patricia 'Patty' Solimene, a 24-year Army veteran and the first female director of the bureau, consistently resisted the effort, explaining that no living person had appeared on US currency since 1866 (when it was outlawed) and that currency typically takes six to eight years to produce. Beach provided bureau staff with mock-up designs in August and September 2025, including one designed by British painter Iain Alexander (who calls himself Trump's 'favorite British artist'). Trump had personally given feedback on the design, endorsing American flag colors and a 250th anniversary logo. Solimene was abruptly reassigned on April 27, 2026 with no explanation. In her farewell email she wrote: 'The buck stopped here.' Brown — the political appointee who had pushed the project — was named acting director. Separately: $100 bills bearing Trump's signature are currently being printed at the bureau's downtown Washington facility, the first time in American history a sitting president's signature has appeared on currency. A bill authorizing the $250 note was introduced in Congress by Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC) in February 2025 but has not received a hearing. Treasury stated it is conducting 'appropriate planning and due diligence.'
cases.outcome: $250 bill not yet produced (requires congressional authorization). Trump signature $100 bills currently being printed. Bureau director reassigned after resisting. Brown (political appointee) now acting director.
cases.tags: Political interference, Design controversy, Historical erasure, Political art, Funding dispute

cases.title: N/A (institutional / UAW Local 2110 second contract negotiations)
cases.institution: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York City
cases.description: Members of UAW Local 2110 at the Whitney Museum of American Art rallied outside the museum's annual fundraising gala on May 19, 2026, distributing flyers, pins and signs as they negotiate their second labor contract. The first contract, ratified March 2023 after 16 months of bargaining, expires next month. The union represents approximately 185 workers across education, curatorial, visitor services, conservation and administrative departments. Whitney management placed police barricades along the museum's Gansevoort Street frontage during the gala, which organizers characterized as antagonistic but did not prevent worker-patron engagement. The museum stated it was 'committed to arriving at a fair, reasonable contract that respects the needs of all parties.' The first contract raised minimum hourly wages from $17 to $22 (retroactive to January 2023), with increases to $24 by June 2025, and provided an average 15% compensation increase plus $1,000 signing bonuses.

cases.title: National Scrollathon (2026)
cases.institution: The Reach, Kennedy Center, Washington DC
cases.description: Steven and William Ladd's participatory textile installation National Scrollathon opens May 29 at the Reach (the Kennedy Center's newer extension), representing 10,000 Americans who created individual scrolls with the artists in all 50 states, five territories and DC. The work features freestanding pillars labeled by state — one side holds the rolled fabric scrolls, the other side photos of participants. The brothers visited every state collecting 25–35 participants per session, who rolled fabric trimmings into scrolls and added messages or symbols. The exhibition was originally scheduled through September 7, but will now close June 29 due to the Kennedy Center's July 6 (operational date) closure — a run cut from over three months to just five weeks. The brothers declined to join the artist boycott despite Trump's takeover, having signed a contract with the Kennedy Center in 2017 for a 250th anniversary commission. Their framing: 'Walking away from the venue we told 10,000 people they would be showing their work at would just be wrong.'
cases.outcome: Exhibition opens May 29. Run truncated from September 7 to June 29 due to July 6 closure.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Labor dispute

cases.title: National Art Museum of Ukraine, National Chornobyl Museum, Yaroslav Mudryi National Library, Kyiv Opera Theatre (and additional cultural sites)
cases.institution: Kyiv, Ukraine (multiple cultural institutions)
cases.description: Russia's massive missile and drone barrage on Ukraine on May 24, 2026 — one of the largest since the February 2022 full-scale invasion — directly hit multiple cultural institutions in Kyiv. Ukraine's culture ministry confirmed damage to: the National Art Museum of Ukraine (heavy building damage; art reported safe); the National Chornobyl Museum (worst damage — approximately 40% of exhibition hall exhibits destroyed, including the entire room containing saved cultural heritage from the Polissia region); the Yaroslav Mudryi National Library of Ukraine; and the Kyiv Opera Theatre. Ukrainian House, site of a current exhibition marking the 40th anniversary of the Chornobyl disaster, was also damaged but reopened within two days with no damage to the exhibition. Russia used 600 drones and 90 missiles in the attack including the hypersonic Oreshnik; approximately 100 people were injured and four killed across Ukraine, with 30 residential buildings damaged in Kyiv alone. Ukraine's culture minister Tetyana Berezhna reported that Russia had by this date destroyed or damaged 1,783 cultural heritage monuments and 2,540 objects of cultural infrastructure in Ukraine since 2022.
cases.outcome: National Chornobyl Museum severely damaged (~40% of exhibits destroyed). National Art Museum building heavily damaged; art safe. Library and theatre damaged. Damage assessment ongoing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: full damage inventory; restoration funding; whether any works lost permanently]
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Historical erasure, Security failure, Geopolitics

cases.title: Van Lévé: Sovereign Visions from the Maroon and Creole Americas and Amazonia (planned exhibition)
cases.artist: Multiple: Julien Creuzet, Gaëlle Choisne, Tabita Rezaire, Zineb Sedira, Hervé Télémaque, and others; Claire Tancons (curator)
cases.institution: Centre Pompidou-Metz, Metz, France
cases.description: The Centre Pompidou-Metz abruptly canceled a major planned exhibition of contemporary Franco-Creole, Caribbean French, and Guyanese art on June 10, 2025, following a tense text message exchange between Guadeloupe-born guest curator Claire Tancons and museum director Chiara Parisi. The exhibition — Van Lévé (Creole for "le vent se lève" / the wind rises) — was planned to run October 31, 2026 through April 5, 2027 and would have been the first major collective survey of French Caribbean contemporary art in a leading French institution. The museum cited budgetary constraints and growing costs; Tancons called the cancellation "brutal and shocking." In late May 2025, Tancons had raised concerns to Parisi about the exhibition overlapping with Maurizio Cattelan's ongoing Endless Sunday show. Over 150 artists and arts professionals signed an open letter condemning the cancellation, published in Le Monde. Signatories included artists set to participate in the show. The open letter framed the cancellation in terms of structural discrimination: "A female Guadeloupean exhibition curator will always be overly ambitious, even if her international reputation is well established and she fundraised to cover nearly half of the budget." Artists pledged to find an alternative venue. The French Minister of Overseas Territories inquired about the cancellation. The Artforum China edition reported this case in a late May 2026 digest, prompting discovery today.
cases.outcome: Exhibition canceled June 2025. No replacement venue announced as of May 2026. Curator and artists seeking alternative French institution. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: whether alternative venue found; whether Centre Pompidou-Metz has faced institutional accountability]
cases.tags: Censorship, Funding dispute, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Institutional crisis, Colonial legacy

cases.title: Bronze statues at Freedom Plaza (including Caesar Rodney equestrian monument)
cases.institution: Freedom Plaza, Washington DC (Pennsylvania Avenue between 13th and 14th Streets NW)
cases.description: Dozens of bronze statues have appeared at Freedom Plaza in Washington DC, installed by the National Park Service as part of America's 250th anniversary programming under the Trump administration. The installation includes an equestrian monument of Caesar Rodney — a signer of the Declaration of Independence known for his overnight horseback ride to Philadelphia to cast Delaware's independence vote — who also enslaved approximately 200 people. The biographies for the statues were reportedly written by David Barton's Christian nationalist organization WallBuilders. The plaza itself has remained closed for months with no reopening date announced. The installation drew immediate social media criticism over the inclusion of an enslaver in 250th anniversary commemorations. Freedom Plaza is steps from the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue and has historically been a major site for protests and public demonstrations.
cases.outcome: Statues installed. Freedom Plaza remains closed. No removal demanded officially. Community criticism ongoing. Caesar Rodney provenance confirmed: removed from Wilmington, DE in June 2020 (BLM era); 13 statues installed at Freedom Plaza May 22, 2026 (see 125-A).
cases.tags: Design controversy, Historical erasure, Political art, Iconoclasm, Political interference

cases.title: Machine (2013)
cases.institution: Kazakhstan Pavilion, Museo Storico Navale, Venice Biennale 2026
cases.description: On May 5, 2026 — the eve of the Biennale professional preview — Asel Kadyrkhanova's mixed-media installation Machine (2013) was dismantled from the Kazakhstan pavilion (Qoñyr: the Archive of Silence) reportedly on order of the Ministry of Culture and Information of Kazakhstan or persons acting on behalf of pavilion organizers. The work consists of three parts: a vintage 1930s typewriter, copies of archived Stalinist-era arrest warrants printed on stationery paper, and red thread. Representatives of the organizers had been pressuring the artist and curator to change the work's central elements prior to installation. The pavilion opened without the work. An international open letter was published on e-flux by over 100 art community members condemning the removal as censorship and demanding an apology from the Ministry of Culture. The letter explicitly notes that May 31, 2026 is a memorial day for victims of political repression in Kazakhstan — making the censorship of an artwork depicting Stalinist terror documents on the eve of that date particularly charged. The Italian Navy-affiliated museum hosting the pavilion (Museo Storico Navale) denied any role in the removal. The D'Uva management company confirmed it had not imposed any restrictions. Curator Syrlybek Bekbota framed Kazakhstan's participation as a "formative stage" and expressed regret the controversy overshadowed the show.
cases.outcome: Work removed from pavilion. Pavilion opened without Machine. Open letter published on e-flux. Ministry has not issued apology. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Ministry of Culture response; whether work shown elsewhere]
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Historical erasure, Geopolitics

cases.title: Seattle Art Museum labor organizing (SAMWU) — May 27 deadline expired
cases.institution: Seattle Art Museum, Seattle, Washington
cases.description: The May 27 voluntary recognition deadline expired with no public announcement from SAM management. Director Scott Stulen's only statement remained "engage in good faith" — not voluntary recognition. cases.title: N/A (systemic policy; affects medieval carvings, stained glass, rare murals in listed UK churches)
cases.institution: Listed churches across UK; St Cuthbert's Church, Great Salkeld, Cumbria (Peel Tower); St Peter's Church, Retford, Nottinghamshire (Phoebe Anna Traquair murals)
cases.description: The UK Labour government ended the Listed Places of Worship Grant Scheme — a 25-year policy renewed by six successive prime ministers allowing listed places of worship to reclaim VAT (20%) on repair and maintenance work. Its expiry means 21,000 churches must now absorb the VAT surcharge on conservation work. National Churches Trust CEO Claire Walker warns that "priceless wall paintings, stained glass, monuments, woodwork and carvings could be damaged beyond repair and lost forever." Two immediate casualties: (1) St Cuthbert's Church, Cumbria: £95,000 Peel Tower restoration faces additional £19,000 VAT, likely unaffordable for a congregation of 15. (2) St Peter's Church, Retford: 1905 murals by Phoebe Anna Traquair (one of England's first professional female artists; the largest surviving Traquair work) suffer from damp requiring urgent specialist restoration — the church faces an additional £50,000 VAT. A new Places of Worship Renewal Fund (£23m/year, England only) replaces the scheme but is less than the previous £42m budget and is not inflation-protected. Museums with free admission can still reclaim VAT on repairs; churches cannot.
cases.outcome: Policy in effect. Churches paying 20% VAT on repairs. New £23m fund replacing previous £42m scheme. Projects being delayed or abandoned. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Conservation, Institutional crisis, Architectural preservation, Political interference

cases.title: La Montagne Sainte Victoire (c. 1888, watercolour)
cases.institution: Fondation Beyeler, Riehen/Basel, Switzerland; current owner unnamed (US-based)
cases.date_controversy: May 2026 (exhibition closed May 25; Fondation Beyeler informed)
cases.description: Provenance researcher Willi Korte, working for the heir of Jewish businessman Gustav Schweitzer (fled Berlin 1935), has presented archival documentation showing Schweitzer loaned this Cézanne watercolour to the Basel Kunsthalle for a 1936 exhibition. Correspondence continued through 1939; the work was returned to Schweitzer's secretary in Paris. How Schweitzer lost ownership thereafter is unknown — but Korte argues it was either sold under duress after Schweitzer fled Germany, or looted in Nazi-occupied territory. Schweitzer died of a heart attack in Manila in 1939 while on a business trip from which he never returned; his secretary was deported from Paris in 1942 and killed at Auschwitz a week later. The watercolour appeared in the Fondation Beyeler's Cézanne retrospective (closed May 25, 2026), loaned by an unnamed private US-based collector. It was not listed on lostart.de. The Fondation Beyeler says it will return the work to the lender and notify the lender of "the suspicion that has been raised." Historian Georg Kreis: with "a heavy cloud of suspicion," the work will become unsaleable, and the heirs should receive compensation.
cases.outcome: Fondation Beyeler notifying lender. Work to be returned to lender. Restitution claim pending resolution between lender and Schweitzer heir. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Art market, Conservation

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, National Mall, Washington DC; US District Court (Judge Carl Nichols)
cases.description: UPDATE: May 21 hearing before Judge Carl Nichols (Trump appointee) on TCLF emergency injunction motion. Nichols questioned whether harm was truly irreparable — the DOJ conceded the paint cannot be removed but argued it could be painted back over in a historically consistent color, which appeared to ease the judge's concern. Nichols did not rule from the bench. Key exchange: DOJ attorney said the pool would look similar when filled with water; Nichols noted it "could be relevant to compare what the Reflecting Pool looks like with dark blue." Washington Post (May 27) reports the paint job is visibly patchy — "different sections of the basin floor display visibly different shades of blue" ranging from charcoal gray to cerulean, with the ends of the pool still unpainted gray cement. Workers were still manually spray-painting as of May 21. Separately: Washington Litigation Group filed a reply brief May 20 revealing a government internal NPS assessment that explicitly acknowledged the law required full Section 106 review — but the agency proceeded with a streamlined exemption anyway on White House and agency leadership instructions to rush for the July 4 deadline. Trump upped the project cost to "less than $20 million" in Oval Office remarks on May 21 — significantly more than his original "$2-3 million" estimate — because he decided the exterior needed work too. Color consultant Jill Morton: "If it is that dark, oh man, that's going to look very, very dismal." Pool expert "Swimming Pool Steve" (Canadian): counterintuitively, a dark pool liner actually makes the water's surface MORE mirror-like, which could increase reflectivity vs. the original gray.
cases.outcome: Hearing held May 21. No injunction issued. No ruling yet. Cost now "less than $20 million." [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Nichols ruling expected]

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing -- DOJ filing in Trump's own words; appeals court stay; parliamentarian firing demand
cases.institution: US District Court (Judge Richard Leon); DC Circuit Court of Appeals; US Senate; White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: Three significant developments reported by Washington Post (May 26). (1) DOJ FILING: On Sunday May 25, Acting AG Todd Blanche and two other senior DOJ officials filed a brief urging Judge Leon to dissolve his order halting aboveground ballroom construction. The filing's language closely mirrors Trump's own rhetoric, including calling the National Trust for Historic Preservation lawsuit a 'charade' and claiming the NTHP had been 'defunded by Congress due to a total lack of respect for them.' (The NTHP has not been defunded.) Trump posted all six pages on Truth Social and White House spokesman Davis Ingle confirmed Trump is 'intimately involved' with the legal case. (2) APPEALS COURT STAY: A federal appeals panel (DC Circuit) has stayed Judge Leon's order halting aboveground construction and is set to hear arguments in the case on June 5. This means above-ground ballroom construction may resume while the appeal is pending. (3) PARLIAMENTARIAN FIRING DEMAND: After Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough ruled that the  billion security funding provision could not be included in the immigration enforcement reconciliation bill (entry 050-B), Trump posted on Truth Social calling for her firing: 'Over the years, she has been brutal to Republicans, but not so to the Dumocrats -- So why has she not been replaced?' Some Republican senators said there were not sufficient votes for ballroom funding regardless of MacDonough's ruling. (4) RELATED DETAILS: 56% of Americans opposed the East Wing demolition in a Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll (28% supported). Alison Hoagland, a historic preservationist who helped the National Trust bring its lawsuit, has been repeatedly targeted by Trump as 'a woman walking her dog' and called a 'known serial plaintiff' in the DOJ filing -- she says she has not personally sued over any Washington matter and was mystified by the description. cases.title: Magnifica Humanitas (encyclical, May 25, 2026) -- paragraph 122 cites Guernica (1937) as example of art resisting normalization of evil, within Chapter Three argument about human limitation as source of moral depth
cases.institution: Museo Reina Sofia, Madrid (location of painting); Vatican (document released)
cases.description: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence), signed May 15 and released May 25, 2026, is primarily a document about AI, human dignity, and the Church's social teaching applied to the technological age. Chapter Three, in the subsection The Limit, the Heart, the Grandeur of the Human Person, contains the passage in which Guernica appears. The full paragraph reads: 'Finitude, when truly accepted, does not diminish us but opens us to recognizing the face of God and others. Indeed, precisely because we experience limits -- vulnerability, suffering and failure -- we can recognize the inviolable dignity of every person, both our own and that of others. In this same experience, we remain capable of intuiting a fraternity greater than ourselves and of perceiving injustice as a scandal. Authentic culture and art preserve this spark, resisting the normalization of evil. For this reason, certain works have taken on an almost prophetic significance: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony can be seen as a desire for unity; Guernica as a denunciation of dehumanization; Schindler's List as a call not to consign the past to oblivion.' The Guernica citation is one clause in one sentence within this passage. Its argumentative function is to illustrate that authentic art -- born from and in response to human limitation and suffering -- carries a kind of moral knowledge that resists the normalization of evil, which no AI could generate. The broader Chapter Three argument is that human vulnerability is not a defect AI should correct but the condition from which solidarity, fraternity, and moral depth arise.
cases.outcome: Encyclical published May 25, 2026. Guernica cited as prophetic anti-dehumanization artwork. No change to Reina Sofia loan status.
cases.tags: Political art, Geopolitics

cases.title: Dallas City Hall (1978)
cases.institution: 1500 Marilla Street, Downtown Dallas, Texas
cases.description: Dallas City Hall (1978), designed by I.M. Pei & Partners as a landmark of Brutalist modernism, faces potential demolition. In August 2025, Dallas City Council commissioned a condition assessment after years of deferred maintenance. Assessment (released March 2026) found no major structural failure but significant systems beyond useful life. Dallas Mavericks CEO Rick Welt submitted a proposal (responding to April 3 Open Call for Concepts from the city) to demolish City Hall and adjacent properties for a  billion 50-acre NBA arena entertainment district. Society of Architectural Historians sent formal letter to Mayor Eric Johnson and City Council on March 3, 2026. On or before May 13, 2026, lawyers for Save Dallas City Hall Coalition served a formal 60-day legal notice to the city, citing violations of its own historic preservation ordinances. Coalition argues city has .6M in ARPA funds for generator replacements (costs ballooned to 7M) plus nearly 8M in unused federal funds that may revert by September 30, 2026. KERA News noted the controversy parallels the Wyland Whaling Wall mural case (093) -- Dallas is simultaneously enabling destruction of both a Modernist civic landmark and a public art landmark in the World Cup lead-up.
cases.outcome: 60-day legal notice served ~May 13. No demolition approved. NBA arena proposal under review. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: San Jose galleon and cargo (~0 billion in gold, silver, emeralds)
cases.artist: N/A (colonial-era shipwreck; multiple state and Indigenous claimants)
cases.institution: Caribbean Sea, ~15 miles off Cartagena, Colombia
cases.description: The San Jose galleon -- a Spanish treasure ship sunk by the British Navy on June 8, 1708 -- was announced discovered by Colombia in 2015 and contains an estimated 7-20 billion in gold, silver, and emeralds: the most valuable and most legally contested shipwreck in the world. Three principal claimants: Colombia (sovereign over its waters), Spain (the ship belongs to Spanish state patrimony under UNCLOS, a convention Colombia is not party to), and Bolivia's Indigenous Qhara Qhara nation (their ancestors were forced to mine the silver). A US salvage company (Sea Search Armada) claims it discovered the wreck in 1981 and is suing Colombia at the UN Permanent Court of Arbitration for .8 billion. Controversy resurfaced in May 2026 when oversight organization VNPCS sent an open letter to Colombia's attorney general alleging: (1) looting and unauthorized interventions in 2016 and 2022; (2) disclosure of the wreck's secret GPS coordinates; (3) lack of transparency from ICANH (Colombian Institute of Anthropology and History), which has repeatedly denied the allegations. ICANH did not respond to Art Newspaper requests. Experts criticize the lack of a science-based recovery strategy.
cases.outcome: Looting allegations renewed May 2026. Multiple parallel legal proceedings. No recovery or repatriation yet. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Conservation, Geopolitics, Indigenous rights

cases.title: AI-generated color version of Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico (1941)
cases.artist: Ansel Adams (original, d. 1984); AI-generated derivative (Danziger Gallery; printed by Esteban Mauchi)
cases.institution: The Photography Show, Park Avenue Armory, New York City (AIPAD 2026); Danziger Gallery
cases.description: Danziger Gallery -- a member of AIPAD (Association of International Photography Art Dealers) -- exhibited and offered for sale at 0,000 an AI-generated colorized version of Ansel Adams iconic Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico (1941) at the AIPAD Photography Show (April 22-26, 2026), without notifying or obtaining permission from the Ansel Adams Publishing Rights Trust. The work is labeled A.I. GENERATED, From the prompt: Make a realistic color version of Ansel Adams iconic Moonrise Over Hernandez, printed by Esteban Mauchi in editions of 10. Trust released a public statement May 23, 2026, condemning the display as unauthorized exploitation of Adams name, reputation, and legacy. Trust was not consulted before the work appeared; once alerted, it contacted gallery owner James Danziger, who did not remove the work. Trust further stated Danziger subsequently leveraged Ansel's name, Moonrise, and the AIPAD presentation while pursuing a proposed commercial AI colorization venture involving other artists' estates. Trust framing: moral rights and artists rights, not opposition to AI per se. Work is legally uncopyrightable as AI-generated.
cases.outcome: Trust statement released May 23. Work still on Danziger website. No legal action confirmed. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Estate alleges the AI piece promotes a broader commercial venture to colorize other artists' works (see 119-A, May 27).
cases.tags: Copyright/ownership, Authenticity, Art market, AI art

cases.description: UPDATE: Two significant developments in the ongoing Chavez reckoning. (1) A Chicana curator at The Cheech Marin Center for Chicano Art published an opinion piece in Hyperallergic (May 25, 2026) explaining why she removed a portrait of Cesar Chavez from the exhibition "Chicano Camera Culture." The curator (Elizabeth Ferrer) frames the decision as not taken lightly: she acknowledges Chavez's labor legacy and the complexity of removing an icon from Chicano cultural space. She notes that the removal process itself became a form of community reckoning. (2) Texas Observer (May 13) published a detailed feature on what should become of the Cesar Chavez National Monument (a federal national monument in Keene, CA, established 2012), documenting how communities — especially Texas farmworker communities — are divided. The article frames the question as: "We have to have the correct individuals at the table that are helping lead these conversations. It should be taken out of politics." NPS manages the monument; no federal decision has been announced. The Chavez holiday in California was renamed Farmworkers Day by LA's County Board of Supervisors in April 2026.

cases.title: DYNAMO (RATM01) and 2026 MFA thesis exhibition / Gaza confrontation installation
cases.artist: Alejandro Valencia (artist); Columbia University MFA Visual Arts Class of 2026
cases.institution: Miriam and Ira D. Wallach Art Gallery, Columbia University, New York City
cases.description: Columbia University's 2026 MFA Visual Arts + Sound Art thesis exhibition includes work by Alejandro Valencia that directly confronts the institution's governance failures around the Gaza genocide — the cohort having matriculated in fall 2024, immediately following the April 30, 2024 forced clearing of student encampments. The show runs through May 24, 2026 (today). cases.title: England national museums foreign visitor admission fee proposal
cases.institution: UK national museums broadly — British Museum, National Gallery, V&A, Natural History Museum, Science Museum, etc.
cases.description: The UK Labour government is 'exploring options' to charge international tourists entrance fees at England's national museums, potentially ending a 25-year policy of free universal admission introduced by Tony Blair's government in 2001. The proposal originated in an independent review of Arts Council England by former Labour MP Margaret Hodge, who recommended levying overseas visitors — but conditional on digital ID infrastructure allowing citizenship verification. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said ministers 'will work with the museum sector to explore the potential opportunities.' The Museums Association and most national institutions oppose the proposal: opponents argue the reputational damage and administrative costs would outweigh projected revenue, which Hodge herself estimated at under £10 million — calling it 'not worth doing.' The British Museum, most visited UK museum (6.1 million visitors in 2025), has not formally endorsed the plan. Enforcement challenges are significant: there is currently no legal requirement to carry ID in the UK. Implementation contingent on a government digital ID card scheme not expected to achieve 'universal coverage' in the near term. The Art Newspaper (May 22) reported most museums largely oppose the proposal. A government update is expected before the end of 2026.
cases.outcome: Policy under exploration. No decision announced. Government update expected before end of 2026. Most museums oppose. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Murder-for-hire conviction in killing of art dealer Brent Sikkema
cases.institution: Federal Court, Southern District of New York; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (murder site)
cases.description: A federal jury in Manhattan convicted Daniel Sikkema, 55, on May 22, 2026 of murder-for-hire conspiracy resulting in death for orchestrating the killing of his estranged husband, prominent New York gallerist Brent Sikkema, 75. Brent Sikkema was stabbed 18 times at his Rio de Janeiro townhouse in January 2024. The alleged hitman, Alejandro Triana Prevez, a Cuban security guard living in Brazil, was arrested four days after the killing and remains in Brazilian custody awaiting trial. Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema used a burner phone to arrange the killing amid contentious divorce proceedings, and bragged to others he would get more money from his husband's death than from a divorce. US Attorney Jay Clayton: 'Daniel Sikkema used a burner phone line to callously order the killing of his husband.' Defense attorney Florian Miedel said they were disappointed and plan to appeal. Daniel Sikkema faces mandatory life in prison. Brent Sikkema co-founded Sikkema Jenkins & Co (Chelsea), representing artists including Vik Muniz, Arturo Herrera, and Kara Walker; the Obamas were among his friends.
cases.outcome: Daniel Sikkema convicted May 22, 2026. Mandatory life sentence. Defense plans appeal. Hitman still in Brazilian custody.

cases.title: Spanish Civil War art confiscations — Prado restitution program (incl. Christ before Pilate, 1450-60, Maestro de Lupiana; Pedro Rico collection; 26,000+ objects total)
cases.artist: Multiple (Sorolla, Bocanegra, Villamil, Jiménez Aranda, Lizcano, and many others); Maestro de Lupiana (Christ before Pilate)
cases.institution: Museo del Prado, Madrid; museums of Gran Canaria, Valencia, Asturias, Málaga; National Museum of Romanticism; National Costume Museum; parishes of Yebes and Pareja (Castilla-La Mancha)
cases.description: A 2022 Spanish Democratic Memory Law has quietly set in motion a wave of restitutions of art confiscated during the Civil War (1936-39) and Franco era, more than 50 years after the dictator's death. During the war, the Republican government established the Board for the Seizure and Protection of Artistic Heritage to safeguard works; after Franco's victory, tens of thousands were confiscated, misappropriated, or lost and never returned. Arturo Colorado Castellary (Complutense University) has identified over 26,000 confiscated objects, of which approximately one-third — more than 8,000 — were never returned to their owners. Over 4,000 were deposited in museums; over 3,300 are missing entirely. The Prado identified 166 confiscated works in its collection and published a public inventory in 2022. In April 2026, the Prado returned two panel paintings confiscated in 1938 to two small parishes (Yebes and Pareja, Castilla-La Mancha), including Christ before Pilate (1450-60, Maestro de Lupiana), which had been displayed in the Prado's Spanish Gothic rooms. Separately, seven paintings from the collection of Pedro Rico (Republican mayor of Madrid, exiled by Franco, collection confiscated as political persecution) were returned from six museums in 2025; five earlier restitutions went to his heirs from Gran Canaria museums in 2024. The Ministry of Culture began investigating in 2024 and has so far identified more than 7,000 confiscated objects in its possession. No formal restitution protocol yet exists — current legislation mandates investigation but not a legal framework for return.
cases.outcome: Restitutions underway since late 2024. Prado leading with 166 identified works; some returned. Ministry identified 7,000+ in its possession. No formal restitution protocol yet. Process described as positive but slow.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Historical erasure, Legal challenge, Ethical museum, Colonial legacy

cases.title: Smithsonian American Women's History Museum (proposed, National Mall)
cases.institution: US House of Representatives; National Mall, Washington DC (proposed site)
cases.description: The US House voted 216-204 to reject a bill that would have located the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum on the National Mall. The museum was authorized by Congress and signed by Trump in 2020 after two decades of effort, but has no permanent physical space. The bill's defeat came after Republicans added three provisions in March 2026 that caused partisan deadlock: (1) language restricting the museum to "biological women," explicitly targeting transgender women and girls; (2) a ban on "diversity" in museum programming; and (3) a provision allowing Trump to override the museum's congressionally designated National Mall site. Democrats had sent a letter in April requesting the original language be restored; House Speaker Johnson refused. The bill's chief sponsor, Republican Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (NY), insisted it was Democrats' "trans obsession" that killed the bill. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (DWC chair) said Republicans "ruined it with your trans obsession and your culture wars." Several Republican men voted against the bill on different grounds — objecting to identity-based museums entirely. The museum's defeat also puts the National Museum of the American Latino (authorized simultaneously in 2020) at risk.
cases.outcome: Bill defeated 216-204 on May 21, 2026. Museum authorized but without a permanent National Mall home. Future of museum uncertain.

Hassan Fartousi (head of Iran's National Commission for UNESCO) confirmed at least 140 culturally and historically significant locations across Iran were affected, beyond the UNESCO-listed sites. At Golestan Palace (UNESCO WH, damaged March 2026), shattered mirrors, broken doors, and ceiling debris remain scattered. The ceasefire (April 7-8) reduced but did not eliminate the threat. Damage documentation continues.

cases.title: Reikado Hall (c. 806 CE) / Kiezu-no-hi "Eternal Flame" (1,200-year continuous flame)
cases.artist: N/A (accidental fire; structure associated with Buddhist monk Kobo Daishi / Kukai, 774-835)
cases.institution: Daishoin Temple, Mount Misen, Miyajima Island, Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima Prefecture
cases.description: A fire destroyed the Reikado Hall at Daishoin Temple on Miyajima Island — a UNESCO World Heritage site — on May 20, 2026. The hall housed the "Kiezu-no-hi" (Eternal Flame), said to have burned continuously for 1,200 years since Kobo Daishi (Kukai) first lit it for ascetic training in 806. The flame also served as one of the source flames for the Flame of Peace at Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park. A temple official moved the flame to a different location before the structure collapsed. No injuries. The fire may have been caused by the flame itself. Eight fire engines and helicopters responded; fire contained by 10:35am. Daishoin said it would work to rebuild immediately. This was the second time Reikado burned down — it also burned in 2005, and a monk preserved the flame then too. A pattern of at least 8 temple and shrine fires across Japan in the first half of 2026 has been noted.
cases.outcome: Hall destroyed. Eternal flame preserved. Rebuilding planned. Cause under investigation.

cases.title: Musée d'Orsay — 'MNR room' (13 unclaimed Nazi-looted works on permanent display)
cases.artist: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Auguste Rodin, Paul Cézanne, and others (works by); wartime provenance unknown
cases.institution: Musée d'Orsay, Paris
cases.description: The Musée d'Orsay opened a permanent room in mid-May 2026 displaying 13 artworks from its holdings of 225 pieces classified as MNR (Musées nationaux récupération) — works recovered from Germany and Austria after World War II that were stolen or sold under duress in France, and whose provenance remains unresolved. The artworks include paintings by Renoir, Degas (a reproduction after Menzel that belonged to Jewish collector Fernand Ochsé, deported and murdered at Auschwitz), and Cézanne (a Mont Sainte-Victoire sold in 1942 to Hitler art dealer Hildebrand Gurlitt, long suspected to be a fake — suspicion now unfounded). The goal is not exhibition but identification: the room invites visitors and the public to help establish provenance and find rightful owners or heirs. Backs of paintings visible through glass for clue examination. 10-year research project funded by a $1.2M donation from American Friends of the Musée d'Orsay. The museum rotates works so more of the 225 can be seen. Context: France's full 225 MNR holdings have been in national museum custody since the late 1940s; fewer than 200 pieces have been restituted since then. The 1998 Washington Principles, the 2023 law enabling restitution of goods looted from Jewish families, and a 2019 government task force coordinate the effort. The project was initiated by Orsay's late director Sylvain Amic before his sudden death.
cases.outcome: Room opened May 2026. 225 works in Orsay custody; 13 on display in rotating schedule. Research project underway. No restitutions announced yet from this display.

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed) — administration cites 1924 congressional report as approval authority
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: Trump administration officials have cited a 1924 congressional report calling for 'two tall columns' at the Columbia Island location as existing congressional authorization for the 250-foot triumphal arch — a legal argument widely dismissed as 'tortured' and 'laughable' by legal experts and historians. cases.title: Stained-glass windows, Notre-Dame Cathedral (6 chapels, Viollet-le-Duc / Claire Tabouret commission)
cases.artist: Eugène Viollet-le-Duc (19th-century originals); Claire Tabouret / Atelier Simon Marq (commissioned replacements)
cases.institution: Notre-Dame Cathedral, Paris, France
cases.description: France's decision to replace six 19th-century stained-glass windows in Notre-Dame Cathedral, designed by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc and Alfred Gérente, with new contemporary works commissioned from French artist Claire Tabouret and glassmakers Atelier Simon Marq (Reims) has ignited a major heritage controversy. The commission was selected in a process overseen by former Centre Pompidou director Bernard Blistène and was publicly championed by President Macron. The National Commission of Patrimony and Architecture (CNPA) voted to veto the project; the government overrode the veto by statute. The windows are in chapels of the nave's southern side and were unaffected by the 2019 fire. The 'La Tribune de l'Art'-led petition to preserve the Viollet-le-Duc windows has gathered over 340,000 signatures — described as the most-signed heritage petition in the world. In April 2026, the permit to remove and replace the windows was posted publicly on the cathedral's railings; heritage groups immediately filed for emergency suspension. On May 19, 2026, the Paris Administrative Court rejected the suspension request from Sites & Monuments and SOS Paris, reasoning that because the new Tabouret windows could theoretically be removed in the future and the original windows will be preserved, the project does not constitute irreversible alteration and does not meet 'urgent' suspension criteria. The judge explicitly did not rule on the project's legality, leaving the path open for appeal. An appeal has been lodged with the Paris Administrative Court of Appeal. A separate prior case on whether the public institution has authority to commission such work (not merely restore) is also under appeal. The Tabouret/Simon Marq windows are expected to be installed by end of 2026.
cases.outcome: Emergency suspension rejected May 19. Appeal filed with Paris Administrative Court of Appeal. Installation of new windows expected end of 2026. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Conservation, Legal challenge, Political interference

cases.title: Wexner Center for the Arts — union demands renaming over Epstein ties
cases.institution: Wexner Center for the Arts, Ohio State University, Columbus, Ohio
cases.description: Wexner Workers United, the union at Ohio State University's Wexner Center for the Arts, sent a formal letter to OSU's president, provost, and board of trustees on May 21, 2026, demanding that the university remove Leslie Wexner's name from the building and begin the process of renaming it. The letter cites Les Wexner's name appearing more than 1,300 times in the Department of Justice's unsealed Epstein files. The union's letter argues that as a contemporary arts center 'we are inherently entwined with the relevant and urgent events of today' and that Wexner's documented association with the Epstein sex trafficking operation taints the institution's identity. This follows months of campus protest at OSU: student architecture students staged a 'REDACTED' tarp over the Wexner name in April 2026 (viral video), hundreds of students and athletes called for removal, and nurses at the Wexner Medical Center held protests. OSU previously denied a December 2025 request to rename the Les Wexner Football Complex. Wexner has not been charged with any crime and denies knowledge of Epstein's criminal activity. He was deposed by Congress on February 18. The Wexner Center for the Arts, designed by Peter Eisenman and Richard Trott and opened in 1989, received at least $15M from Wexner. Leslie Wexner is the founder of L Brands (Victoria's Secret, Bath & Body Works, Abercrombie & Fitch).
cases.outcome: Formal demand letter sent May 21. OSU has not yet responded. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía — director threatened over missing artworks
cases.institution: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid
cases.description: Spain's parliamentary joint Congress-Senate commission (responsible for Court of Auditors relations) passed a resolution 20-13 demanding the Reina Sofía complete a full updated inventory of its holdings by December 31, 2026 — or face the Ministry of Culture dismissing director Manuel Segade. The measure was backed by the conservative Popular Party with far-right support; the ruling Socialist Party abstained. The museum acknowledged longstanding inventory problems but attributed them to the 1988 merger with the former Spanish Museum of Contemporary Art, which created documentation gaps never fully resolved. The text also calls for a 'total and absolute' audit including works on loan, deposited artworks, and pieces whose whereabouts remain unclear. Segade has been director since 2022, overseeing an ambitious program of collection diversification and feminist acquisition. The Reina Sofía also faces the separate Guernica loan dispute (entry 101) and is now under political pressure from an opposition-aligned parliamentary resolution.
cases.outcome: Resolution passed. December 31, 2026 deadline set. Director dismissal threatened if not met. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Outwin Boochever Portrait Competition / 'America's Presidents' exhibition / multiple Smithsonian galleries
cases.artist: Jared Soares, Al Rendon, Rachel Cox, Kameron Neal (Outwin competitors); multiple Smithsonian institutions
cases.institution: Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery, Washington DC; multiple Smithsonian institutions
cases.description: NYT investigation (May 21, 2026) documents Smithsonian wall text suppression across multiple fronts: (1) OUTWIN COMPETITION: In the NPG's prestigious 'Outwin Boochever Portrait Competition' exhibition (through August 2026), most wall text was eliminated — artists submitted explanatory language last summer and were told it would not be used. Photographer Jared Soares (2nd prize): his image of a Black man falsely accused via facial recognition AI appears with only title and artist name, stripped of the story of AI misidentification. He considered withdrawing and tried unsuccessfully to get a QR code linking to context. Photographer Al Rendon: his image of the bedroom of 9-year-old Uvalde victim Jackie Cazares (parents standing beside her made bed) appears without text identifying her as a Uvalde victim — text that accompanied the same image at the Witte Museum in Texas. First-prize winner Kameron Neal (surveillance video installation, 1960-80 footage) pushed back after initially being told all text would be removed; museum included three sentences after negotiation. (2) TRUMP WALL TEXT: 'America's Presidents' exhibition — Trump impeachment language was removed months ago, returned in revamped form that references the two impeachments but does not state why he was impeached (shorter than previous version). (3) WHITE HOUSE DOCUMENT DEMAND: Trump White House demanded eight Smithsonian institutions turn over thousands of documents including wall texts for review, seeking to replace 'divisive or ideologically driven language with unifying, historically accurate and constructive descriptions.' (4) BRITISH MUSEUM: Separately, ~27,000 people signed petition against British Museum changing 'Palestine' on ancient artifact labels to Canaan/kingdoms of Israel and Judah/Judea, framing the change as historically inaccurate and politically motivated. (5) GRASSROOTS MONITORING: Georgetown historian Jessica Dickinson Goodman is part of a citizen effort monitoring Smithsonian language changes. NPG spokeswoman called the label-free Outwin approach 'experimental.'
cases.outcome: Wall text suppressed in Outwin competition. Trump portrait impeachment language returned in shorter form. White House document demand active. Monitoring effort underway. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions — NKA funding scandal
cases.institution: National Cultural Fund (NKA), Budapest; Hungarian parliament (extraordinary committee session)
cases.description: UPDATE: A major cultural funding scandal has emerged in the final weeks of the Orbán government, deepening the case for de-Orbánization. Telex (May 8) and Daily News Hungary revealed that outgoing Culture Minister Balázs Hankó distributed hundreds of millions of forints through the National Cultural Fund (NKA) by bypassing professional expert committees and awarding grants directly to Fidesz-affiliated entities: (1) A company registered in February 2026 under the name of the official photographer of Fidesz's favored violinist Zoltán Mága received 500 million HUF (approx. €1.4M) — the same amount as all independent Budapest theaters received in 2025. (2) A company owned by an employee of the Fidesz parliamentary faction (Dávid Zsolt Párkai) received 450 million HUF (approx. €1.2M); Párkai's apartment had been used by a fugitive former Polish deputy justice minister wanted on corruption charges. (3) When confronted on television, Hankó defended the grants as a matter of 'cultural taste' and said decisions followed the principle of 'supporting those who value patriotism, a life-affirming attitude and traditions.' Incoming Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr (Tisza) has called for an immediate and comprehensive investigation and pledged to restore the NKA's independence. There is suspicion of covert campaign financing. An extraordinary parliamentary committee session has been called; interim reports ordered from beneficiaries. Incoming PM Magyar promised criminal charges if violations are found.
cases.outcome: Investigation ordered. Tarr pledged to restore NKA independence. Criminal charges possible. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Stonewall National Monument (interpretive materials and Pride flag removal)
cases.institution: Stonewall National Monument, Christopher Street, Greenwich Village, Manhattan, New York
cases.description: After Trump returned to office, the Stonewall National Monument — the first and only US national monument dedicated to LGBTQ+ history, designated by President Obama in 2016 — was subjected to two federal actions: (1) Trump administration removed the rainbow Pride flag from the monument's flagpole, one of several LGBTQ+ symbols removed from federal properties under executive orders. After public protest, New York City officials re-raised the Pride flag (date unconfirmed in sources). (2) Many references to transgender people's role in the Stonewall uprising were excised from the monument's interpretive website and materials, as part of the broader administration program of removing transgender representation from federal agencies. On May 20, 2026, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed Stonewall on its 2026 '11 Most Endangered Historic Places' list — the first time the monument has appeared on the list — for 'federal actions undermining representation in LGBTQ+ history.'
cases.outcome: Monument physically intact but interpretive materials altered. Pride flag re-raised. On NTHP 2026 Endangered list.
cases.tags: Historical erasure, Political interference, Censorship, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Centre Pompidou Hanwha (Seoul branch opening June 4, 2026)
cases.artist: N/A (institutional / Hanwha Foundation of Culture / Centre Pompidou Paris)
cases.institution: 63 Building, Yeouido, Seoul, South Korea; proposed Busan branch at Igidae Park
cases.description: The Centre Pompidou Hanwha — a four-year licensing partnership in which Hanwha Foundation of Culture (subsidiary of conglomerate Hanwha) paid approximately €20M for the right to use the Centre Pompidou brand — opens June 4, 2026 in Seoul's main financial district, with an inaugural Cubism exhibition. My concern is that once Hanwha launches Pompidou Seoul, other companies will scramble to bring in their own branches from abroad.' (2) Busan political controversy: The city of Busan signed an MOU with Centre Pompidou for a second Korean branch at Igidae Park, opening 2031, at a cost of 108.3 billion won ($78M) in public funds. Public protest over ecological impact of the building at Igidae Park. People Power Party candidate Park Hyoung-joon defended it as investing in cultural tourism. The mayoral race is ongoing. (3) V&A MOU: London's V&A reportedly signed an MOU with Seoul's Dongjak district for yet another branch — Seoul accumulating multiple Western museum brand franchises.

cases.title: N/A (institutional / whistleblower complaint)
cases.institution: Palm Springs Art Museum, Palm Springs, California
cases.description: An anonymous whistleblower filed a detailed complaint alleging multiple instances of financial misconduct and governance failures at the Palm Springs Art Museum. Allegations: (1) improper transfer of funds between accounts to address 'severe cash crunches'; (2) deaccessioning proceeds used for operating expenses (acknowledged by museum, characterized as an 'internal loan' to be repaid by 2030, $544,403 outstanding as of June 2024); (3) former director Adam Lerner forced out on 'trumped-up' staff complaints without interviewing other qualified candidates before promoting an internal hire (chief curator to director without open search); (4) a $3 million discrepancy in the investment account balance; (5) a nominating committee chair (Patsy Marino) removed from the process to block candidates who might institute a financial review. The museum commissioned an investigation, which it says found no wrongdoing. It declined to release the full investigation report to ARTnews. Museum statement: 'The investigation confirmed a long-standing, Board-acknowledged practice of using such proceeds for purposes beyond strictly the acquisition of art during periods of operating stress.' At least eight board members resigned since spring 2025. An outside accounting firm conducting the annual audit attached a 'letter of material weakness' to the 2024 books in January 2025.
cases.outcome: Museum internal investigation complete; no wrongdoing found per museum statement. Report not publicly released. Board resignations continuing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Senator Biermann Ratjen Medal / Medal for Art and Culture in Hamburg
cases.institution: Hamburg, Germany
cases.description: The city of Hamburg renamed its prestigious culture prize — the Senator Biermann Ratjen Medal — to the Medal for Art and Culture in Hamburg after historical research revealed that its namesake, Hans-Herbert Biermann-Ratjen, had Nazi ties. Biermann-Ratjen served as Hamburg's Senator for Cultural Affairs from 1954 to 1965. The renaming follows a pattern of German cities and institutions reviewing honorific namesakes from the postwar period whose Nazi-era conduct has come under scrutiny. No further details on the specific nature of the ties or the timing of the research findings were reported at the time of this entry.
cases.outcome: Prize renamed. No legal challenge.

cases.title: Palestine Uprooted: Nakba Past and Present (exhibition)
cases.artist: Multiple (Palestinian Canadian artists, video testimonies, photography)
cases.institution: Canadian Museum for Human Rights, Winnipeg, Manitoba
cases.description: Shurat HaDin – Israel Law Center (Israeli legal advocacy organization) sent a formal seven-page legal demand letter dated May 14, 2026 to the CMHR's board of trustees and senior leadership, threatening legal action over the planned exhibition 'Palestine Uprooted: Nakba Past and Present' scheduled to open June 27, 2026. The letter alleges the federally funded museum is abandoning its educational mandate by presenting a 'one-sided, politicized, and historically incomplete' portrayal of the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, and claims the exhibition could fuel antisemitism and violate Canadian federal law. CMHR confirmed the letter is under review and that the exhibition remains on schedule. This is reportedly the first time Shurat HaDin has threatened a Canadian museum, and the first time a Canadian museum has devoted an exhibition to the Nakba from the perspective of Palestinian Canadian survivors. Independent Jewish Voices (Winnipeg) defended the exhibition: 'The Nakba is exactly the sort of stories that Canada's premier human rights museum should be telling.'
cases.outcome: Exhibition scheduled June 27, 2026. Legal letter under review. Museum has not altered plans. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Galleria Borghese expansion (proposed)
cases.institution: Galleria Borghese / Villa Borghese Pinciana, Rome
cases.description: Details emerged about a privately funded €900,000 feasibility study and international architecture competition, sponsored by Italian engineering firm Proger, to explore whether additional exhibition and visitor space could be added to the 17th-century Villa Borghese Pinciana grounds. Heritage preservation organizations Italia Nostra Roma and Amici di Villa Borghese immediately objected to any new construction within one of Rome's most historically sensitive landscapes. Museum director Francesca Cappelletti held a press conference May 18 clarifying that no project exists yet — the competition brief has not even been issued — and pushed back on 'highly premature' criticism. She noted the public debate had generated useful suggestions including adaptive reuse of existing structures. The museum's operational constraints driving the study: 360-visitor timed slots, 2-hour windows (approx. 4,000/day), weeks-long advance reservations, works in storage, poor accessibility for disabled visitors. Record 630,760 visitors in 2025, up from ~506,000 a decade ago. Subterranean expansion (as at Frick Collection NY or Städel Frankfurt) has been raised as one hypothetical option, but Cappelletti notes Roman subsoil requires extensive archaeological study. Competition winner could be selected by end of 2026 per ANSA.
cases.outcome: Feasibility study funded; competition not yet launched; no project exists. Heritage objections filed. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: competition brief expected; winner potentially by end of 2026]
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Institutional crisis

cases.title: Guernica (1937)
cases.institution: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid; proposed loan to Guggenheim Bilbao
cases.description: The Spanish Ministry of Culture refused the Basque government's formal request to loan Pablo Picasso's Guernica to the Guggenheim Bilbao for a nine-month exhibition (October 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027), which would mark the 90th anniversary of both the founding of the first Basque government and the April 26, 1937 bombing of the Basque city of Guernica by Franco-allied Nazi and Italian forces. Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun cited a 16-page Reina Sofía conservation report (March 25) finding the painting too fragile to be moved: extensive micro-crack networks, paint loss revealing ground layer at top edge, sensitivity to any vibration during transport. Guernica has not left Madrid since 1981. Basque President Imanol Pradales (EAJ-PNV) warned the refusal would be 'a serious political mistake,' framing the transfer as 'a symbolic and political reparation to the Basque people and a message to the world.' He invoked the removal of Franco's body from the Valley of the Fallen: 'Did they take Franco out of his tomb... and they are not capable of taking a painting from Madrid to the Basque Country?' Pradales also threatened political consequences — the PNV backs PM Sánchez's minority coalition government. Guarnica's mayor proposed that if moved, the natural site would be the town itself, not Bilbao. Madrid conservative president Isabel Díaz Ayuso dismissed the loan as 'provincial mindset'; PP official Juan Bravo: if technicians say no, politicians have 'little more to say.' The Reina Sofía has refused every previous Guernica loan request (MoMA 2000, Canada 2006, Basque 2007, Japan 2009, Korea 2012). Separately, 24 preparatory drawings and a Guernica variation will be loaned to Gernika-Lumo as a compromise.
cases.outcome: Loan refused by Culture Minister April 7–8. Reina Sofía conservation report published March 25. Diplomatic crisis ongoing between Madrid and Basque government. Compromise: 24 preparatory drawings + variation loaned to Gernika-Lumo.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Conservation, Geopolitics, Political interference, Institutional risk

cases.title: "Gaza Love" (2014–)
cases.institution: Gaza Square (Main Street / Palestine Way), South Paterson, New Jersey
cases.description: On May 17, 2026 — Palestine Day — the city of Paterson, New Jersey unveiled Gaza Square on a five-block stretch of Main Street (previously renamed Palestine Way in 2022) with a permanent sculpture by activist artist Kyle Goen. Goen's 'Gaza Love' design, realized in three dimensions, borrows the colors of the Palestinian flag and invokes the typography of Robert Indiana's iconic LOVE series (1964–). Goen has been distributing prints of 'Gaza Love' as a free organizing tool since 2014, during protests against the Gaza War; prints were also prominent throughout the 2021 Strike MoMA movement. The 3D sculpture was fabricated by a local Paterson signage business and sponsored by the local business association, the Palestinian American Community Center, and several cultural and faith-based organizations. Paterson has a large diasporic Palestinian community. Goen: 'I call the work "Gaza Love" to communicate that love is solidarity — that it's resistance. Love isn't passive.' 'Art is so compromised with capitalism. It's important that artists are doing this work... We have to recall what shapes our moral compass.' The sculpture sits outside the South Paterson library branch.
cases.outcome: Monument unveiled May 17, 2026. Permanently installed. No removal demanded.
cases.tags: Political art, Protest art, Community objection, Geopolitics, Public art

cases.title: Whaling Wall 82 / Ocean Life (1999)
cases.institution: Former Texas Utilities Building, Akard Street, Downtown Dallas, Texas
cases.description: UPDATE: Cease and desist formally filed by Dallas law firm Kessler Collins, P.C. on behalf of Wyland. Defendants named: 3PZ Property Company LLC (building owner entity), Dallas Convention & Visitors Bureau, City of Dallas, and FIFA (Americas) Inc. The letter states: 'Whether by negligence, flagrant disregard, or both, the result is the same — an irreversible destruction of a federally protected work of art in the name of a temporary promotional campaign.' Attorneys argue VARA required a written waiver from Wyland before any work was done, and no such waiver exists. Wyland confirmed to ARTnews he has hired the firm to pursue legal action: 'It's protected under VARA if anything is. I'm willing to take these people on and really set a precedent. I can't save the wall but I can try to save and protect other artists.' 'The law does not yield to World Cup schedules, commercial timelines, nor the indifference of property owners.' No formal VARA complaint filed in court as of May 20. Wyland Foundation president Steve Creech: 'This is part of a global conservation movement that has spent decades using art to connect people to the importance of protecting our oceans and clean water.' The naming of FIFA (Americas) Inc. as a defendant is analytically significant — it adds an international sports governance body to the accountability chain alongside the city and property owner.
cases.outcome: Formal cease and desist served. Defendants named. No VARA lawsuit filed yet as of May 20. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: formal VARA complaint filing expected]
cases.tags: Removal, Legal challenge, Artists rights, Community objection

cases.title: Multiple Iranian cultural heritage sites (Golestan Palace, Naqsh-e Jahan Square, trans-Iranian Railway, 131+ sites)
cases.institution: Iran (multiple sites); UNESCO; Society for Iranian Archaeology
cases.description: UPDATE: More than 200 scholars and cultural heritage professionals — including leading academics at universities across the US, Europe, and beyond — signed a joint statement published by the Society for Iranian Archaeology condemning 'irreversible damage' to Iran's heritage caused by US-Israeli missile strikes. The statement criticizes states and international institutions for an 'inadequate response' and raises concerns about potential violations of international law, including the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in Armed Conflict. It specifically flags Pete Hegseth's declaration that US forces would not be constrained by 'stupid rules of engagement' as 'deeply alarming.' Iranian archaeologists separately launched an interactive map geolocating damaged cultural sites. Iranian officials report over 131 museums, historical buildings, and cultural sites damaged. The Trans-Iranian Railway (UNESCO World Heritage Site) has also been threatened; Iranian cultural minister sent official letter to UNESCO about it. The Golestan Palace (UNESCO WH, Qajar-era) was struck March 3. Stanford scholar Bijan Rouhani notes the Rome Statute explicitly categorizes deliberate attacks on historic monuments as war crimes; the 2017 al-Mahdi ICC conviction (Timbuktu) is the applicable precedent.
cases.outcome: 200+ scholars' letter published April 15. Ceasefire announced April 7-8 but status uncertain. 131+ sites damaged per Iranian officials. No ICC proceedings initiated.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Geopolitics, Conservation, Historical erasure, Legal challenge

cases.title: N/A (institutional / Southbank Centre board chair)
cases.institution: Southbank Centre, London; UK Independent Press Standards Organisation
cases.description: UPDATE: Scale of public support for Misan Harriman dramatically exceeds initial reporting. Over 97,000 people filed complaints with IPSO (UK's Independent Press Standards Organisation) — described by Harriman as potentially the most in British newspaper history. The open letter defending him, originally signed by 245 including Tracey Emin, Greta Thunberg, Mark Ruffalo, Peter Doig, and Aimee Lou Wood, has grown to over 20,000 signatures. Additional context: the conservative media campaign against Harriman began the day after PM Keir Starmer's remarks about tackling antisemitism, in which he referenced Arts Council England's powers to 'suspend, withdraw and claw back funding' where institutions 'promote or platform antisemitism.' Harriman told Hyperallergic: 'I've organized for Black Lives Matter, championed women's rights, LGBTQ+ rights, transgender protections, and for the Ukrainians during the war, and no one has had a problem until I started speaking out against Israel's genocide in Palestine.' The Telegraph's articles focused on: (1) Harriman resharing a post questioning why the Golders Green stabbing was classified as antisemitic terrorism given the attacker also stabbed a Muslim man; (2) Harriman quoting Susan Sontag on the Holocaust ('10% of any population is cruel no matter what...') which the Telegraph and Reform MP Robert Jenrick framed as comparing Reform voters to Nazis. Former Israeli peace negotiator Daniel Levy publicly defended Harriman. Southbank Centre confirmed all board members 'have the right to exercise their freedom of expression within the law.'
cases.outcome: Harriman remains as Southbank Centre board chair. 97,000+ IPSO complaints filed. Media campaign ongoing.
