cases.title: Stone lintel by Mayuy (c. AD 600–900)
cases.artist: Mayuy (Maya artist, c. AD 750, Piedras Negras)
cases.institution: Mexican Consulate General, New York → Mexico (repatriated April 16) → now claimed by Guatemala
cases.description: A rare Maya limestone lintel — depicting a ritual scene associated with ruler Cheleew Chan K'inich and bearing the signature of Mayuy, an elite artist described by archaeologist Stephen Houston as 'the Michelangelo of the pre-Columbian era' — was repatriated to Mexico on April 16, 2026 after an unnamed US businessman delivered it to the Mexican Consulate in New York. Hours after the official repatriation ceremony, experts determined the lintel had come not from Mexico but from the Guatemalan Petén Basin. Guatemala's cultural ministry conducted technical analysis (bibliographic research, comparative studies, archaeologist consultations) and concluded the work is part of Guatemala's cultural heritage, not Mexico's. Guatemala has now formally requested repatriation from Mexico through diplomatic channels. The lintel was originally documented in the 1950s, before being illegally removed from the Guatemalan jungle and entering the international antiquities market. It is part of a series of four lintels now divided between private US collections and the Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth. Houston devoted the opening chapter of his 2021 book A Maya Universe in Stone to this specific lintel. The confusion stems from the fact that Maya territory once extended across both sides of the Usumacinta River, now the Guatemala-Mexico border.
cases.outcome: Lintel repatriated to Mexico April 16. Guatemala formally requested repatriation from Mexico via diplomatic channels May 2026. 'Very positive attitude' from Mexico reported by Guatemala's minister. No timeline announced. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Mexico's formal response; diplomatic resolution timeline; status of the three related lintels]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Indigenous rights, Authenticity, Geopolitics

cases.title: Hair Dress (2024) / Nervina Hair Dress (2024–25)
cases.institution: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York — Costume Art exhibition (opened May 10, 2026)
cases.description: British artist Anouska Samms and New York-based fashion designer Yoav Hadari collaborated on a garment called Hair Dress — a dress with human hair woven through it — while both were residents at London's Sarabande Foundation (founded by the late Alexander McQueen). Samms holds intellectual property rights over the specific hair textile used in the work. The Met expressed interest in purchasing the collaboration in 2024 and including it in its Costume Art exhibition; those plans were shelved in December. The Met's Costume Art exhibition opened May 10, 2026 (following the Met Gala). Samms was alerted to the presence of a dress she says is materially identical to their collaboration — now titled Nervina Hair Dress and credited solely to Hadari — when the Sarabande Foundation tagged her on social media congratulating her on the show she didn't know she was in. Hadari acknowledges Samms holds IP rights over 'the specific textile' but says those rights do not extend to the design, name, concept, or construction of Nervina Hair Dress, which he says he designed independently. After Samms raised the issue with the Met, the museum told her the dispute was between her and Hadari; it declined to comment 'out of respect for the artists and their ongoing dispute.' Samms argues the Met is 'committing its own acts of copyright and moral rights infringement' under English law and is now seeking US legal advice. She says curator Andrew Bolton and his team knew about her, knew Hadari had acknowledged her textile IP, and had agreed to credit her in the original acquisition — making the museum's current neutral position a deliberate choice not to act.
cases.outcome: Dress displayed in Costume Art without Samms credit. Met declined to act pending artist-to-artist resolution. Samms seeking US legal counsel. No lawsuit filed yet. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: US legal action; Met response]
cases.tags: Copyright/ownership, Legal challenge, Authenticity, Institutional risk

cases.title: Sijena Monastery murals ('Sistine Chapel of Romanesque Art', c. 1200)
cases.institution: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya (MNAC), Barcelona; Royal Monastery of Sijena, Aragón
cases.description: Spain's most contentious interregional cultural heritage dispute has escalated in 2026. Background: 12th-century Romanesque murals from the chapter house of the Sijena Monastery (Aragón) were removed in 1936 after a Civil War fire and transferred to Barcelona for restoration; they have been displayed at MNAC since 1961. In May 2025, Spain's Supreme Court ordered their return to Aragón. In March 2026 the Huesca court set a 56-week deadline for MNAC to comply. In April 2026, MNAC filed an appeal contesting the timetable's technical feasibility — conservators note the 132 sq. meter work (72 fragments) is extremely fragile, and cutting and transport risks are severe. Former Catalan culture ministers filed a separate lawsuit against the Huesca judge. A small protest by the Catalan National Assembly erupted when Aragonese technicians arrived to inspect the murals. The latest escalation, reported May 15, 2026: Catalonia has formally sent Aragón a €791,000 demand for repayment of the acquisition cost (paid in 1983 and 1992), preservation, and upkeep costs. Aragón calls it legally unfounded; Catalonia gives 30 days before proceeding to court.
cases.outcome: 56-week return deadline set April 10. MNAC appealed the timetable April 22. Former Catalan ministers sued the Huesca judge March 25. Catalonia sent €791,000 compensation demand to Aragón May 15 (30-day window before court action). Multiple parallel legal proceedings active. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: MNAC appeal outcome; Aragonese response to Catalonia's compensation demand; court deadline compliance]

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing — Senate parliamentarian strikes $1B provision
cases.institution: US Senate; White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough ruled on May 16, 2026 that the $1 billion White House ballroom security provision inserted by Senate Republicans into the $72 billion immigration enforcement reconciliation bill violated budget reconciliation rules. Democrats announced the ruling Saturday night. MacDonough — the nonpartisan Senate arbiter — determined the provision did not qualify for reconciliation (which requires 51 votes), meaning it would instead need 60 votes to pass. Since all Democrats oppose it, this effectively kills the provision in its current form. Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans said 'technical adjustments are ongoing' and were revising the measure. Senate Democrats: 'We cannot let Republicans waste our national treasure on a mission of chaos and corruption.' Sen. Schumer: 'Senate Democrats fought back — and blew up their first attempt.' Secret Service director Sean Curran had briefed Republican senators the prior week, distributing a breakdown showing only $220M of the $1B would go directly to the White House project; the remainder to other security programs. Republicans now face a politically difficult vote if they restructure the provision. Democrats plan to force repeated votes on ballroom-related spending regardless. The parliamentarian also ruled on May 15 that some central Homeland Security funding elements violated reconciliation rules for technical reasons.
cases.outcome: $1B provision struck by parliamentarian May 16. Republicans revising. 60-vote threshold now required — effectively kills it without bipartisan support. Judge Leon injunction still in effect blocking above-ground construction. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Republican restructuring attempt; whether revised provision survives parliamentarian; Senate floor vote timeline]

cases.title: El triunfo de la naturaleza (replica) / 'The Triumph of Nature' (Perito Moreno glacier painting, replica)
cases.artist: Helmut Ditsch (b. 1962, Villa Ballester, Argentina; resides Vienna, Austria)
cases.institution: Casa Rosada (Argentine presidential palace), Buenos Aires; Ditsch studio, Vienna
cases.description: Helmut Ditsch — the most commercially valuable living Argentine artist, whose original Perito Moreno glacier painting sold for €1.6M (record for an Argentine artist) — publicly demanded the return of a high-quality replica of his work that had been on loan to Argentina's Casa Rosada (presidential palace) for 13 years. The work was removed in March 2026 during the legislative debate over Argentina's Ley de Glaciares (Glacier Protection Law), a politically charged environmental legislation that Milei's government opposes. Ditsch was not informed of the removal, received no response to three weeks of requests, and publicly stated: 'Che, ¡no se roben mi obra!' (Don't steal my painting!). He emphasized the work was a loan, not a gift — the government never purchased it — and that loan terms required notification before any movement. The government has not responded publicly. The removal's timing — coinciding with the glacier law debate — suggests the glacier-honoring painting became politically inconvenient for the Milei government. Infobae published the story May 18, 2026.
cases.outcome: Painting removed March 2026. Artist demanding return since then. Government unresponsive as of May 18, 2026. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Removal, Political interference, Institutional risk, Self-censorship

cases.title: Don Colossus (2026)
cases.institution: Trump National Doral Miami, Miami, Florida
cases.description: A 22-foot bronze statue of Donald Trump covered in gold leaf — nicknamed 'Don Colossus' — was unveiled May 6, 2026 at Trump National Doral Miami, commissioned by the $PATRIOT cryptocurrency group for $500,000 (later $360,000 after revisions; sculptor withheld until full payment). The statue depicts Trump's fist-raised gesture from the July 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, PA. Ohio sculptor Alan Cottrill described the project as the most chaotic of his 400+ commission career: late payments, constant demands to digitally slim Trump's appearance (including his 'turkey neck'), last-minute installation (drove through the night, not invited to the ceremony), and a copyright dispute over the group using statue images to market the $PATRIOT meme coin. Cottrill held the statue in an undisclosed Ohio location until $96,750 in outstanding fees were wired on April 22. Evangelical backlash erupted immediately: Florida pastors called the dedication ceremony 'golden calf' idolatry; Pastor Mark Burns, who led the dedication, insisted 'this is not a golden calf — it is about honor.' Trump defended the statue on social media. Hyperallergic's essay framed it as comparable to a Moloch idol. Separate: a bronze Trump/Epstein 'Titanic'-pose statue appeared on the National Mall in March 2026; a smaller gold-painted replica showed Trump embracing Epstein the same month — both by critics/protesters and separately noted by Time magazine coverage.
cases.outcome: Statue installed and unveiled May 6, 2026. Standing at Trump National Doral. Sculptor's copyright dispute settled. No vandalism — viral image confirmed fabricated by Snopes. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: sculptor hinted at copyright/payment lawsuit re: $PATRIOT coin's unauthorized use of statue images]
cases.tags: Design controversy, Political art, Religious objection, Copyright/ownership, Art market fraud

cases.description: Wyland's 82nd Whaling Wall — a large-scale marine life mural completed in 1999 and gifted to the City of Dallas, depicting life-sized whales and ocean wildlife — was partially painted over beginning the week of May 12, 2026 by crews working for the North Texas FIFA World Cup 2026 Organizing Committee. The property owner is Slate Asset Management; the city referred all questions to the North Texas FIFA World Cup Organizing Committee, which issued a statement saying the new work "captures the current historical moment and reflects the energy, unity, and global spirit surrounding the World Cup 2026" and that "a portion of the original mural will remain preserved as a tribute to its lasting impact." Wyland says he was never contacted — calling the claim that he was asked permission "a lie with a capital L" — and is calling the destruction "shameful" and "really disrespectful on every level." He has sent a cease and desist notice to the organizing committee and says he is considering VARA legal action. He argues that the mural, though gifted to the city, remains his intellectual property and is protected under the Visual Artists Rights Act.
cases.outcome: 80% of mural painted over as of May 15-16. Cease and desist sent. VARA legal action threatened. Painting of new World Cup mural continuing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Trump portrait wall text / National Portrait Gallery presidential exhibition revamp
cases.artist: N/A (institutional wall text; portrait by Vanessa Horabuena referenced)
cases.institution: National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, Washington DC
cases.description: The Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery unveiled a revamped presidential exhibition on May 15, 2026, restoring language about Trump's two impeachments to his wall text — language that had been removed months earlier under scrutiny and which historians had noticed. The updated text lists the impeachments as factual data points alongside the Abraham Accords, Operation Warp Speed, January 6, and the George Floyd protests, without explaining why he was impeached. The White House acknowledged "appreciation" for restoring "fair and accurate description" but complained about missing "accomplishments." The White House is also partnering with the NPG on a planned exhibition featuring multiple Trump portraits — including works by speed painter Vanessa Horabuena, who has drawn religious images at Trump's parties. Separately: (1) Jefferson's slaveholding is still mentioned, but language was softened to include a Jefferson quote about the "deplorable entanglement." (2) Rutherford B. Hayes text changed "white terrorist groups" to "militias," which the WaPo had previously flagged. (3) NPG director was earlier fired by Trump, then resigned. (4) NPG historian Mindy Farmer led the revamp, says it began in 2022 and that Trump's complaints "played no role." (5) Smithsonian spokesperson: "The Smithsonian makes full content decisions." (6) Georgetown historian James Millward (part of a grassroots Smithsonian language-monitoring effort): "There is no sign of them caving to White House pressure with these changes. If they had, those facts about the impeachment wouldn't be there."
cases.outcome: Revamped exhibition unveiled May 15. Impeachment language restored. White House "appreciation" plus complaint about missing accomplishments. Planned Trump multi-portrait exhibition in development. White House partnering with NPG on future show.

cases.title: National Endowment for the Humanities — DOGE grant terminations; appeal status
cases.institution: US District Court, SDNY; NEH

Additional details from discovery now public: DOGE members Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh admitted using ChatGPT without defining "DEI" for the chatbot. Grants containing words including "history," "culture," and "identity" were flagged as DEI-related. The court found DOGE "blatantly used" race and gender as criteria. Fox and Cavanaugh, described by McMahon as having "no experience in anything remotely related to the humanities," were the operative decision-makers, not NEH's own leadership. Cavanaugh, when asked if he regretted harming grant recipients, replied he did not because he believed it would reduce the federal deficit — and then admitted when pressed that the grants had not in fact reduced the deficit. The ruling covers two separate cases: American Council of Learned Societies v. NEH (1:25-cv-03657) and Authors Guild v. NEH (1:25-cv-03923). The government was ordered to rescind termination letters; payment of grant funds remains a separate matter for the Court of Federal Claims.
cases.outcome: Permanent injunction stands. No appeal confirmed as of May 16. Government must rescind termination letters. Grants not yet paid. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: watch for government appeal filing]

cases.title: Neue Galerie collection (incl. Klimt "Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I")
cases.artist: Gustav Klimt, Egon Schiele, Oskar Kokoschka, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Max Beckmann, and others
cases.institution: Neue Galerie New York / Metropolitan Museum of Art, Manhattan
cases.description: The Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Ronald S. Lauder Neue Galerie New York announced on May 14, 2026 that they will merge in 2028 — creating the richest collection of 20th-century Austrian and German Modernism outside Europe under one institution. The Neue Galerie's collection, building (William Starr Miller House, a Beaux-Arts mansion at Fifth Avenue and 86th Street), and endowment will transfer to Met ownership; the museum will be renamed "The Met Ronald S. Lauder Neue Galerie" and will continue operating from its current location as the Met's third campus alongside Fifth Avenue and The Cloisters. Ronald S. Lauder (heir to Estée Lauder fortune, Neue Galerie co-founder) and his daughter Aerin Lauder Zinterhofer will donate 13 additional works from personal collections including Klimt's "Die Tänzerin," Kirchner's "Die Russische Tänzerin Mela," and works by Dix and Grosz. Lauder is a long-time Met trustee who previously donated $1B+ in Cubist works. Neue Galerie closes for renovations May 27; reopens autumn 2026 for 25th anniversary. The Met is currently in a $1.5B capital campaign. Adele Bloch-Bauer I, acquired by Lauder for $135M, will remain at the Neue Galerie location. The Hyperallergic report noted that Lauder has come under scrutiny for backing Trump and Israel and serving as president of the Zionist World Jewish Congress; pro-Palestinian protesters previously called on MoMA (where he is honorary chair) to sever ties.
cases.outcome: Merger announced May 14, 2026. To be finalized in 2028 pending approvals. Neue Galerie closes for renovation May 27.

cases.title: Art Dubai 2026 (20th anniversary edition)
cases.institution: Madinat Jumeirah, Dubai, UAE
cases.description: Art Dubai's 20th anniversary edition was originally planned for mid-April 2026 with ~120 exhibitors from 35+ countries. The US-Israel war against Iran — which began in late February 2026 — disrupted UAE airspace, halted airline flights, and stopped art logistics, forcing postponement. On March 19, Art Dubai announced a rescheduled "special edition" for May 14–17 at Madinat Jumeirah in an "adapted format." Around 75 exhibitors dropped out; the reduced edition features ~50 galleries, approximately two-thirds from the region. Fee structure was revised: no stand fees, instead a percentage of sales capped at stand fee equivalent; galleries unable to participate were assessed stand fees rolled to 2027. The Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale in Riyadh and ISEA2026 Dubai also postponed. The Art Newspaper reported the reduced fair opened May 14–15 with "healthy sales" and was framed by organizers as "reflection of resilience." Gallery One from Ramallah is among the Arab galleries present. A related UAE fair — World Art Dubai — separately postponed entirely to November 1–22 in Expo City Dubai, citing need for "more favorable travel and market conditions." Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is still set to open by end of 2026.
cases.outcome: Art Dubai 2026 special edition now open May 14–17. Reduced scale (~50 galleries vs. 120 planned). Healthy early sales reported. World Art Dubai separately postponed to November.

cases.title: Wellcome Collection Jain manuscripts (2,000 items, incl. Kalpasutra, c. early 16th century)
cases.institution: Wellcome Collection, London → Birmingham Centre of Jain Studies, University of Birmingham
cases.description: The Wellcome Collection announced on May 14, 2026 that it will restitute approximately 2,000 Jain manuscripts acquired in 1919 — the largest group of Jain manuscripts outside South Asia — to the UK Institute of Jainology for deposit at the University of Birmingham. A Memorandum of Understanding was signed at the House of Commons on May 14. The manuscripts were acquired in 1919 by Henry Wellcome's Indian agent Paira Mall at 'a low price and against the best interests of their original owners' (5 rupees each) from an unidentified Jain temple in the Punjab area, in a place named in acquisition documents as Patli or Pattli, in what is now Pakistan. Around 1,200 came from this single temple source; ~800 from other unidentified sources, also in present-day Pakistan. Some manuscripts remain wrapped in the 1919 newspapers in which they were packed for transport. The collection ranges from an early 16th century illustrated Kalpasutra (a central Jain scripture) to 19th century documents and includes what may be the earliest surviving copy of the first medical treatise in early Hindi (1592). The destination is unusually a UK institution rather than the country of origin: the temple's location is now in Pakistan, where virtually no Jain community survives after partition in 1947; the fragmented Indian Jain community has no single appropriate institution; and the UK Institute of Jainology at Birmingham was judged the best available custodian. The physical transfer begins in 2026 and may take several years. Deaccession requires formal approval from Wellcome governors and the Charity Commission. Wellcome head of collections Adrian Plau: private discussions are underway with other institutions about further transfers from the Wellcome's 265,000-item manuscript holdings.
cases.outcome: MoU signed May 14, 2026. Physical transfer beginning 2026, may take several years. Formal deaccession approval pending from Wellcome governors and Charity Commission.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Indigenous rights, Colonial legacy, Ethical museum, Conservation

cases.title: Multicultural Community Center (MCC) artwork removal — ethnic studies mural, MLK poster, 'Free Palestine' sign
cases.artist: Multiple (ethnic studies student artists, collective works)
cases.institution: Multicultural Community Center, Martin Luther King Jr. Student Union, UC Berkeley, California
cases.description: In February 2026, UC Berkeley administrators stripped all artwork from the walls of the Multicultural Community Center — a student space founded in the aftermath of the 1999 ethnic studies hunger strike — including a large-scale colorful mural depicting heroes of the ethnic studies movement, a poster of Martin Luther King Jr., and a 'Free Palestine' sign that had been displayed for years. Campus fire marshals were cited as justification (signage violated fire code); the MCC had been abruptly closed in November 2025 following complaints that some students felt unwelcome. Chancellor Rich Lyons confirmed the reopening on February 11, 2026, but with all political art removed and new restrictions on event scheduling. Student interns on the art committee initially complied with removing some items but refused to take down the mural and the 'Free Palestine' sign — when they returned, those too had been removed. Students responded by staging a censorship-themed exhibition in the MCC's main space, mounting free-standing sculptures commemorating the missing works, and displaying posterboards with quotes about art and social change. Red tape outlines marking where artworks had hung were also subsequently removed. ASUC senators questioned how the artwork removal reconciles with campus free expression policies. Berkeleyside published a major feature April 22, 2026; KPFA covered the case May 12-13.
cases.outcome: MCC reopened February 2026 with all political art removed. Restrictions on event programming remain. No restoration announced.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Campus art, Political interference, Campus censorship

cases.title: Southbank Centre -- Misan Harriman under media pressure; open letter defense
cases.institution: Southbank Centre, London, UK
cases.description: Misan Harriman, the chair of the Southbank Centre (one of the UK's largest publicly funded arts venues, home to the Royal Festival Hall and Hayward Gallery), has become the target of a sustained campaign in conservative UK media outlets over posts he shared on social media. The nature of the posts is not fully specified in available reporting but connects to the broader pattern of cultural leaders being pressured for social media content related to Palestine/Gaza. Multiple prominent figures -- including Greta Thunberg and Hugh Bonneville -- signed an open letter defending Harriman. Harriman's position as chair of a major publicly funded institution makes this pressure analogous to the Basma al-Sharif case in Germany (entry 023): the controversy is not about the institution's programming but about the individual's social media activity. The Southbank Centre receives substantial public funding from Arts Council England.
cases.outcome: Harriman remains in post. Open letter defense published. Media campaign ongoing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

cases.title: Gulag Museum rebrand; Memorial banned as extremist; Yeltsin Center removals
cases.institution: Gulag Museum, Moscow; Yeltsin Presidential Center, Yekaterinburg; Memorial (human rights organization)
cases.description: The Kremlin is systematically eliminating Soviet-era repression history from Russian cultural institutions. Three parallel actions: (1) GULAG MUSEUM: Independent investigative outlet Verstka (April 13) reported exhibitions at the Gulag Museum in Moscow are being packed up and moved. The museum, founded in 2001, will reportedly be rebranded to focus on Nazi crimes rather than Stalinist repression -- redirecting the memory of state violence entirely onto an external enemy. (2) MEMORIAL BANNED: On April 9, Russia's supreme court ruled that Memorial -- the human rights movement founded to document Stalin-era crimes -- is an extremist organization and banned it. This is the culmination of a decade of pressure since Memorial was designated a "foreign agent" in 2016; Memorial had also been dissolved by the Justice Ministry in 2021. The court characterized Memorial as "anti-Russian," devoted to destroying "historical, cultural, spiritual and moral values." (3) YELTSIN CENTER: Within days of the Memorial ruling, the Yeltsin Presidential Center in Yekaterinburg (known for its liberal interpretation of Russian history) removed all mention of Memorial from its materials.
cases.outcome: Gulag Museum exhibitions being removed. Memorial declared extremist organization April 9. Yeltsin Center removing Memorial references. No institutional resistance reported.

cases.title: Portrait of a Young Girl (Toon Kelder)
cases.institution: Private home near Utrecht, Netherlands; Goudstikker collection provenance (Amsterdam)
cases.description: Art detective Arthur Brand announced that "Portrait of a Young Girl" by Dutch painter Toon Kelder -- one of more than 1,100 paintings plundered from Amsterdam art dealer Jacques Goudstikker by Nazi occupiers -- has been found hanging in a hallway of a home near Utrecht belonging to the heirs of Hendrik Seyffardt, a notorious Dutch collaborator and SS commander during the German occupation. Brand was contacted several months ago by an anonymous family member of Seyffardt (the family has since changed its name), who reached out in the hope that the work could be restituted to its rightful owners. The painting has been in the family's possession since at least the postwar period. The Goudstikker case is one of the most significant Nazi-looted art restitution cases: Goudstikker fled the Nazi occupation in 1940, dying in a shipboard accident en route to England; his gallery and collection were seized by Reichsmarschall Hermann Goering's agents. After decades of legal proceedings, the Dutch government restituted approximately 200 works to Goudstikker's heirs in 2006. This painting was apparently not among those restituted at that time.
cases.outcome: Painting located. Restitution claim expected. No formal claim filed yet. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Art market, Conservation

cases.title: Louvre Crown Jewels Heist / Institutional Crisis -- French parliamentary commission report
cases.institution: Assemblee nationale, Paris; French museums (Louvre, national museums)
cases.description: UPDATE: A French parliamentary commission formed in the wake of the October 2025 Louvre heist published its report on May 13, 2026, proposing 40 recommendations for major reforms to French museum security and collections management. The commission characterizes the condition of French museum collections as "worrying" and raises alarms about multiple threat categories beyond the heist itself. The report is formally titled "Protection du patrimoine national -- securisation des musees." Recommendations cover security staffing, surveillance infrastructure, inventory management, conservation conditions, and the governance relationship between museum administrations and the state. The heist, in which 8 pieces of Crown Jewels valued at 88M euros were stolen in an 8-minute daylight robbery, exposed chronic understaffing and security failures that the commission found to be systemic rather than exceptional.
cases.outcome: 40 recommendations published. French government response pending.

cases.title: America250 vs. Freedom250 rivalry -- "Prayer at Valley Forge" iconography; Rededicate 250
cases.artist: Arnold Friberg (original painter, d. 2010); Freedom 250 / Freedom Trucks (deploying image)
cases.institution: Freedom Trucks (nationwide); National Mall, Washington DC (May 17 event); federal agency social media
cases.description: UPDATE/ENRICHMENT: NYT feature (May 14) documents how Arnold Friberg's "Prayer at Valley Forge" painting (1976 Bicentennial commission) has become quasi-official iconography for the Trump administration's 250th anniversary programming. The image appears on the back of the Freedom Trucks (PragerU/Hillsdale-produced history exhibits touring schools, already logged as part of 069), in social media posts from federal agencies including the Department of Defense and Department of Labor, and as the promotional image for "Rededicate 250" -- a White House-backed National Mall event on May 17 featuring religious leaders, Republican officials, Pete Hegseth, and Eric Metaxas. The prayer event runs three hours on "God's providence in American history." The historical problem: the Valley Forge prayer episode was likely invented in the decade after Washington's death by evangelical pastor and bookseller Mason Locke Weems (the same source who invented the cherry tree story). Washington scholars note he was not evangelical, rarely mentioned Jesus, and believed strongly in religious freedom including for non-Christians. Friberg, a Mormon illustrator who made his name with Book of Mormon cycle paintings and "The Ten Commandments" designs for Cecil B. DeMille, explicitly intended the painting as a counter to "rebellious cynicism" of Vietnam-era protesters. The image has circulated in evangelical right circles as evidence of America's "biblical foundation" (David Barton/WallBuilders). Its elevation to quasi-official status under Trump represents a shift from civil-religion commonplace to Christian nationalist political statement.
cases.outcome: Rededicate 250 event scheduled National Mall May 17. Freedom Trucks continuing national tour. Federal agencies actively using image. No removal or objection from administration.
cases.tags: Political interference, Political art, Historical erasure, Funding dispute

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed) -- no-bid contract scheme; site testing begins
cases.artist: Nicolas Leo Charbonneau (architect); AECOM Services (engineering firm); Trump administration
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Memorial Circle, Washington DC; NPS; White House Office of Administration
cases.description: UPDATE: Washington Post investigation (May 14) reveals the Trump administration planned to begin environmental assessment work at the arch site by piggybacking on an existing White House contract with AECOM Services -- a firm already holding up to $695M in White House contracts (two five-year agreements: $500M signed 2024, $195M signed 2025). NPS acting director Jessica Bowron emailed White House officials on April 22 asking whether the agency could extend the White House-AECOM contract to cover the arch site, acknowledging it was "a little further afield than Lafayette Park." White House official Heather Martin replied "Yes of course" within one hour. Contracting experts called the move unusual and legally questionable: the Economy Act permits inter-agency transfers only when an agency lacks its own procurement capability. The arch site is on NPS land across the Potomac, not the White House campus. Stan Soloway (former Pentagon acquisition official): "It's a real stretch to say that a contract for work on the White House campus has any relevance at all to an arch a mile away." Interior Dept. spokesperson called the Post's "assertion on contract sourcing incorrect," saying leaked emails were "draft/deliberative" and not final. An anonymous administration official confirmed NPS was likely to use one of the White House's "existing contracts." Site testing was to begin the week of May 11 per court filings; heavy machinery was observed at the site May 12.
cases.outcome: Site testing underway week of May 11. No-bid contract scheme documented. NPS authorization for construction not yet issued per May 7 court filing. Veterans lawsuit active. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: NCPC approval still required; veterans lawsuit; whether no-bid contract is formally challenged]
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Political interference

cases.title: Underground Railroad chute / Merchant's House Museum (1832)
cases.institution: Merchant's House Museum, 29 East 4th Street, Manhattan, New York
cases.description: A vertical passageway approximately two feet square, built into the walls of the Merchant's House Museum in Manhattan, has been identified as a rare surviving purpose-built Underground Railroad hiding place — one of the only such spaces in a publicly accessible building in the United States. The chute connects a basement pantry to second-floor bedrooms via wooden-slat ladder rungs; it was accessed via a concealed hatch behind a built-in hallway dresser. The house was built in 1832 for hatter Joseph Brewster and his wife Susanna, recently identified through archival research as fervent abolitionists who supported racially integrated churches, signed antislavery petitions, and were part of an Underground Railroad network extending from Staten Island to Canada. The chute has no plausible architectural explanation other than as a purpose-built refuge for freedom-seekers. The museum's western wall — which contains the hideaway — adjoins a one-story garage now slated for demolition to make way for a commercial building. Preservation architect Michael Devonshire warns that by the time vibration monitors detect serious damage, 'it's too late' to prevent structural collapse. The developer offered vibration monitoring but has not agreed to structural safeguards. The museum is leading opposition to the development.
cases.outcome: Museum opposing development. Developer offered vibration monitoring only. No legal challenge filed yet. No NYC LPC ruling reported. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Historical erasure, Demolition, Landmark dispute, Racial/ethnic sensitivity

cases.title: SADDEXLEEY — Somalia's first-ever Venice Biennale pavilion / domestic artists excluded
cases.artist: Somalia Arts Foundation (SAF); Warbixinta Cidda; Ayan Farfah, Asmaa Jama, Warsan Shire (diaspora artists); Fabio Scrivanti (Italian co-curator)
cases.institution: Venice Biennale 2026 — Somalia national pavilion, Palazzo Caboto, Venice
cases.description: Somalia's inaugural national pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale, titled SADDEXLEEY (a Somali triadic poetry form), features three diaspora-based Somali artists: Somali-Swedish painter Ayan Farfah, Somali-Danish poet and filmmaker Asmaa Jama, and Somali-British poet Warsan Shire. The Somalia Arts Foundation (SAF), describing itself as Somalia's first contemporary art institution, publicly condemned the absence of Somalia-based artists from the selection. SAF founder Sagal Ali: 'Artists and arts organizations based in Somalia, those who have spent years rebuilding the cultural sector from within, were not meaningfully consulted, included, or recognized in a process that should have belonged to the nation more broadly.' Separately, the Somali queer collective Warbixinta Cidda criticized the appointment of Italian graphic designer Fabio Scrivanti (a project manager at Venice Art Factory consulting firm) as co-curator, citing Italy's colonial history in Somalia beginning in the 19th century.
cases.outcome: Pavilion open. Controversy ongoing. No curatorial change announced. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Community objection, Geopolitics, Institutional risk, Colonial legacy

cases.title: Berlinale 2026 / German Booksellers Prize / Kunstfonds jury surveillance (Weimer censorship cluster)
cases.artist: Multiple (Tricia Tuttle, Berlinale; three unnamed bookshops; Kunstfonds jury)
cases.institution: Berlin International Film Festival; Leipzig Book Fair; Kunstfonds Foundation; Buchenwald Memorial — Germany
cases.description: Germany's new Federal Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer (CDU/CSU-SPD coalition, appointed May 2025 under Chancellor Friedrich Merz) has pursued a systematic campaign across multiple cultural institutions. (1) BERLINALE: Following pro-Palestinian speeches at the 76th Berlinale closing ceremony (February 22, 2026) — including Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib accusing Germany of being a 'partner in genocide' — Weimer called an extraordinary supervisory board meeting threatening to fire director Tricia Tuttle. 3,000+ industry figures signed open letters; Tuttle retained her position with an advisory council/code-of-conduct framing. (2) BOOKSELLERS PRIZE: In March 2026, Weimer excluded three left-wing bookshops (Berlin, Gottingen, Bremen) from the German Booksellers' Prize — already selected by independent jury — citing Verfassungsschutz intelligence findings. He then canceled the Leipzig Book Fair ceremony entirely. (3) KUNSTFONDS SURVEILLANCE: Weimer requested the names of all Kunstfonds Foundation jury members within three days, internally described as needed because 'significant political pressure is building here.' Kunstfonds jurors publicly denounced it as 'political interference' violating Article 5(3) of Germany's Basic Law. (4) BUCHENWALD: On April 13, 2026, Weimer was heckled and called 'fascist' by survivors and relatives at Buchenwald concentration camp commemoration.
cases.outcome: Berlinale: Tuttle retained (March 4, 2026) with advisory council/code-of-conduct recommendations. Booksellers Prize: ceremony canceled; exclusions not reversed. Kunstfonds: jury protests ongoing; no Weimer retraction. Weimer remains in post.

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation — cost explosion; no-bid contract; new lawsuit
cases.institution: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, National Mall, Washington DC; US District Court (DDC)
cases.description: UPDATE: The cost of the Reflecting Pool renovation has ballooned from Trump's stated $1.8M to $13.1 million — over seven times the original figure. On May 8, Interior Dept. added $6.2M to the existing no-bid contract with Atlantic Industrial Coatings (a Virginia firm Trump chose because it had worked on pool resurfacing at his Sterling, VA golf club), bringing the total to $13.1M. Federal contracting records show the $13.1M figure matches exactly the contractor's own April offer, including a 20% profit margin. Contract awarded without competitive bidding under an 'urgent' exemption citing the 250th anniversary July 4 deadline; the specific 'serious injury' to the government was not publicly identified. On May 11, the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) and its founder/CEO Charles A. Birnbaum filed suit (Case 1:26-cv-01593, DDC) against DOI, Secretary Doug Burgum, NPS, and Acting Director Jessica Bowron. The complaint argues: (1) Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act required DOI/NPS to consult with interested parties before making changes to the Reflecting Pool, which is part of the National Mall Historic District listed on the National Register of Historic Places. No consultation occurred. (2) The 2008 NPS Programmatic Agreement streamlined review only for actions 'repainting in the same color as existing, or in similar colors or historic colors' — painting the basin vivid blue explicitly falls outside the streamlined exemption. (3) The dark grey, achromatic basin was 'not incidental to the design. It was the design' — cited in the 1999 NPS Cultural Landscape Report as a character-defining feature creating 'the illusion of greater depth and a more profound reflection.' (4) NEPA review also bypassed. The complaint calls the resurfacing 'part of a pattern — epitomized most notably by the rush to destroy the East Wing of the White House — in which this Administration willfully disregards legal limits established by Congress.' Birnbaum personally authored the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties with Guidelines for the Treatment of Cultural Landscapes (1996) — the governing federal framework for the Reflecting Pool.
cases.outcome: Renovation underway. Cost: $13.1M (no-bid; 7x stated figure; matches contractor's profit-padded proposal to the dollar). TCLF lawsuit filed May 11 (Case 1:26-cv-01593, DDC). Section 106 consultation never initiated. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: court ruling; whether judge halts painting; completion timeline]

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation — PROMULGATED
cases.institution: Élysée Palace / French government; Le Journal Officiel
cases.description: RESOLUTION: The French repatriation framework law was formally promulgated by President Macron on Saturday, May 10, 2026, and published in the official gazette Le Journal Officiel on Sunday May 11. The law is now in force. Final sequence: (1) Senate unanimously adopted the CMP-reconciled text Thursday May 8 (343 votes in favor, none against). (2) National Assembly unanimously adopted it Wednesday May 7. (3) Macron signed it Saturday May 10 during a trip to Africa, making his remarks at the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi on Monday May 11: 'I believe we have built something irreversible and unstoppable.' The law allows the French government to return cultural property without requiring individual parliamentary votes for each item. It covers objects acquired between November 1815 and April 1972. A bilateral scientific committee (French and country-of-origin experts) must review each request; Parliament also gets a vote on individual cases. Military items excluded.
cases.outcome: RESOLVED. Law promulgated May 10, 2026. In force. Pending restitution requests from Algeria, Mali, Benin, Chad, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, Ghana now have active legal pathway.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Legislative action, Ethical museum

cases.title: Seated Man with a Cane (1918)
cases.institution: New York Supreme Court; Geneva freeport (current location of painting)
cases.description: After an 11-year legal battle, NY Supreme Court Judge Joel M. Cohen ruled April 3, 2026 that billionaire art dealer David Nahmad must return Modigliani's Seated Man with a Cane (1918) to the estate of Oscar Stettiner, a Jewish antiques dealer whose Paris gallery was looted during the Nazi occupation. Nahmad's Panamanian holding company, International Art Center S.A., purchased the painting at Christie's London in 1996 for £2M; it has been in a Geneva freeport since. The Panama Papers (2016) revealed Nahmad as the holding company's sole owner after years of denial. Cohen found the painting identical to the looted work and that Stettiner 'never voluntarily relinquished it.' He criticized Christie's 1996 provenance catalog as 'flawed and misleading — whether by error or design.' On May 5, Nahmad filed a motion to review, citing a newly published Modigliani catalogue raisonné by Marc Restellini and eyewitness testimony claiming Mondex misidentified the painting.
cases.outcome: Ruling entered April 3, 2026 ordering return. Nahmad filed motion to review May 5. Return not yet executed. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Art market, Authenticity, Geopolitics

cases.title: The Migrant Child (2019)
cases.institution: Palazzo San Pantalon, Venice; Arsenale Tesa 113 (unveiling); Venice canals (boat tour)
cases.description: Banksy's 2019 Venice mural depicting a child refugee in a life vest holding a pink flare — painted illegally on Palazzo San Pantalon in the Santa Croce district — was removed from the deteriorated facade in July 2025 after years of saltwater damage eliminated roughly a third of the image. Banca Ifis, which acquired the palazzo in 2024 at the Italian Ministry of Culture's request, funded and supervised a full conservation-restoration by Federico Borgogni. The restored work was unveiled May 7 at Tesa 113 in the Arsenale during the Biennale Arte 2026 preview, then toured Venice's canals by boat May 8–9. Banca Ifis says it consulted people close to Banksy but could not confirm direct artist permission. The 2023 decision to restore the work rather than allow it to decay in situ generated debate among street art purists. The work is one of only two officially attributed Banksy pieces in Italy. Banca Ifis also launched an educational initiative, Migrant Child – Rights at Work, for Italian secondary schools in 2026–27.
cases.outcome: Restoration complete. Work unveiled May 7. Canal boat tour May 8–9. Return to Palazzo San Pantalon pending.
cases.tags: Conservation, Unauthorized public art, Removal, Migration, Protest art

cases.title: Tatlin's Whisper #6 / Fall of Freedom (national arts resistance platform)
cases.institution: Times Square (Father Duffy Square), Manhattan, New York; galleries, museums, theaters nationwide
cases.description: Cuban artist and activist Tania Bruguera staged her landmark participatory performance "Tatlin's Whisper #6 (Havana Version)" (2009, on loan from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum) in Times Square on May 1, 2026 (International Workers' Day/May Day), in partnership with "Fall of Freedom." The performance — a microphone, a raised platform, and one minute of uncensored speech per participant — originated at the 2009 Havana Biennial as a platform for free speech denied under Cuban authoritarianism. Its staging in Times Square on May Day 2026 explicitly frames current US governance as analogous: "I think it's important to create connections between situations that apparently have nothing to do with each other, for example, repression in Cuba and what is happening in the United States," Bruguera told Hyperallergic. Fall of Freedom is a new national arts resistance platform launched May 1, 2026, calling on galleries, museums, libraries, comedy clubs, theaters, and concert halls across the country to host exhibitions and performances defying "authoritarian forces sweeping the nation." Times Square Arts Director Anna Starling: "We are honored to bring Tatlin's Whisper #6 back to the Crossroads of the World, this time on May Day, to open up a temporary public forum where speech itself becomes the artwork." Bruguera has been repeatedly detained by Cuban authorities for her artistic and civic work.
cases.outcome: Performance completed May 1. Fall of Freedom platform launched, ongoing.
cases.tags: Political art, Protest art, Resistance, Censorship

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation — definitively adopted
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale / Sénat, Paris
cases.description: RESOLUTION: The French repatriation framework law was definitively adopted by both chambers of parliament. Sequence: (1) The CMP (commission mixte paritaire) produced a unified compromise text on April 30, reconciling the Assemblée nationale's April 13 amended text with the Senate's January 2026 version. (2) The National Assembly voted unanimously 141-0 on Wednesday May 6. (3) The Senate voted unanimously on Thursday May 7. Culture Minister Catherine Pégard declared: "L'instant est historique." The law now awaits formal promulgation by President Macron (15-day constitutional clock from May 7 = approximately by May 22). The law enables restitutions by government decree without requiring individual parliamentary votes, covering cultural property acquired between 1815 and 1972. Two scientific and parliamentary commissions must consult on each case. Pending requests from Algeria, Mali, Benin, Chad, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, Ghana, Senegal now have a legal pathway once promulgated. Approximately 150,000 African objects held in ~230 French public museums. Separately: a bill for repatriation of Kali'na human remains from Guyana is expected before the Senate on May 18.
cases.outcome: Both chambers adopted unanimously. Awaiting Macron promulgation by approximately May 22. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Macron signature; Kali'na bill Senate May 18; first restitution requests under new framework]

cases.title: Eisenhower Executive Office Building — NCPC hearing outcome, May 7
cases.institution: Eisenhower Executive Office Building, Washington DC; National Capital Planning Commission
cases.description: The National Capital Planning Commission held a 1.5-hour hearing May 7 on Trump's proposal to paint the EEOB's granite exterior white at an estimated cost of $7.5M+. The NCPC unanimously approved cleaning the exterior but declined to approve the painting proposal, instead requesting additional information: how the silicate paint would affect the historic granite, ongoing maintenance costs, and whether less intrusive alternatives (such as exterior lighting) could achieve the desired 'brightening' without painting. Preservationists and public commenters had filed more than 2,000 comments opposing the paint. A federal lawsuit challenging the proposed paint job is already pending. The NCPC is chaired by Will Scharf, a senior Trump White House aide — a conflict of interest flagged in entry 050 (White House ballroom). Commission's decision to request more information rather than approve or deny leaves the project in procedural limbo; a future NCPC hearing will address the paint proposal.
cases.outcome: NCPC approved cleaning only; declined to approve painting; requested additional information. Future hearing required. Lawsuit pending.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Landmark dispute, Legal challenge

cases.title: National Endowment for the Humanities — DOGE grant terminations ruled unconstitutional
cases.artist: Multiple grantees (scholars, writers, research institutions nationwide)
cases.institution: National Endowment for the Humanities / US District Court, Southern District of New York
cases.description: DOGE used ChatGPT to identify and terminate over 1,400 NEH grants totaling $100M+, targeting any grant the AI flagged as DEI-related, without defining DEI for the chatbot before using its outputs. Grants canceled included Holocaust education programming at Seton Hall University, a virtual reality demonstration of Indigenous culture at Mesa Verde and Wupatki National Monuments, and a book about HIV in prisons. ChatGPT incorrectly flagged as DEI an anthology titled 'In the Shadow of the Holocaust: Short Fiction by Jewish Writers from the Soviet Union.' On May 7, 2026, US District Judge Colleen McMahon (SDNY) permanently barred the administration from terminating the grants, ruling DOGE violated the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal protection clause, and had no statutory authority. 'DOGE had no statutory authority to terminate NEH grants,' McMahon wrote. She called the case 'a textbook example of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.' The court rejected the government's argument that ChatGPT's misclassifications absolved it of constitutional responsibility: 'ChatGPT was the Government's chosen instrument for purposes of this project, and DOGE's use of AI to identify DEI-related material neither excuses presumptively unconstitutional conduct nor gives the Government carte blanche to engage in it.' Government ordered to rescind termination letters; not immediately required to pay grant funds (only the Court of Federal Claims can compel payment). Appeal not confirmed as of May 9. Case brought by Authors Guild, American Council of Learned Societies, American Historical Association, Modern Language Association, and individual grantees.
cases.outcome: Judge permanently barred grant terminations May 7, 2026. Government ordered to rescind termination letters. Appeal not confirmed. Ruling does not immediately compel payment.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Funding dispute, Legal challenge

cases.title: Vaillancourt Fountain — demolition and accidental fire
cases.institution: Justin Herman Plaza, San Francisco, California
cases.description: Demolition of the 1971 Brutalist Vaillancourt Fountain began May 4 after the California appeals court denied a final injunction request from the preservation coalition Friends of the Plaza. On May 6, construction crews accidentally ignited debris inside the fountain's cantilevered steel tubes during torch-cutting; a San Francisco Arts Commission spokesperson confirmed the fire was controlled with continuous water spraying, with no major damage. Demolition is continuing. The city's rationale centered on asbestos contamination; the Friends of the Plaza alleged asbestos was pretextual — the city wanted to remove an aesthetically unpopular work without engaging the preservation question on its merits. The fountain, commissioned by the San Francisco Arts Commission in 1969 and completed in 1971, was one of the largest public art installations on the West Coast. The preservation fight lasted years.
cases.outcome: Demolition underway as of May 8. Court denied preservation injunction. Work continuing.
cases.tags: Demolition, Architectural preservation, Legal challenge, Public art

cases.title: Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB) exterior — proposed painting
cases.institution: Eisenhower Executive Office Building, 17th Street & Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump is pursuing the painting of the entire granite exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB) — a National Historic Landmark and National Register of Historic Places site completed in 1888 — bright white. Trump stated the current gray granite is 'a really bad color.' The White House Office of Administration proposed two options: painting the entire exterior, or painting most of it while leaving the granite base unpainted (the full paint is preferred). Estimated cost: at least $7.5 million, per White House facilities official Ryan Erb at a May 7 NCPC hearing. Preservationists, architects, and historians have raised alarms that granite is not designed to receive paint and that silicate paint would trap moisture, accelerating stone deterioration — potentially irreversible damage to an 1888 landmark. More than 2,000 public comments submitted to the NCPC were strongly opposed. The Commission of Fine Arts (Trump-appointed) directed White House to present more information at a future date at an earlier hearing; at the May 7 NCPC hearing, commissioners unanimously approved cleaning the building's exterior but declined to approve the paint proposal, instead requesting additional information including a third-party assessment of the granite's condition and details on the proposed silicate paint. A federal lawsuit against the proposed paint job is already working its way through court. The NCPC is chaired by Will Scharf, a Trump White House aide — the same conflict-of-interest pattern flagged in entry 050 (White House ballroom: NCPC chair simultaneously serving the project's patron).
cases.outcome: NCPC review May 7: approved cleaning, declined to approve painting, requested additional information. CFA previously directed more information. Federal lawsuit pending. No painting approved as of May 8. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: NCPC future hearing; CFA decision; court ruling]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Landmark dispute, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Political interference

cases.title: Die große Nacht im Eimer (The Big Night Down the Drain, 1962–63) / Der nackte Mann (The Naked Man, 1962)
cases.institution: Galerie Werner & Katz, West Berlin, West Germany
cases.description: RETROSPECTIVE ENTRY, occasioned by Baselitz's death April 30, 2026. At his first solo exhibition in October 1963 at Galerie Werner & Katz in West Berlin, two paintings were seized by the public prosecutor's office two days after opening on grounds of 'infringement of public morality' (Unsittlichkeit): Die große Nacht im Eimer (depicting a distorted figure with an exaggerated phallus, widely read as a Hitler-like figure masturbating) and Der nackte Mann (a nude youth gripping a monstrous phallus). A friend of gallerist Michael Werner had reportedly already tipped off the German News Agency's local paper B.Z. — making the seizure partly a self-fulfilling, intentional scandal. Baselitz was charged with offending public morality. Criminal proceedings lasted until October 1965, when the case was dismissed and the paintings returned. The episode made Baselitz famous and effectively launched his career in the West. His stated intention was to provoke a reckoning with post-war German amnesia: 'I proceed from a state of disharmony, from ugly things.' Both paintings are now held at Museum Ludwig, Cologne. Die große Nacht im Eimer is widely considered one of the landmark works of postwar European art.
cases.outcome: Resolved 1965: criminal case dismissed, paintings returned. Both now at Museum Ludwig, Cologne.
cases.tags: Censorship, Obscenity, Legal challenge, Political art

cases.title: American Folk Art Museum labor dispute
cases.artist: UAW Local 2110 workers; American Folk Art Museum (institutional)
cases.institution: American Folk Art Museum, New York City; Mandarin Oriental, Columbus Circle (picket site)
cases.description: Workers at the American Folk Art Museum picketed the museum's annual gala at the Mandarin Oriental hotel in Columbus Circle on May 6, joined by UAW Local 2110 organizers. Approximately 36 union members and supporters marched for two hours, holding signs reading 'For Folk's Sake' and 'Self Taught, Not Self Funded,' chanting against poverty wages and union busting. Management offered $21.50/hour max by year three; union demanded $30/hour by year three, plus health care and hybrid schedule guarantees. cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale — May 8 strike; Fainaru legal threats detail
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Arsenale and Giardini; Via Garibaldi (rally)

cases.title: US museum building repairs crisis (GAO-26-108485 report)
cases.institution: Museums nationwide — approximately 16,700 public and private nonprofit museums, 50 states and DC
cases.description: A March 2026 Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108485), covered today by The Art Newspaper and ARTnews, documents a systemic crisis in US museum infrastructure. Key findings from a survey of approximately 300 museums and 17 site visits: (1) About 85% of museums (13,700) have a backlog of deferred maintenance and repair needs. (2) About 77% (12,300) have at least one building system in poor condition putting collections at risk. (3) About 73% (11,900) cite at least one health or safety concern. (4) Nearly half have physical accessibility barriers. (5) About half report more than $100,000 in deferred maintenance each. (6) Only 11% expect the backlog to shrink in three years. Root cause: federal IMLS funding legally may not be used for construction or capital improvements — only programs and services. Museums rely primarily on private donations for structural needs. Rural and tribal museums face compounding challenges. The report provides Congress with data as it considers IMLS reauthorization, which lapsed in 2025. Trump's FY2027 budget proposes eliminating IMLS; Congress has continued funding at $291.8M for FY2026. Example cited in report: a small museum in Alaska with a $212,000 annual budget needing $289,000 in building repairs. Federal museums excluded from scope.
cases.outcome: GAO report published March 2026. Covered today. No federal legislative response yet. IMLS authorization lapsed; Trump budget proposes elimination.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Institutional crisis, Conservation

cases.title: America250 vs. Freedom250 rivalry; 'History Rocks!' cancellations; 'Rededicate 250' National Mall event
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC; schools nationwide; 250.gov
cases.description: Two organizations compete to shape the US 250th anniversary (July 4, 2026). America250 is the bipartisan congressional commission established in 2016 (co-chaired by Bush and Obama, 350-member Congressional caucus). Freedom250 is a Trump-aligned public-private partnership launched December 2025, operating through 250.gov with fewer public reporting requirements. Congress appropriated $150M to the Department of Interior; most is now expected redirected to Freedom250. The IMLS originally awarded America250 a $10M grant for six Freedom Truck mobile exhibitions; this was redirected to Freedom250 in December, with exhibits now organized by PragerU and Hillsdale College, presenting American history without reference to slavery or Indigenous genocide. Education Secretary Linda McMahon's 'History Rocks!' school tour — billed as nonpartisan — has been canceled at 4+ locations (Massachusetts, Alabama, two in Connecticut) and met with protests at others (Wisconsin, New Jersey, Illinois). Cancellations are driven by the tour's exclusive sponsorship by the America 250 Civics Education Coalition, composed entirely of conservative and religious organizations (Turning Point USA, Moms for Liberty, Heritage Foundation, America First Policy Institute). 'Rededicate 250' event planned for National Mall on May 17 includes far-right Christian nationalist speakers; White House described it as a 'large-scale revival.' Freedom250 events include a UFC fight on the White House Ellipse (June 14) and an IndyCar race on the National Mall. Corporate sponsors including Mastercard, SAP, Deloitte, and Lockheed Martin are listed for Freedom250. Congress has appropriated a total of $150M; America250 has received ~$25M, Freedom250 ~$22M; final allocation unresolved.
cases.outcome: Both programs operating in parallel. Freedom250 controls increasing share of federal funding. 'History Rocks!' cancellations continuing. 'Rededicate 250' National Mall event scheduled May 17. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: May 17 event; further History Rocks! cancellations; congressional oversight]
cases.tags: Political interference, Funding dispute, Historical erasure, Political art, Censorship

cases.title: Marine, Amsterdam (1874) / Adolphe Monet Reading in a Garden (1867) — Rouen hearing held; ruling pending
cases.institution: Tribunal judiciaire de Rouen
cases.description: The Rouen court hearing in the Wildenstein/Monet 'vitiated consent' case took place today, May 7, 2026, as scheduled. No written ruling has been published online as of end of session. French civil courts typically deliberate days to weeks before issuing written judgments. The case centers on sellers' claim that Marine, Amsterdam's original canvas had been lost (replaced during a transfer process) before the 2004 exchange with Wildenstein, constituting vice du consentement under French civil law. The prior jurisdictional challenge by Wildenstein attorney Philippe Plantade was resolved in favor of the Rouen tribunal. If vitiation is found, the 2004 exchange could be nullified, affecting Adolphe Monet Reading in a Garden (currently on loan at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, owned after resale by Wildenstein) and Marine, Amsterdam (currently owned by Larry Ellison).
cases.outcome: Hearing held May 7. No ruling published yet. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: search for ruling in coming days/weeks]

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale — May 6 protests at Israeli and Russian pavilions
cases.artist: ANGA protesters; Pussy Riot; FEMEN; Belu-Simion Fainaru (Israeli pavilion)
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Arsenale and Giardini
cases.description: On Day 1 of the professional preview (May 6), major protests occurred at both contested pavilions. (1) ANGA organized a demonstration of 200+ people at the Israeli pavilion in the Arsenale, blocking the entrance for approximately 30 minutes. Protesters chanted 'silence is complicity' and 'shame on you,' distributed leaflets, held 'No Artwashing Genocide' banners. (2) Pussy Riot and FEMEN staged a separate protest at the Russian pavilion, lighting pink, blue, and yellow flares; approximately 50 activists attempted to enter before being pushed back by police. Tolokonnikova (Pussy Riot): Russia's cultural presence is part of its 'hybrid warfare campaign.' A statue outside the Russian pavilion was draped in a Ukrainian flag. Russian pavilion temporarily closed after the protest before reopening for press/industry. (3) ANGA announced a 24-hour cultural sector strike for May 8, backed by Italian trade unions ADL Cobas, Unione Sindacale di Base, and Confederazione Unitaria di Base. Strike calls on pavilion teams and art workers to close their venues for the day. Rally planned at Viale Garibaldi (near Arsenale) at 4:30pm Friday. cases.title: Las Playas Intaglio (c. 1000 CE)
cases.institution: Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge, Southwest Arizona (US-Mexico border)
cases.description: On April 23, 2026, a contractor building Trump's 'Smart Wall' border reinforcement ran heavy construction equipment through the Las Playas Intaglio, a 272-foot-long fish-shaped geoglyph etched into the desert pavement of Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge in Southwest Arizona. Approximately 60–70 feet of the intaglio were damaged. The intaglio is estimated to be at least 1,000 years old and is a sacred site for ancestors of the Tohono O'odham Nation, which lies east of the refuge. CBP confirmed the damage on May 1, describing it as 'inadvertent,' and stated that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott was 'engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.' The remaining portion of the site was secured. The intaglio's existence and cultural significance had been extensively documented, including in US Supreme Court amicus filings during Trump's first term. Preservation archaeologist Aaron Wright, who visited the site in April out of concern about Smart Wall construction and filmed it days before the damage, told Hyperallergic: 'It's a grim reality that the nation's heritage basically dangles on the whim of an administration. We have these environmental laws in place, but then we have other laws that basically nullify them at the will of the executive.' Trump's border emergency declaration superseded standard environmental review processes under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). During Trump's first term, contractors also damaged a Hohokam burial ground in the same region. Smart Wall construction also threatens Quitobaquito Springs in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. Florida Governor DeSantis similarly invoked emergency orders to build the 'Alligator Alcatraz' prison on sacred Miccosukee land.
cases.outcome: 60-70 feet of 272-foot intaglio damaged April 23. CBP confirmed damage May 1. Remaining site secured. Tribal leadership consultation underway. No restoration announced.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Indigenous rights, Historical erasure, Political interference

cases.title: Tlali (2026)
cases.institution: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), Geffen Plaza, Los Angeles CA
cases.description: Mexican artist Pedro Reyes unveiled Tlali (2026), a four-metre-tall Olmec-inspired volcanic-stone sculpture of a female face, installed on the exterior of the new David Geffen Galleries building at LACMA as a permanent commission. An open letter signed by nearly 80 Mexican cultural figures, published April 23 in the Spanish-language criticism site Cubo Blanco, alleges the work is a revised version of a commission Reyes received in 2021 to replace Mexico City's 1877 Columbus statue on the Paseo de la Reforma — a project that was canceled after objections from more than 300 cultural figures and collectives. The objections in 2021 centered on: (1) Reyes is a male, non-Indigenous artist commissioned to represent 'the Indigenous woman'; (2) the work 'reproduces the silencing and invisibilisation of women's struggles and their Indigenous communities'; (3) it exhibits 'neo-indigenist overtones' and a 'vagueness typical of 19th-century national statuary.' The 2023 letter objects to the LACMA commission on the same grounds, and adds: the title was shortened from 'Tlalli' (Nahuatl for Earth) to 'Tlali' to 'appeal to anglophones'; a Nahuatl word is used for an Olmec-inspired work (a different culture); and the original Mexico City site was ultimately transformed into the Glorieta de las Mujeres que Luchan (Roundabout of the Women Who Fight), a feminist anti-monument against gender violence and femicide, making the export of the rejected sculpture to a US museum feel like a disrespect to that struggle. LACMA describes the work as 'entirely different in purpose and meaning' from the 2021 Mexico City proposal, noting the face's features were reshaped and the commission offers 'a new location, context and opportunity for discussion.' LACMA director Michael Govan said the visible armature was central to discussions with the artist: 'Museums are a kind of armature for history.' Reyes did not respond to press requests.
cases.outcome: Sculpture installed permanently at LACMA. Open letter published April 23 with ~80 signatories. No removal demanded. No LACMA retraction. LACMA defending commission.
cases.tags: Community objection, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Indigenous rights, Authenticity, Design controversy

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing — Senate Republicans insert $1B security funding into immigration bill
cases.institution: US Senate; White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: Senate Republicans inserted $1 billion for White House East Wing 'security enhancements' into a roughly $70 billion immigration enforcement funding bill released May 5. The provision was added by the Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair: Sen. Charles Grassley). The bill does not mention the ballroom explicitly, but the money is directed to 'security adjustments and upgrades, including within the perimeter fence of the White House compound to support enhancements by the Secret Service relating to the East Wing Modernization Project, including above-ground and below-ground security features.' A bar on spending for 'non-security elements' is included. Trump had previously insisted the renovation would be funded by private donations. White House spokesman Davis Ingle praised the security funding. After the April 25 WHCD shooting (see 050-A), some congressional Republicans proposed $400M in direct federal funding for the ballroom; Democrats blocked that. The $1B immigration-bill provision is a second attempt, packaged with immigration enforcement funding to use the filibuster-proof reconciliation process. If enacted, it could clear the legal obstacles Judge Leon identified — he ruled the project required congressional approval. Democrats signaled immediate opposition: Sen. Schumer called it 'a Trump ballroom.' Sen. Brian Schatz noted all senators would get 'an up or down vote on the ballroom.' Democrats plan to use it as a 2026 midterm election issue.
cases.outcome: Senate provision released May 5. Bill advancing via reconciliation. Judge Leon injunction still in effect. Democrats opposing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Senate vote timeline; whether $1B provision survives; whether enactment clears Judge Leon's injunction.]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Political interference, Design controversy

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed) — NYT sightline analysis; CFA post-approval revision letter
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: The New York Times published a detailed 3-D model analysis on April 29 showing how the proposed 250-foot arch would affect sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House (Robert E. Lee's mansion, built by enslaved people, atop Arlington National Cemetery). Key findings: from the Lincoln Memorial, the arch columns would frame Arlington House; from Arlington House, the arch would obscure much of the Lincoln Memorial. The reciprocal sightline between the two memorials was intentionally designed a century ago as a 'symbolic link between north and south' (NPS). Following its April 17 concept approval, the Commission of Fine Arts sent a letter backing the proposed location but endorsing only a smaller version — requesting removal of gilded statues at the top and more openings within columns to reduce obstruction of monumental views. NCPC approval still required; Trump has filled NCPC with allies. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has framed breaking ground as a 'fitting way' to commemorate America's 250th anniversary in July. Administration has not released cost details; expects combination of private and public funds, with construction to complete by end of Trump's term.
cases.outcome: CFA approved concept April 17 with revision requests (smaller, fewer gilded elements, more column openings). NCPC approval still required. Lawsuit pending. Administration targeting July groundbreaking.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Political art, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Marine, Amsterdam (1874) / Adolphe Monet Reading in a Garden (1867) — Rouen hearing tomorrow
