cases.title: White House Correspondents Dinner shooting / ballroom rationale
cases.institution: Washington Hilton, Washington DC
cases.description: On the evening of April 25, 2026, gunman Cole Tomas Allen (31, Torrance, California) stormed the White House Correspondents Dinner at the Washington Hilton, armed with a shotgun, handgun, and multiple knives. Allen ran past the main magnetometer security checkpoint near the ballroom stairs and exchanged fire with Secret Service agents; one agent was struck in a bullet-resistant vest and is expected to recover. No other injuries. Allen taken into custody. Acting AG Todd Blanche told CNN the suspect appeared to be targeting Trump administration officials. Trump, Melania, VP Vance, and cabinet members were evacuated to a secure area; Trump departed at approximately 9:45 PM. Approximately 2,600 attendees including RFK Jr., Rubio, Kash Patel, and Lee Zeldin were present. This was the first WHCA Dinner Trump attended as a sitting president. Security note: Washington Hilton lobby remained open to regular hotel guests during the dinner, per standard practice; security screening was located inside at the checkpoint directly outside the ballroom rather than at hotel entrance. At a press conference afterward, Trump almost immediately cited the venue's security as rationale for the White House Ballroom, calling the Washington Hilton "not a particularly secure building" and using the incident as justification for having a dedicated presidential events venue. Trump also said the shooting would not stop him from "winning the war in Iran."
cases.outcome: Suspect in custody; arraignment Monday April 27. Motive under investigation. Ballroom construction injunction still in effect.
cases.tags: Security failure, Political interference, Design controversy, Landmark dispute

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing demolition
cases.artist: McCrery Architects (Jim McCrery, lead); Clark Construction; AECOM (engineering)
cases.institution: White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: In July 2025, Trump announced plans to demolish the White House East Wing and replace it with an 89,000 sq ft state ballroom, framed as providing a larger venue than the East Room for state dinners. McCrery Architects (classical design firm) selected as lead; Clark Construction as builder; AECOM as engineer. Cost announced at $200M, rose to $300-400M by October 2025. Trump said private donors and corporations would pay; construction began September 2025 and continued through the October 2025 federal government shutdown (OMB memo confirmed private funding). East Wing demolished October 20, 2025 -- demolition became an impromptu tourist attraction; Presidential Emergency Operations Center (WWII-era underground bunker) dismantled as part of site prep. Design problems widely reported: exterior grand staircase leading to a wall with no door, columns blocking sightlines, fake windows, staircase breaking symmetry of Olmsted-designed 1930s driveway. NYT published design flaw critique March 29, 2026; Trump revealed revised design the next day. National Trust for Historic Preservation sued December 2025 for failure to observe federal historic preservation guidelines. DOJ argued February 2026 that halting construction raised "national security implications." NCPC approved final design 8-1 on April 2, 2026. Judge Richard Leon issued preliminary injunction March 31 halting above-ground construction, finding no law "comes close" to giving Trump authority to build such a structure without Congressional approval. Revised April 16 order: above-ground construction blocked; below-ground work (including classified military complex) permitted. Trump confirmed a "massive complex" being built underground; Secret Service said pausing would "hamper its statutory obligations." FY2026 White House renovation budget: $377M (866% increase from FY2025). ADAO filed FOIA lawsuit over asbestos inspection records. Rose Garden previously paved with stone patio (2025). White House Correspondents Dinner shooting April 25, 2026: Trump immediately cited venue security as rationale for ballroom -- see entry 050-A.
cases.outcome: Above-ground construction enjoined (April 16 order). Below-ground/national security work proceeding. NTHP lawsuit active. ADAO FOIA lawsuit active. NCPC approved final design April 2. Appeals ongoing.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Demolition, Landmark dispute, Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Political art, Historical erasure

cases.title: Post-Orban de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian cultural institutions broadly; Magyar/Tisza government (forming)
cases.description: Two weeks after Orban's defeat, no major cultural institution director changes have been announced. Péter Magyar's cabinet is expected to be sworn in by mid-May 2026. Hyperallergic piece (April 17) from a Budapest-based curator now in the US remains most detailed account of what needs to happen: Orban-loyalist museum directors "should step aside"; Ludwig Museum director Julia Fabényi (who in 2019 censored a work depicting Orban) is the key name to watch. The Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) -- constitutionally elevated by Fidesz with grant-allocation and board powers across cultural sector -- is the central institution to restructure. Tisza's supermajority gives it legal authority. EU frozen 17B euros in rule-of-law funds being discussed as leverage. State broadcaster suspension (Magyar vowed to suspend news broadcasts until independent standards restored) remains most concrete cultural-sector action to date. No cultural institution appointments confirmed as of April 26.
cases.outcome: Government transition ongoing. No cultural institution appointments yet. Cabinet formation mid-May 2026.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Censorship, Funding dispute, Self-censorship

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spolies durant la colonisation
cases.institution: French parliament / Elysee Palace
cases.description: As of April 26, 2026, the repatriation framework law passed unanimously by both chambers has not yet been formally promulgated by Macron. Updated Wikipedia entry on the Sarr-Savoy report states the law "proceeds to a joint parliamentary committee for further review," suggesting a commission mixte paritaire (CMP) process may be required before promulgation. Art Newspaper confirmed the April 13 vote was unanimous. Law covers 1815-1972 acquisitions, requires state (not individual) petitions, uses bilateral scientific committee, excludes military objects and public archives. Pending claims from Algeria, Mali, Benin, Chad, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast, and Madagascar will have legal pathway once promulgated. France returned Djidji Ayokwe drum to Ivory Coast (taken 1916) in early 2025 as a precursor.
cases.outcome: Passed both chambers. Possible CMP process underway. Promulgation pending -- not yet signed by Macron as of April 26.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Legislative action, Ethical museum

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale: Golden Lion jury ICC exclusion statement
cases.artist: Jury: Solange Farkas (chair), Elvira Dyangani Ose, Zoe Butt, Marta Kuzma, Giovanna Zapperi
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Giardini and Arsenale
cases.description: The five-member jury for the 2026 Venice Biennale announced April 23-24 that it will not consider for the Golden Lion or Silver Lion awards any national pavilion whose country's leaders are currently charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court. The statement does not name countries but directly affects Russia (Putin under ICC arrest warrant for Ukraine war crimes) and Israel (Netanyahu under ICC arrest warrant for Gaza). The jury framed the decision as consistent with the late Koyo Kouoh's curatorial vision for In Minor Keys. The Biennale's press office distanced itself, noting the jury acts autonomously. Israeli artist Belu-Simion Fainaru responded that the jury's action created a hostile and degrading environment and constitutes discrimination based on national origin, noting that the Biennale's own stated policy rejects exclusion. ANGA praised the decision but criticized the jury for not naming Israel explicitly and invited jurors to sign ANGA's open letter (now 200 signatories). Finland's political boycott of the Russian pavilion remains in place. Hyperallergic's guide to the Biennale also confirmed the US was named in the ANGA open letter (along with Israel and Russia) -- unprecedented triple exclusion demand.
cases.outcome: Jury exclusion from awards announced April 23. Both pavilions proceeding. Preview opens May 6.
cases.tags: Geopolitics, Protest, Boycott, Institutional risk

cases.title: Hold My Hand in Yours exhibition
cases.artist: Elana Mann; AMBOS (Art Made Between Opposite Sides); 12+ artists
cases.institution: Frederick R. Weisman Museum of Art, Pepperdine University, Malibu, California
cases.description: Pepperdine University administrators visited the Weisman Museum on October 1, 2025, and directed that two works be turned off or obscured as overtly political content: Elana Mann's video Call to Arms 2015-2025 (a decade-spanning documentation of protest performances using arm-shaped megaphones) and AMBOS's Con Nuestros Manos Construimos Deidades, a collaborative sculpture by 240+ people including refugees and asylum-seekers near the US-Mexico border, which included an embroidered patch reading "Save the Children" and "Abolish ICE." University cited longstanding practice of avoiding political content consistent with its nonprofit status. Both artists withdrew their work. At least 12 other artists withdrew in solidarity, forcing early closure of the exhibition (originally scheduled through March 2026). Museum director Andrea Gyorody resigned October 24. Pepperdine Fine Arts faculty issued statement of full support for the artists. NCAC and College Art Association issued joint open letter calling the nonprofit-status rationale "misguided and untenable." Case resurfaced April 26, 2026 when Wende Museum (Culver City, CA) premiered Mann's related performance Whirlwinds, Tornadoes, Basement at its Spring 2026 opening, explicitly noting it as a work recently removed by administrators at Pepperdine's Weisman Museum after being deemed political in nature.
cases.outcome: Exhibition closed early October 2025. Director resigned. NCAC/CAA letters sent. No restoration. Mann's related work premiering at Wende Museum today, April 26.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Campus art, Political interference, Campus censorship

cases.institution: Élysée Palace / French government
cases.description: UPDATE: As of April 25, 2026, the repatriation framework law passed unanimously by both the Senate (January 2026) and National Assembly (April 13, 2026) has not yet been formally promulgated by President Macron. One source (France in English) notes the law 'now proceeds to a joint parliamentary committee for further review,' suggesting a possible additional procedural step before promulgation. Under French constitutional procedure, the president has 15 days to promulgate a law or refer it to the Constitutional Council; the deadline would fall approximately April 28–29. No Constitutional Council referral reported. Expected to be promulgated imminently. cases.title: N/A (systemic / multiple artists and cultural institutions)
cases.institution: Multiple galleries, auction houses, public cultural spaces across India
cases.description: A pattern of cultural self-censorship has deepened in India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP government, documented in multiple 2026 reports. HRW published April 17, 2026 that India documented 40+ instances of social media content takedowns or account blockings in March 2026 alone, many targeting satire or criticism of Modi, with platform compliance response windows shortened from 36 to 3 hours. Gallery director Shireen Gandhy (Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai) told The Art Newspaper April 21 that 'everything that has been happening in America when Trump took over in January [2025] has happened here' and that 'there is a certain amount of self-censorship among artists. There's never a direct response.' Gandhy was one of few exhibitors at Art Basel Qatar to bring work responding to current political situations. Meanwhile India's art market itself is at historic highs — a Raja Ravi Varma painting sold for $18M in April at Saffronart. MediaNama documented censorship of a student's vlog of Modi's airport inauguration, social media posts linked to Caravan Magazine reporting, mimicry videos, and opposition political content.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Self-censorship systemic. No single precipitating incident. Art market paradoxically thriving.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Political interference

cases.title: National Museum of Sudan and 20+ additional museums and cultural sites
cases.institution: National Museum of Sudan, Ethnographic Museum, Natural History Museum, Khalifa House Museum, Nyala Museum, El Geneina Museum (Khartoum and Darfur region)
cases.description: The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) has caused destruction and looting of more than 20 museums, with financial damage exceeding $110 million. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) occupied the National Museum of Sudan in June 2023, looting over 100,000 archaeological artefacts including ancient gold, jewellery, and ceremonial items from the Napatan and Meroitic civilizations. By March 2026, approximately 60–90% of the National Museum's holdings had been destroyed or removed (varying estimates from NCAM director Ghalia Garelnabi). Looted objects have appeared for sale on eBay and through European and African art dealers. In February 2026, the RSF was accused of burning the library of the College of Forestry at Sudan University of Science and Technology and using musical instruments as fuel. SAF forces recaptured Khartoum in March 2025; January 13, 2026, some recovered artefacts were displayed in a ceremony in Port Sudan. UNESCO has documented 1,700+ objects, trained police and customs officers, and appealed to international institutions. ICRC condemned attacks. Lack of media coverage compared to Afghanistan and Iraq has limited international responsiveness.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Some artefacts recovered and displayed January 2026. SAF retook Khartoum March 2025. Museum interior destroyed. UNESCO documentation ongoing. No accountability proceedings. UNESCO implementation underway (see 047-B): five priority museums assessed (Kerma, Gebel Barkal, Red Sea, El Damer, Sennar), 1,737 artefacts digitally inventoried, El Damer collection relocated to Kerma, 500 heritage/customs/judiciary professionals trained (reported May 18, 2026).
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Geopolitics, Historical erasure, Security failure

cases.title: US Pavilion Venice Biennale 2026 -- Andres Serrano proposal / not selected

cases.description: Background to entry 045: Serrano publicly submitted and promoted a proposal in July 2025 to turn the US Pavilion into a Trump mausoleum titled The Game: All Things Trump -- a multi-media installation of 1,000+ Trump memorabilia items ($200,000+ collection) including a 2004 Trump portrait, Jan. 6 footage from his 2022 film Insurrection, and archival US history footage. Serrano framed it as apolitical: I observe, I don't judge. Trump had been photographed holding Serrano's book at Mar-a-Lago. Far-right blogger Curtis Yarvin simultaneously submitted a competing proposal to Trumpify the Venice Biennale. Serrano was not selected -- Alma Allen announced November 2025 (see entry 045). Serrano's Piss Christ (1987) was itself a central NEA culture-wars controversy in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump announced on April 23 that renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is already underway. He described the pool as filthy and dirty and said a friend prompted his inspection. Trump toured the site with Secret Service and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. A contractor proposed removing and replacing the granite at a cost of $300M over three years; Trump rejected this and instead called contractors from his real estate career, who agreed to resurface the pool for $1.5M-$2M. Work began two weeks prior to the announcement. Trump chose the color American flag blue for the new industrial-grade pool coating. The pool was last renovated in 2012 at a cost of approximately $30M. The reflecting pool is a National Historic Landmark and site of major civil rights and antiwar protests including Martin Luther King Jr.'s I Have a Dream speech (1963) and the 1971 Vietnam War protests. No Section 106 review, congressional approval, or National Capital Planning Commission process has been publicly announced. The renovation follows Trump's demolition of the White House East Wing (halted by federal court), the proposed triumphal arch (CFA approved April 17), and the White House Rose Garden paving.
cases.outcome: Renovation underway. No legal challenge filed yet. No public review process announced.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Landmark dispute, Political art, Design controversy, Funding dispute

cases.title: US Pavilion, Venice Biennale 2026 / Alma Allen: Call Me the Breeze
cases.artist: Alma Allen (sculptor); Jeffrey Uslip (curator); Jenni Parido / American Arts Conservancy (commissioner)
cases.institution: US Pavilion, Giardini, Venice Biennale
cases.description: The 2026 US Pavilion selection process was upended when the Trump administration stripped the NEA of its traditional role and handed oversight to the State Department, which added application language banning DEI and requiring promotion of American values/policies and American exceptionalism. Artist Robert Lazzarini was reportedly selected first but dropped. Utah-born, Mexico-based sculptor Alma Allen was announced November 2025 without the usual advisory committee of museum directors and curators. Commissioner Jenni Parido is a former pet supply shop owner running a newly formed nonprofit (American Arts Conservancy) with no track record. Curator Jeffrey Uslip resigned from his last major US post in 2016 amid racial insensitivity charges. Allen's two galleries (Mendes Wood DM and Olney Gleason) dropped him for accepting; he now shows with Perrotin. Artists William Eggleston and Barbara Chase-Riboud declined to participate. Robert Storr (Yale): America will be known as having squandered a major opportunity to show serious work. Allen broke silence April 23 in Time Sensitive podcast: described the response as a little stressful but said it was worth it. CNN April 23 feature describes the pavilion as chaotic. Biennale opens May 9.
cases.outcome: Pavilion proceeding. Biennale opens May 9.
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Funding dispute, Institutional risk

cases.title: transfeminisms / "There are other skies"
cases.artist: Zainab Fasiki, Alex Martinis Roe, Fatima Mazmouz, Ada Pinkston, Bahia Shehab, Lorena Wolffer, Cassils, Martine Gutierrez, and others
cases.institution: Scottsdale Museum of Contemporary Art (SMoCA), Scottsdale, Arizona
cases.description: A traveling feminist exhibition originated by Mimosa House (London) as 'transfeminisms' — a major survey of women, queer, and trans artists — was significantly altered before opening at SMoCA. The exhibition was retitled 'There are other skies,' shortened by two months, and had its artist lineup reduced. Chief curator Jennifer McCabe resigned from SMoCA in October 2024, and co-curators (Daria Khan, Maura Reilly) say they were sidelined after her departure and told of changes without input. Khan: the show was 'violently edited.' SMoCA CEO Gerd Wuestemann maintains changes were 'pragmatic' and driven by space, budget, and timeline constraints. Context: Scottsdale City Council had voted to cut DEI funding; Arizona legislature introduced anti-trans bills in the same session. The case entered national discourse when NBC News cited it as part of a pattern of LGBTQ art censorship at US museums in August 2025.
cases.outcome: Exhibition shown in altered form. No retraction or restoration. Case now part of documented national pattern.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Funding dispute

cases.title: Basma al-Sharif censorship chain (Goethe-Institut / Düsseldorf / Osnabrück)
cases.institution: EMAF (European Media Art Festival), Kunsthalle Osnabrück
cases.description: UPDATE: The 39th EMAF (European Media Art Festival) opened today, April 22, in Osnabrück. Al-Sharif's short film 'Morning Circle' (Morgenkreis) is being screened despite ongoing political controversy. Landschaftsverband Osnabrücker Land joined the city of Osnabrück and Lower Saxony PM Lies in publicly distancing from the festival over al-Sharif's inclusion. Festival director Katrin Mundt defended the decision on grounds of artistic freedom: 'We have shown her films for years. They were selected not only by us but also by Jewish Israelis.' City of Osnabrück confirmed its €150,000 annual funding remains intact. The WSWS (April 16) published analysis characterizing the Foreign Ministry's reprimand of the Goethe-Institut as 'coded language for censorship and repression.' The festival theme is 'An Incomplete Assembly' — the irony that an exhibition about incomplete assemblies is itself under pressure for assembling Palestinian voices was noted in the taz.
cases.outcome: Festival open April 22–26. Al-Sharif film showing. Patronage withdrawn. Funding intact. Multiple governmental bodies distancing from festival.

cases.title: Exhibition catalogues ("Music Is Black"; "Fabergé: Romance to Revolution")
cases.artist: Gus Casely-Hayford (introduction author); multiple exhibition artists
cases.institution: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
cases.description: UPDATE: Index on Censorship responded April 21 calling V&A case 'deeply worrying' and 'exactly the kind of censorship' its 'Banned by Beijing' campaign warns about. CEO Jemima Steinfeld: the museum 'landed in this compromised place because the Chinese printers were apparently more competitively priced.' Sara Chen (Museum Association analyst) described it as 'externalised censorship' operating 'through contracts, deadlines, cost pressures and infrastructural dependence.' British Museum declined to answer questions about its own Chinese-printed publications. Tate and British Library said they have never encountered censorship issues with their Chinese printers.
cases.outcome: Catalogues printed with censored content. V&A has not retracted. Index on Censorship public response adds institutional accountability pressure.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Political interference, Institutional risk

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott
cases.institution: Kennedy Center, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: Washingtonian magazine (April 18) published extensive staff accounts of year of turmoil inside Kennedy Center. Staff built an underground Signal chat network out of fear management was monitoring Microsoft Teams. Former programming manager Cathleen O'Malley describes the atmosphere as 'snarky, intimate, dismayed, disgusted.' Former staffer says ticket sales were 'near 50% unsold — worst since 2018' (figure DOJ did not dispute in filings). Multiple staff theories on closure purpose: (1) to hide boycott embarrassment, (2) to break unions — International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees locals have contract negotiations in September 2026. National Symphony Orchestra is now effectively homeless. Washington National Opera departed after 55 years. O'Malley: 'We thought it was as solid as the marble building.' Outlet notes that when it closes July 4, the KC will be the second building near it bearing Trump's name that sits empty (Trump Hotel is the first).
cases.outcome: Closure proceeding July 4. Staff accounts of systematic dismantling now on record.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Labor dispute, Censorship

cases.title: Arthur Ashe Memorial Mural
cases.artist: Hamilton Glass (and Sir James Thornhill, restorer)
cases.institution: Battery Park, Richmond, Virginia (Arthur Ashe tunnel, Dupont Circle)
cases.description: A federal judge ordered Patriot Front, its founder Thomas Rousseau, and members William Ring and Jacob Brown to pay over $470,000 in punitive damages for the October 2021 defacement of a mural honoring Richmond-born tennis legend and civil rights activist Arthur Ashe in the majority-Black Battery Park neighborhood. Patriot Front members spray-painted the mural with white nationalist logos and stickers, caught on video they filmed themselves. The lawsuit, filed in 2022 by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law on behalf of Battery Park residents, argued the vandalism was intended to intimidate Black residents and violated their civil rights under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. Patriot Front advocates for a white ethnostate. Battery Park residents testified to anxiety and stress when accessing the park after the attack. The mural had been restored in 2022 by Sir James Thornhill, one of the original artists. Civil penalties against the group aim to disrupt Patriot Front's organizing network.
cases.outcome: Judgment entered April 2026. $470,000+ punitive damages ordered. Mural restored (2022). Criminal charges not filed — McEachin's office declined.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Legal challenge, White nationalism
outlets: Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law

cases.title: "30 Mil Motivos" (mural)
cases.institution: Centro Cultural Osvaldo Soriano / Biblioteca Municipal Leopoldo Marechal, 25 de Mayo al 3100, Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires Province
cases.description: A mural by the late Mar del Plata artist Osmar Freites, created in 2014 to commemorate the 30,000 people disappeared during Argentina's last military dictatorship (1976–1983), was painted over in its entirety with white paint. Freites, deeply committed to human rights work, died in 2015. The mural was located on the exterior wall adjacent to the city's public cultural center and library. Councilmember Melisa Centurión (Acción Marplatense) accused the local municipal government — aligned with the Milei national government — of 'insólito vandalism' against collective memory. The municipal government denied direct responsibility, claiming the wall belongs to a private residence and that paint-over occurred during routine maintenance. Opposition bloc (Unión por la Patria) introduced a project in the Concejo Deliberante demanding investigation of possible cultural heritage crimes, an official apology to Freites's family and human rights organizations, and restoration of the work. Centurión invoked the language of 'blanqueamiento' (whitewashing) — both literal and figurative.
cases.outcome: Mural painted over. Investigation project filed in Concejo Deliberante. Municipal government denies responsibility.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Historical erasure, Community objection, Removal, Political interference

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian Academy of Arts, Ludwig Museum, Hungarian National Museum, Budapest arts institutions broadly
cases.description: UPDATE: Hyperallergic (April 17) published in-depth analysis from Budapest-based curator describing Orbán's 16-year cultural dismantling and calling on Orbán-loyalist museum directors to step aside. Author draws explicit parallel to Trump's second term US from their vantage point now living in the US. Urgent Matter (April 14) noted Tisza's supermajority gives it power to unwind the constitutionally elevated Hungarian Academy of Arts and restructure cultural funding. EU could unlock €17B in frozen funding tied to rule-of-law conditionality. Art Newspaper (April 16) quoted gallery and artist figures expressing cautious optimism but noting Magyar is center-right — changes may be slower than hoped. No major institutional appointments yet confirmed as of April 20.
cases.outcome: Government transition underway. No institutional appointments announced yet. Tisza cultural program still vague.

cases.title: Desviaciones: Festival de Artes Escénicas y Disidencia Sexual (2nd edition)
cases.artist: Multiple (Dian C. Guevara, Susy Shock, Silvio Lang, Daniel Mariblanca, others)

cases.description: UPDATE: After deputies' formal inquiry (oficio), the Ministry of Culturas reduced the festival's grant allocation, citing that some programming was not included in the original funding application. Festival opened as scheduled April 20 with inauguration set for April 22 at the Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos. cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed)
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: U.S. Commission of Fine Arts approved the arch concept on April 17, 2026, allowing the project to move forward for design adjustments. Public comments had been 'overwhelmingly in opposition — over 99%.' Commission secretary noted opposition centered on waste of money (cited by ~50% of commenters), 'inappropriate imperial or political symbolism,' and design critiqued as 'gaudy, oversized, incompatible.' Despite all this, commissioners voted to approve. Trump claimed private donations would fund it; however NOTUS reported NEH spending plan reserves $2M in special initiative funds plus $13M in matching grants. DC Preservation League joined other groups in suing over Kennedy Center renovation — a related but separate action.
cases.outcome: Concept approved by CFA April 17 despite 99%+ public opposition. Lawsuit pending. Design adjustments proceeding.

cases.title: "Contorsiones" erotic sculpture installation
cases.institution: Malecón, Puerto Vallarta, Mexico
cases.description: Erotic sculptures installed on the Puerto Vallarta Malecón as part of Semana del Arte Puerto Vallarta 2026 (World Art Day, April 15). Within one day, Councilwoman Laurel Carrillo Ventura, chair of the Culture Committee, requested removal, citing public objections on social media that the works "promoted sexuality in a liberal way." The director of the Instituto Vallartense de Cultura, Ricardo Martínez, told her the works were only scheduled for April 15 (World Art Day). Councilwoman nonetheless urgently demanded removal. Works removed after a single day of display.

cases.title: New Deal murals and site-specific artworks in four DC federal buildings (Ben Shahn, Philip Guston, Harold Weston, Magafan sisters, Seymour Fogel, Richmond Barthé, and others)
cases.artist: Ben Shahn, Philip Guston, Harold Weston, Ethel and Jenne Magafan, Seymour Fogel, Richmond Barthé, and others
cases.institution: Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building; Robert C. Weaver Federal Building (HUD HQ); GSA Regional Office Building (301 7th St SW); Liberty Loan Building — all Washington DC
cases.description: Trump administration GSA has flagged 46 federal buildings for 'accelerated disposal,' including four in Washington DC that preservationists consider at risk of demolition. The centerpiece is the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building (former SSA headquarters, 'Sistine Chapel of the New Deal'), housing integral fresco murals by Ben Shahn (The Meaning of Social Security), Philip Guston (Reconstruction and the Wellbeing of the Family), Magafan sisters, and others. Because many works are painted directly on walls, demolition would destroy them permanently. The GSA Fine Arts Collection includes 26,000 works, ~23,000 from the New Deal era. Senators Whitehouse and Schumer sent inquiry letter; 400+ artists/historians signed preservation petition; Joyce Kozloff, Martha Rosler, and Eve Ensler wrote to the Jewish Museum (which responded supportively). Preservation groups filed suit. Art Newspaper reported February 2026. GSA added the 301 7th St SW building (Harold Weston 22-panel mural cycle) to list April 10, 2026.
cases.outcome: Cohen building still occupied as of early 2026; required to be sold within 2 years of vacating (per Congressional mandate in water bill). GSA has engaged art conservation professionals to assess New Deal art condition. Preservation lawsuit (Cultural Heritage Partners v. Trump) active in DC district court — retired GSA official's declaration specifically mentions demolition as near-term possibility. No demolition yet. Staff being moved out gradually. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Removal, Demolition, Funding dispute, Political interference, Historical erasure, Labor dispute

cases.title: Exhibition catalogues ("Music Is Black"; "Fabergé: Romance to Revolution")
cases.artist: Gus Casely-Hayford (introduction author); multiple exhibition artists
cases.institution: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
cases.description: The Victoria and Albert Museum removed maps and images from at least two exhibition catalogues at the request of its Chinese printer, C&C Offset Printing, which cited China's General Administration of Press and Publication (GAPP). Deleted content included a 1930s British imperial trade route map (flagged merely because it showed China's borders) and an image of Lenin. Internal emails showed staff confusion — 'it's a historic map showing British colonial rule so nothing to do with China — just shows China on the map and that seems to be enough to warrant rejection!' — but the museum proceeded, saying edits were 'minor.' Guardian FOI investigation published April 14–15, 2026 revealed the practice. British Museum (chaired by former Chancellor George Osborne) declined to answer questions about its own Chinese-printed publications. Tate and British Library said they use Chinese printers but have not changed content.
cases.outcome: Catalogues already printed with censored content. No retraction by V&A.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Self-censorship, Institutional risk

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed), Columbia Island, Washington DC
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump is pursuing construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, on the Potomac side of the Lincoln Memorial. The arch originated from a 2025 proposal by architecture critic Catesby Leigh (Claremont Institute) calling for a non-'huge' arch of no more than 60 feet. Under Trump the project quadrupled: 76 feet → 164 feet (to surpass Arc de Triomphe) → 250 feet (to mark America's 250th anniversary). When asked by a CBS reporter whom the monument was for, Trump replied: 'Me.' Architect Charbonneau's design features gold eagles and lions. The Commission of Fine Arts (Trump appointees) was scheduled to review April 17. NEH has reserved $15M; total cost unspecified. Vietnam War veterans sued to block construction, citing the Commemorative Works Act of 1986 and arguing it obstructs sightlines between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. The Trump administration claims 1920s congressional authority for 'two tall columns' on Columbia Island suffices. Even original proponent Leigh now objects: 'It's way too big for that site.' Historian Sarah Bond: 'Trump is using Washington DC as emperors used Rome.'
cases.outcome: Commission of Fine Arts approved concept April 16, 2026 (5 of 7 Trump-appointed members present; unanimous vote among present). 100% of ~1,000 public comments opposed. Design revisions requested (remove Lady Liberty figure and eagles atop arch; reconsider lions). NEPA and NHPA reviews still required — these require public input and stakeholder consultation including Arlington National Cemetery, NPS, and DC SHPO. Veterans group lawsuit active. Groundbreaking timeline unconfirmed.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Political art, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Landmark dispute

cases.title: Cultural heritage destruction during 2026 Iran war
cases.institution: Isfahan (Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Shah Mosque, Chehel Sotoun), Tel Aviv White City, Habima Theater, Rafi'-Nia Synagogue, Tehran, Jerusalem Old City
cases.description: During the US-Israel military conflict with Iran beginning February 28, 2026, cultural heritage sites have been damaged or destroyed on multiple sides. Israeli strikes on Isfahan on March 9 damaged Naqsh-e Jahan Square (UNESCO World Heritage Site), Chehel Sotoun, Ali Qapu, the Shah Mosque, and Jameh Mosque. March 8 strike damaged Falak-ol-Aflak castle (Blue Shield emblem present). April 7: Rafi'-Nia Synagogue in Tehran fully destroyed by Israeli Air Force. Iranian missile strikes February 28 damaged UNESCO World Heritage White City of Tel Aviv (two Bauhaus buildings). The Habima Theater — Israel's national theater — was struck directly, windows shattered. Jerusalem's Old City (UNESCO WH) was targeted March 16; missile fragments fell near Temple Mount, Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Western Wall — no casualties. UNESCO urged protection of heritage sites March 11. Russia's Foreign Ministry reported April 1 strike in Tehran caused structural damage near St. Petersburg Orthodox Church.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Multiple UNESCO World Heritage Sites damaged. No accountability proceedings initiated as of April 18.

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale – Israeli Pavilion / ANGA boycott campaign
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Arsenale
cases.description: UPDATE: Artist Belu-Simion Fainaru issued a public statement April 6 opposing cultural boycotts: 'Art thrives on openness, and any narrowing of that space diminishes it.' ANGA published a second open letter March 17 with 183 total signatories demanding exclusion of Israel, Russia, and the US. The letter cites the US-Israel war against Iran as context. Finland's political leadership also announced it will not attend if Russia is present (see 017-A). With Israel, Russia, Iran, and the US all entangled in the current Middle East war, the Biennale opening on May 9 is framed by multiple sources as a stage for geopolitical positioning as much as art. Palestine still has no national pavilion because it is not recognized by Italy.
cases.outcome: Israel participating with Fainaru's 'Rose of Nothingness.' Boycott campaign active. Biennale opens May 9.

cases.title: Russia return to Venice Biennale 2026
cases.institution: Venice Biennale; Finland Ministry of Education and Culture
cases.description: UPDATE: Finland's Ministry of Education and Culture announced April 17 that Finnish political leadership will not attend the Venice Biennale if the Russian Pavilion goes on view. Some Finnish public officials will still attend to support Finnish arts. Finnish officials had previously signed the 22-nation open letter calling Russia's presence 'deeply troubling.' EU Commission separately warned Biennale it could lose a €2 million grant for its 2028 edition if it fails to address concerns about potential violation of EU sanctions. Italian Vice-Premier Salvini sharply criticized EU position as 'vulgar blackmail.' Italian Culture Minister Giuli expressed disapproval by visiting Lviv rather than the Biennale restoration. cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian Academy of Arts, National Film Institute, Budapest museums, public broadcaster (multiple)
cases.description: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz-KDNP party was defeated in a landslide on April 13, 2026 by Péter Magyar's Tisza party, ending 16 years of rule. During that period Orbán systematically centralized cultural institutions, gave the conservative Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) unprecedented grant-allocation powers, purged independent curators and museum directors, restricted LGBTQ+ content in cultural programming (2021 law used to fire Hungarian National Museum director in 2023), and aligned arts funding with Christian-nationalist ideology. Arts community celebrating. Hungarian art scene now faces what Hyperallergic describes as a 'watershed moment' comparable to 1989. Tisza has a projected two-thirds supermajority giving it power to rewrite laws governing cultural institutions. Film commissioner Csaba Káel (National Film Institute) already announced departure. Public broadcaster leadership expected to change quickly. Hungarian Academy of Arts' role expected to be reformed. Artists who boycotted co-opted institutions now face decisions about re-engagement. Tisza cultural program currently vague but promises 'institutional autonomy.'
cases.outcome: Fidesz defeated; Tisza governing. The May 31, 2026 voluntary-resignation deadline for Orbán-era appointees (incl. cultural-institution heads) passed without high-profile resignations — President Tamás Sulyok refused, citing the Venice Commission. De-Orbánization shifting toward constitutional-removal mechanisms. Cultural-institution-director turnover still unresolved as of June 1, 2026. Ongoing transition. (See 036-W.)
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Censorship, Funding dispute, Self-censorship

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale, Paris; French museums (Quai Branly, Louvre, etc.)
cases.description: French National Assembly unanimously passed (170 votes) a framework law on April 13, 2026 to facilitate return of cultural property looted from the colonial empire. Law applies to objects acquired between 1815 and 1972. Requests must pass a bilateral scientific committee (French and country-of-origin researchers) and a parliamentary commission. National Rally wanted to limit restitution to countries with 'cordial' relations with France — amendment failed. Countries with pending requests include Mali, Algeria, and Benin. Culture Minister Catherine Pégard: the law 'opens a new page of our History.' Completes 2023 framework laws covering Nazi-looted property and human remains.
cases.outcome: Assemblée nationale passed amended text unanimously April 13-14. CMP (commission mixte paritaire) PENDING — required because AN amended the Sénat text. Not yet promulgated. CMP must reconcile both chambers' versions before final adoption.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Legislative action, Ethical museum

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale – Israeli Pavilion / ANGA boycott campaign
cases.artist: Belu-Simion Fainaru ('Rose of Nothingness'); 74+ signatory artists (open letter)
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Arsenale, Sala d'Armi G
cases.description: Israeli sculptor Belu-Simion Fainaru confirmed representing Israel with 'Rose of Nothingness' — 16 pipes dripping black water into a pool, referencing Paul Celan's concept of 'black milk.' Placed in Sala d'Armi G of the Arsenale (Israel's Giardini pavilion under renovation). ANGA launched new campaign demanding Israel's exclusion, threatening 'full artist and audience boycott.' The March open letter from 74 artists also called for exclusion of Russia and the United States. La Biennale maintained institutional neutrality. L'Internationale confederation of cultural institutions published statement urging reversal of the Arsenale placement, noting it constitutes 'explicit institutional endorsement' unlike the Giardini. Biennale opens May 9, 2026.
cases.outcome: Pavilion confirmed in Arsenale. Boycott campaign active. Biennale opens May 9.

cases.title: NEA grant cancellations (hundreds of grants, nationwide)
cases.institution: National Endowment for the Arts, Washington DC; arts organizations in all 50 states
cases.description: Trump administration's 2026 budget proposed eliminating the NEA, NEH, and Institute of Museum and Library Services. Hours after the budget proposal, hundreds of NEA grants were canceled. 'Challenge America' program — which funded small organizations serving underserved communities — eliminated for FY2026. Organizations required to sign agreement not to operate DEI programs to receive any federal arts funding. Multiple senior NEA staff resigned. As of April 2026, surviving grants framed under nationalistic 'America250' priorities. Arts groups face choice between signing anti-DEI agreements or forgoing funding. Local Richmond impact: Studio Two Three had a $30,000 grant canceled. Oregon Humanities lost 40% of its operating budget. Portland Playhouse learned of grant cancellation on opening night. Lawsuits filed against NEH/DOGE over dismantling.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. NEA operating with reduced mandate and DEI restrictions. Elimination requires Congressional action; Congress has resisted. Multiple lawsuits pending.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Political interference, Censorship, Institutional crisis

cases.title: West Side Wall murals (multiple works)
cases.institution: CVS/ex-Rite Aid lot, 5217 California SW, West Seattle, Washington
cases.description: A multi-artist rotating mural installation including a Desmond Hansen baseball mural on the street face and evolving community works in the alley, developed over three years at a CVS-leased wall in West Seattle. A community complaint triggered a city abatement letter to CVS; CVS, unaware of the oral permission arrangement, painted over everything. No written agreement had formalized the artistic arrangement. Hansen pursuing restoration and a formal written agreement with CVS and the property owner (an investment firm) to prevent recurrence.
cases.outcome: As of March 2026: CVS management (acquisitions director and district manager) is supportive of restoration. Hansen waiting for written city acknowledgment that restoration will not trigger another abatement action. No formal written agreement yet. Restoration has not begun. New subjects being considered (Kraken/Sounders instead of Mariners). [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: written agreement and restoration not yet confirmed]
cases.tags: Removal, Community objection, Public art

cases.title: Friends Association mural (untitled)
cases.institution: 113 W. Chestnut Street, West Chester, Pennsylvania
cases.description: A commissioned mural painted in 2022 by then-West Chester University student Noah Burns for the Friends Association (a homelessness prevention nonprofit) faces potential removal after the building changed ownership. The work depicts a Black individual with arms outstretched, representing community, housing, and family — created with support from the borough's Public Arts Commission. New building occupant submitted a removal request to the West Chester Public Arts Commission. Burns received the key to the city at the 2022 dedication. No ordinance currently protects the artwork. The artist expressed grief over the potential loss but acknowledged he has moved to Philadelphia.
cases.outcome: As of April 4, 2026: mural still stands but new building owner actively exploring removal. No borough ordinance protects it. Mayor and council contacted by Friends Association CEO but no protective action taken. No PAC ruling reported. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Removal, Community objection, Artists' rights, Racial/ethnic sensitivity

cases.title: "I Told You I Loved You and I Wanted Genocide to Stop" (student mural)
cases.artist: UNC student artists (multiple), Hanes Art Center
cases.institution: Hanes Art Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
cases.description: Student-created pro-Palestinian mural quoting poet June Jordan had hung in the Hanes Art Center lobby for over a year. Night before fall 2025 semester, Chancellor Lee Roberts and Interim Provost Jim Dean ordered facilities workers to board it up with white plywood without notifying the art and art history department. Chair Annette Lawrence arrived to her 9 a.m. class to find it covered. Mural subsequently removed and reported 'damaged beyond repair.' A mock museum placard was affixed: 'UNC Chancellor's Office, a practice in censorship, 2025.' UNC had been under federal investigation for allegedly failing to protect Jewish students from antisemitism, with funding consequences at stake. Mural included inverted red triangle symbol, contested between pro-Palestinian and Jewish student groups. Resurfaced in April 2026 via MERIP article on censorship and surveillance at US universities.
cases.outcome: Mural destroyed during removal. No restoration.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Self-censorship, Campus art, Campus censorship

cases.title: "Free Palestine" watermelon mural
cases.institution: Nevermore boutique, Brookland Park Blvd & North Ave, Richmond VA Northside
cases.description: Additional coverage and April 8 town hall update on mural already logged as Entry 021 (April 14 scan). Community town hall at Richmond Public Library on April 8 drew a full auditorium. Building owner Teresa Sharpe confirmed the mural will remain and she will add a context plaque. Artist Lauren YS (California-based) confirmed intention was Palestinian solidarity, not racist imagery. VCU professor Faedah Totah explained watermelon's role as Palestinian resistance symbol since 1967 Israeli ban on Palestinian flag. Panelist Silly Genius (muralist) defended the mural as speaking to a global issue. The mural is in a predominantly Black neighborhood facing gentrification; the controversy centers on whether a symbol of Palestinian resistance can also invoke anti-Black racist stereotypes in its US context.
cases.outcome: Mural remains. Context plaque planned. No removal.
cases.tags: Community objection, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Public art, Geopolitics

cases.title: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a New Nation exhibit
cases.institution: President's House, Independence National Historical Park, Philadelphia
cases.description: April 9, 2026: Federal appeals court ordered exhibit panels to remain unchanged as legal fight continues. Ruling blocks Trump administration from removing or altering the 16 restored panels. However, NPS simultaneously published digital images of proposed replacement 'new exhibits' on its website — replacement panels that describe Washington as expressing 'discomfort' with slavery and enslaved people as having 'a modicum of autonomy.' Avenging the Ancestors Coalition condemned the online update as sanitizing history while technically complying with the court's physical order. Michael Coard: 'The federal government is playing games.' Opposition briefs were due April 13. Congressman Brendan Boyle introduced 'Protecting American History Act' in February.
cases.outcome: Appeals court blocks physical changes as of April 9. NPS website revised with softened language. Some panels still not restored. Litigation ongoing.
cases.tags: Censorship, Historical erasure, Legal challenge, Political interference

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott
cases.institution: Kennedy Center, Washington DC
cases.description: Kennedy Center leadership conducting tours for Congressional members to justify $257M renovation project ahead of July 2026 closure. New executive director/COO Matt Floca leading bipartisan tours showing infrastructure damage. In official press statement, institution now refers to itself as 'the Trump Kennedy Center.' Separate from Beatty lawsuit and preservation lawsuit: a third legal action filed challenging renovation as permanently destroying 'historic fabric,' 'monumental core vistas,' and 'memorial purpose.' Before renaming, ticket sales reportedly near 50% unsold — worst since 2018 (per DOJ filings that did not dispute the figure). Trump attended 'Chicago' opening March 31. Mark Twain Prize for Bill Maher set for June 28, just before July closure.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Three parallel lawsuits. Closure July 2026 approaching. Renovation tours underway.

cases.title: N/A (systemic policy)
cases.artist: N/A (affects all performing artists in China)

cases.description: China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism has required all performance companies to submit full scripts, program lists, and safety plans for approval. cases.title: American Sublime (retrospective) / Trans Forming Liberty (2024)
cases.institution: Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery (planned, then pulled); Baltimore Museum of Art
cases.description: Sherald pulled her career retrospective 'American Sublime' from the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery after learning the museum might exclude her painting 'Trans Forming Liberty,' which depicts the Statue of Liberty as a Black trans woman. Museum reportedly feared provoking Trump. Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch proposed replacing the painting with a video including anti-trans viewpoints as 'context.' cases.title: European museum collections of human remains / colonial repatriation
cases.institution: Museum Vrolik (Amsterdam), UK museums (263,000+ items), German museums, French institutions
cases.description: NYT feature on European museums confronting colonial-era human remains. Central case: Museum Vrolik in Amsterdam, where Dutch customs official Menucha Latumaerissa tracked down Moluccan skulls taken from Amtufu village in 1912 by a Dutch colonial army medical officer. Skulls had been used for 'race science' — craniometry and anthropometry to invent racial hierarchies justifying colonial subjugation. Skulls now repatriated; empty stands displayed in exhibition 'Imagine: The Future of Human Remains from Colonial Contexts' (through Jun 2027). Broader European pattern: Karolinska Institute (Stockholm) repatriated 122 skulls since 2015 but can't identify origins of many more. Berlin Museum of Prehistory spent $4M researching 1,500+ skulls — some African countries declined repatriation due to political obstacles. Charité hospital (Berlin) repatriated 216 remains since 2011 across 10 ceremonies. No EU-wide legislation exists; US has NAGPRA (1990) but Europe relies on patchwork of local laws. Germany creating Coordination Council (Apr 2026). France Senate passed framework (Jan 2026).
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Germany creating formal council. France passed framework. UK debating legislation. Netherlands has active repatriation program. No single resolution — this is a continental-scale institutional reckoning.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Ethical museum, Human remains, Legislative action
